Protocols such as ICP (Internet Cache Protocol) let caches ask each other. CDNs (Content Distribution Network) are a modern, large-scale form of cooperating caches.

↑ Section 2.2

Section 2.3: Electronic Mail in the Internet

11 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11

Also asked in: Assignment 1 Q1.6

Q1

What are the differences between POP (Post Office Protocol) and IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol)?

Answer

  • Where mail lives: POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) typically downloads messages to one device and deletes them from the server ("download-and-delete"; there is also "download-and-keep"). IMAP keeps messages on the server; your devices view and manage them there.

  • Folders: POP3 has no server folders — organising happens on your device. IMAP lets you create folders on the server and move messages between them.

  • Multiple devices: with POP3 your phone and laptop get out of sync. With IMAP every device sees the same mailbox state (read/unread flags, folders, deletions).

  • State: POP3 keeps no state between sessions. IMAP keeps state (folders, flags) across sessions.

  • Partial download: IMAP can fetch just headers or parts of a message (good on slow links); POP3 fetches whole messages.

  • Complexity: POP3 is very simple; IMAP is richer and more complex.

↑ Section 2.3
Q2

What are user agents and mail servers in electronic mail respectively?

Answer

  • User agent: the mail program people use to read, write, reply to, forward and save messages — e.g., Outlook, Apple Mail, Thunderbird, the Gmail app or website. It sends outgoing mail to the user's mail server and retrieves incoming mail from the mailbox.

  • Mail server: the always-on machine that holds each user's mailbox (incoming messages) and a message queue of outgoing messages, and uses SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) to send and receive mail with other mail servers. Each server acts as an SMTP client when sending and an SMTP server when receiving.

↑ Section 2.3
Q3

What does the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) do?

Answer

SMTP transfers email messages from a sender's mail server to the recipient's mail server (and from the user agent to its own server). It is a push protocol running over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) (port 25, or 587 for submission from user agents), which provides reliable delivery.

↑ Section 2.3
Q4

What are the basic operations of SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol)?

Answer

After the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection is set up (port 25), SMTP has three phases:

1. Handshake (greeting): the server says 220 ready; the client says HELO / EHLO with its name; the server replies 250.

2. Transfer of messages: MAIL FROM: <alice@crepes.fr> (sender) → 250 OK; RCPT TO: <bob@hamburger.edu> (recipient, repeat for each) → 250 OK; DATA → 354 start mail input; the client sends the headers and body, ending with a line containing only a period . → 250 accepted.

3. Closure: QUIT → 221 closing.

Several messages can be sent over the same TCP connection (persistent). Each command gets a numeric reply code.

↑ Section 2.3
Q5

Why does SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) need a message queue?

Answer

Because the receiving mail server might not be reachable when the message is sent (down, busy or network problems). The sending server puts outgoing messages in a queue, tries to deliver them, and if it fails it keeps the message and retries periodically (for example every 30 minutes). If delivery still fails after several days, it removes the message and sends the sender a "delivery failed" notice. The queue also lets the user agent hand off a message instantly without waiting for the remote server.

↑ Section 2.3
Q6

How would you compare SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) with HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)?

Answer

Similarities: both transfer files/objects from one host to another; both use TCP (Transmission Control Protocol); both use persistent connections; both use ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) text command/response messages with header lines and numeric status codes.

Differences:

  • Push vs pull: HTTP is mainly a pull protocol (the client fetches what it wants); SMTP is a push protocol (the sending server pushes the message to the receiving server).

  • Encoding: SMTP requires the whole message (headers and body) to be 7-bit ASCII, so binary attachments must be encoded (MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), base64); HTTP has no such restriction.

  • Objects: HTTP puts each object in its own response; SMTP puts all parts of a message (text and attachments) into one multipart message.

↑ Section 2.3
Q7

What formats might a mail message have?

Answer

A message has a header and a body separated by a blank line (RFC (Request for Comments) 5322 format). Headers include From:, To:, Subject:, Date:, Cc:, plus Received: lines added by each server.

Formats of the body:

  • Plain text (7-bit ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) — the original format).

  • MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) formats, declared with Content-Type: and Content-Transfer-Encoding: headers: HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) email, non-ASCII text (UTF (Unicode Transformation Format)-8, other languages), images, audio, video, PDFs (Portable Document Format) and other attachments (usually base64-encoded), and multipart messages that combine several of these.

↑ Section 2.3
Q8

What are mail access protocols? How do they differ from a mail transfer protocol, such as SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol)?

Answer

Mail access protocols let a user agent retrieve (pull) mail from the user's mailbox on the mail server: POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3), IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol), and HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) (for web mail such as Gmail in a browser).

Difference from SMTP: SMTP is a transfer (push) protocol that delivers mail to a mail server. It cannot be used to fetch mail because pulling is not what SMTP does, and a user's device is often offline and has no fixed address to push to. Access protocols handle pulling, plus things SMTP knows nothing about: user login, listing, downloading, deleting and organising messages in folders.

↑ Section 2.3
Q9

What does Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3) do?

Answer

POP3 is a very simple mail access protocol (TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 110, or 995 with TLS (Transport Layer Security)). It works in three phases:

1. Authorisation: the user agent sends user <name> and pass <password>.

2. Transaction: the agent lists messages (list), retrieves them (retr <n>), and marks them for deletion (dele <n>).

3. Update: after quit, the server deletes the marked messages.

It is typically used in download-and-delete mode (mail moves to one device) or download-and-keep. It keeps no state between sessions.

↑ Section 2.3
Q10

What does IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) protocol do?

Answer

IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) (TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 143, or 993 with TLS (Transport Layer Security)) lets a user manage mail that stays on the server: create and use server-side folders, move messages between them, search the mailbox on the server, keep read/unread and other flags, and fetch only parts of messages (just headers, or one attachment). It keeps the user's state across sessions, so all devices (phone, laptop, web) see the same mailbox.

↑ Section 2.3
Q11

What are the differences between POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) and IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol)?

Answer
POP3 IMAP
Downloads mail to the device, usually deletes it from the server Keeps mail on the server
No server-side folders Server-side folders; move messages between them
Doesn't keep state across sessions Keeps state (folders, flags) across sessions
Hard to use from multiple devices Designed for multiple devices — all stay in sync
Downloads whole messages Can download headers or parts only
Simple, uses little server storage More complex; uses server storage
Port 110 / 995 Port 143 / 993
↑ Section 2.3

Section 2.4: Domain Name System

17 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17
Q1

What is DNS (Domain Name System)? What is DNS used for?

Answer

DNS (Domain Name System) is (1) a distributed database of names and records, held in a hierarchy of name servers, and (2) an application-layer protocol that lets hosts query that database.

Used for:

  • Name-to-IP (Internet Protocol) translation (the main job): www.athabascau.ca → 3.167.56.46.

  • Host aliasing: mapping easy alias names to the real (canonical) name.

  • Mail server aliasing: finding the mail server for a domain (MX (Mail Exchanger record) records).

  • Load distribution: spreading requests over many server IP addresses.

  • Reverse lookups (IP → name) and other data (TXT (Text record) records for email security, etc.).

↑ Section 2.4
Q2

How does the Domain Name System work?

Answer

When you type a name:

1. Your computer (the DNS (Domain Name System) client, "stub resolver") sends a query over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 53 to its local DNS server.

2. If the local server has the answer cached, it replies at once.

3. Otherwise it asks a root server, which replies with the addresses of the TLD (Top-Level Domain) servers for the ending (e.g., .ca).

4. It asks a TLD server, which replies with the authoritative server for the domain (e.g., athabascau.ca).

5. It asks the authoritative server, which replies with the IP (Internet Protocol) address (A/AAAA record).

6. The local server caches the answer (for its TTL (Time-to-Live)) and sends it back to your computer, which then opens the connection to that IP address.

↑ Section 2.4
Q3

Why is DNS (Domain Name System) so important for the Internet community?

Answer

Because almost every Internet activity starts with a DNS lookup — web browsing, email delivery (MX (Mail Exchanger record) records), apps, cloud services. Without it, people would have to remember numeric addresses, and addresses could never change without breaking everything. DNS also lets services move, scale and balance load (CDNs (Content Distribution Network) rely on it), and it is a core part of the Internet's resilience. If DNS fails, the Internet effectively "goes down" for users even though the network still works.

↑ Section 2.4
Q4

In DNS (Domain Name System), what is host aliasing? Why is it needed?

Answer

Host aliasing lets a host with a complicated canonical name (e.g., relay1.west-coast.enterprise.com) have one or more simpler alias names (e.g., www.enterprise.com, enterprise.com). DNS stores a CNAME (Canonical Name record) record mapping the alias to the canonical name.

Needed because: users want short, memorable names; organisations can move a service to a different machine by changing one record without users noticing; and one server can host several names (and a mail server and web server can share the same alias name).

↑ Section 2.4
Q5

What is load distribution in DNS (Domain Name System)?

Answer

Load distribution spreads traffic across replicated servers. A busy site (e.g., cnn.com) runs many servers with different IP (Internet Protocol) addresses; the DNS database holds a set of IP addresses for one name. When clients ask, the DNS server returns the whole set but rotates the order of the addresses in each reply. Clients usually use the first address, so requests are spread across the servers. (CDNs (Content Distribution Network) use more advanced DNS tricks to send users to nearby servers.)

↑ Section 2.4
Q6

What problems does a centralized DNS (Domain Name System) design have?

Answer

A single, centralized DNS server would have:

  • A single point of failure — if it crashes, the whole Internet's naming fails.

  • Huge traffic volume — it would have to answer billions of queries.

  • Distance — it would be far from most users, so lookups would be slow.

  • Maintenance — one database would have to be updated for every new host in the world.

In short, it would not scale.

↑ Section 2.4
Q7

Why is a distributed database important for DNS (Domain Name System)?

Answer

Because a distributed database solves all the scaling problems above: the load is spread over millions of servers; there is no single point of failure (many copies at every level); servers are close to users; and each organisation maintains its own records (authority is delegated), so updates happen locally. Caching across the hierarchy makes it fast.

↑ Section 2.4
Q8

What are root DNS (Domain Name System) servers? What roles do they play?

Answer

Root DNS servers are the top of the DNS hierarchy. There are 13 logical root servers (named A to M, run by 12 organisations) replicated as well over a thousand physical instances worldwide using anycast, overseen by IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority)/ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers).

Role: when a local DNS server can't answer from its cache, it asks a root server, which tells it the addresses of the TLD servers for the requested top-level domain (e.g., the servers for .com or .ca). Root servers do not know individual host addresses.

↑ Section 2.4
Q9

What is a top-level domain (TLD) server?

Answer

A top-level domain (TLD) server is responsible for one top-level domain — generic ones like .com, .org, .net, .edu, .gov and country codes like .ca, .uk, .jp. It knows the authoritative DNS (Domain Name System) servers for every domain registered under it (e.g., the .com TLD servers know who is authoritative for amazon.com). Companies such as Verisign run .com; CIRA (Canadian Internet Registration Authority) runs .ca.

↑ Section 2.4
Q10

What are authoritative DNS (Domain Name System) servers?

Answer

An authoritative DNS server holds the official records for an organisation's domain (e.g., the hosts in athabascau.ca) and gives the final, definitive answer — the actual IP (Internet Protocol) address for a name. Every organisation with public hosts must provide one (its own servers or a service provider such as a cloud DNS or its ISP (Internet Service Provider)), usually with a primary and secondary copy.

↑ Section 2.4
Q11

What are so-called local DNS (Domain Name System) servers?

Answer

A local DNS server (also called the default name server or resolver) is the one your computer asks first. It is provided by your ISP (Internet Service Provider), company or university (or a public service like 8.8.8.8 / 1.1.1.1), and your address is configured automatically by DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol). It is not strictly part of the hierarchy — it acts as a proxy: it takes your query, does the searching through root, TLD (Top-Level Domain) and authoritative servers, caches answers, and returns the result.

↑ Section 2.4
Q12

What are recursive queries and iterative queries in DNS (Domain Name System)?

Answer

  • Recursive query: the asker hands the whole job to the server: "find the answer for me." The server must return the final answer (doing any further queries itself). Typically your computer → local DNS server.

  • Iterative query: the server replies with the best it knows — either the answer or "I don't know, but ask this server next" (a referral). The asker then contacts the next server itself. Typically local DNS server → root → TLD (Top-Level Domain) → authoritative.

Recursive puts the burden on the contacted server; iterative spreads the work. The usual pattern is one recursive query (host to local server) followed by iterative queries.

↑ Section 2.4
Q13

Why is DNS (Domain Name System) caching needed?

Answer

Caching speeds up lookups (answers come from a nearby server immediately) and reduces DNS traffic and load on root and TLD (Top-Level Domain) servers. When a DNS server learns a mapping, it keeps it for the record's TTL (Time-to-Live) (e.g., a day or two); local servers also usually cache TLD server addresses, so root servers are rarely visited. The downside is that a cached entry can be out of date until its TTL expires.

↑ Section 2.4
Q14

What are resource records (RRs) in DNS (Domain Name System)? What is the format of resource record?

Answer

A resource record (RR) is one entry in the DNS database. Format: (Name, Value, Type, TTL (Time-to-Live)) — TTL says how long a cache may keep it. The meaning of Name and Value depends on the Type:

Type Name Value Example
A host name IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address (relay1.bar.foo.com, 145.37.93.126, A)
AAAA host name IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) address (www.example.com, 2001:db8::1, AAAA)
NS (Name Server record) domain host name of an authoritative server for it (foo.com, dns.foo.com, NS)
CNAME (Canonical Name record) alias name canonical (real) name (foo.com, relay1.bar.foo.com, CNAME)
MX (Mail Exchanger record) domain (alias for mail) canonical name of its mail server (foo.com, mail.bar.foo.com, MX)

Others: PTR (Pointer record) (reverse lookup), SOA (Start of Authority record) (zone info), TXT (Text record) (text, e.g., SPF (Sender Policy Framework)), SRV (Service record) (service location).

↑ Section 2.4
Q15

What are DNS (Domain Name System) messages? What is the format?

Answer

There are two kinds of DNS messages — query and reply — and both use the same format:

  • Header (12 bytes): a 16-bit identification number (a reply uses the same ID (Identifier) as its query), flags (query or reply; authoritative answer; recursion desired; recursion available), and four counts giving the number of entries in each of the sections below.

  • Question section: the name being asked about and the type (A, MX (Mail Exchanger record)…).

  • Answer section: the resource records that answer the question.

  • Authority section: records for other authoritative servers.

  • Additional section: helpful extra records (e.g., the IP (Internet Protocol) address of a mail server named in an MX answer).

↑ Section 2.4
Q16

What can the nslookup command do for you?

Answer

nslookup sends DNS (Domain Name System) queries from the command line so you can look up and troubleshoot DNS:

  • find the IP (Internet Protocol) address for a name (nslookup www.athabascau.ca) or the name for an IP (reverse lookup);

  • query specific record types (nslookup -type=MX (Mail Exchanger record) gmail.com, -type=NS (Name Server record), -type=AAAA, -type=CNAME (Canonical Name record));

  • ask a specific DNS server (nslookup www.mit.edu 8.8.8.8);

  • see whether an answer is authoritative or from cache.

PowerShell equivalent: Resolve-DnsName www.athabascau.ca -Type A (and -Type MX, -Server 8.8.8.8).

↑ Section 2.4
Q17

What roles does ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) do?

Answer

ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) coordinates the Internet's unique identifiers:

  • manages the DNS (Domain Name System) root zone and policy for top-level domains (creating new gTLDs, delegating country-code TLDs);

  • accredits domain-name registrars and sets registration rules and dispute processes;

  • through IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority), allocates IP (Internet Protocol) address blocks to the regional Internet registries (ARIN (American Registry for Internet Numbers), RIPE (Réseaux IP Européens)…), AS (Autonomous System) numbers, and protocol parameters and port numbers.

↑ Section 2.4

Section 2.5: Peer-to-Peer File Distribution

11 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11

Also asked in: Assignment 1 Q2.4

Q1

What is a peer-to-peer network application?

Answer

A P2P (Peer-to-Peer) application is one in which end systems (peers) communicate directly with each other, with minimal or no reliance on always-on dedicated servers. Each peer acts as both client and server — it requests content from other peers and provides content to them. Peers are usually users' own computers, which come and go and change IP (Internet Protocol) addresses. Examples: BitTorrent, older Napster/Gnutella/Kazaa, early Skype, blockchain networks, and peer-assisted delivery (some game and OS (Operating System) updates).

↑ Section 2.5
Q2

What are the differences between client-server applications and peer-to-peer applications?

Answer
Client-server Peer-to-peer
Always-on server with a fixed, well-known address No always-on server needed; peers are intermittently connected with changing addresses
Clients talk only to the server, not to each other Peers talk directly to each other
Server does all the uploading; capacity is fixed Every peer uploads too, so capacity grows with users (self-scaling)
Must buy big servers/data centres and bandwidth Cheap for the provider — users supply the resources
Easy to manage, secure and control Harder to manage: churn, security, incentives, ISP (Internet Service Provider)-unfriendly traffic
Examples: Web, email, Netflix Examples: BitTorrent, blockchain
↑ Section 2.5
Q3

How is P2P (Peer-to-Peer) used for file distribution?

Answer

The file is broken into chunks. A peer joining the distribution gets a list of other peers (from a tracker or DHT (Distributed Hash Table)), downloads chunks from several peers at once, and as soon as it has a chunk it uploads that chunk to other peers. So every peer that is downloading is also redistributing. Eventually every peer has all chunks and reassembles the file. The server (seed) only has to upload each chunk at least once; the peers do the rest.

↑ Section 2.5
Q4

Why is it said that P2P (Peer-to-Peer) architecture is self-scalable?

Answer

Because each new peer adds both demand and supply. A new peer wants the file (adds work) but also contributes its upload bandwidth to serve others (adds capacity). So total upload capacity (u_s + Σu_i) grows at the same rate as total demand (N·F). The distribution time in the formula approaches F/u as N grows — it stops growing with N — whereas client-server time keeps growing linearly with N.

↑ Section 2.5
Q5

What is the file distribution problem?

Answer

The file distribution problem asks: how long does it take to get a copy of one large file (size F) from one server to a large number (N) of hosts? — i.e., what is the minimum distribution time, the time until all N peers have the whole file. It is used to compare client-server and P2P (Peer-to-Peer), given server upload rate u_s, peer upload rates u_i and peer download rates d_i.

↑ Section 2.5
Q6

How is distribution time calculated for a P2P (Peer-to-Peer) file distribution system?

Answer

The minimum distribution time is the largest of three lower bounds:

D_p2p = max( F / u_s ,  F / d_min ,  N·F / (u_s + Σ u_i) )

  • F/u_s: the server must upload the file at least once.

  • F/d_min: the slowest peer must download all F bits.

  • N·F/(u_s + Σu_i): N·F bits must be uploaded in total, using the combined upload capacity of the server and all peers.

See "How the formulas work" above for a worked example, and Assignment 1 Q2.4 for a 3×3 table.

↑ Section 2.5
Q7

What does the BitTorrent system do?

Answer

BitTorrent is a P2P (Peer-to-Peer) protocol for distributing large files:

  • The set of peers sharing a file is a torrent (swarm); a tracker keeps a list of peers in it (or a DHT (Distributed Hash Table) does, in "trackerless" mode).

  • The file is split into equal chunks (typically 256 KB (Kilobytes)). A new peer gets a list of peers, connects to some ("neighbours"), and starts trading chunks.

  • Which chunks to ask for: rarest first — request chunks that the fewest neighbours have, so rare chunks spread quickly.

  • Whom to send to: tit-for-tat — upload to the 4 neighbours sending to you at the highest rate (re-evaluated every 10 s); every 30 s also upload to one random neighbour ("optimistically unchoke"), which lets newcomers start and helps find better partners.

  • Peers may leave once done ("leechers" become "seeds" if they stay).

↑ Section 2.5
Q8

Where are distributed hash tables (DHTs) used?

Answer

DHTs are used wherever a P2P (Peer-to-Peer) system needs a database without a central server — to store and look up (key, value) pairs across peers:

  • BitTorrent's trackerless mode (Mainline DHT, based on Kademlia) — finds which peers have a torrent.

  • IPFS (InterPlanetary File System), eMule/Kad and other P2P file-sharing systems.

  • Distributed storage/databases — Amazon's Dynamo, Apache Cassandra, Riak (consistent hashing).

  • Some blockchain/peer-discovery systems (Ethereum's node discovery).

↑ Section 2.5
Q9

How does circular DHT (Distributed Hash Table) work?

Answer

  • Each peer gets an ID (Identifier) (e.g., 0 to 2^n − 1), and each key is hashed into the same ID range.

  • Peers are arranged in a ring (circle) in order of ID. A (key, value) pair is stored at the key's successor — the first peer whose ID is equal to or just after the key.

  • Each peer only knows its immediate successor (and often predecessor). A query for a key is passed around the ring from peer to peer until it reaches the peer responsible, which replies.

  • Lookups then cost about N/2 messages on average. To speed this up, peers keep shortcuts to peers farther around the ring (as in Chord), reducing lookups to about O(log N) messages with only O(log N) neighbours each.

  • For churn, each peer tracks its first and second successors and pings them; if the successor leaves, the second becomes the first.

↑ Section 2.5
Q10

What is an overlay network? How does it work?

Answer

An overlay network is a logical (virtual) network built on top of the physical Internet. Its nodes are the participating peers, and its "links" are logical connections between pairs of peers (e.g., TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections, or simply "knowing each other's IP (Internet Protocol) address"). An overlay link may cross many physical routers, but the overlay ignores that. Routers are not part of the overlay.

How it works: each peer keeps a list of its overlay neighbours; messages (queries, chunks) are forwarded peer to peer along overlay links, while the underlying Internet actually carries them. The overlay can be reshaped at will (e.g., a ring for a DHT (Distributed Hash Table), or BitTorrent's neighbour sets). Examples: BitTorrent swarms, DHT rings, CDNs (Content Distribution Network), VPNs (Virtual Private Network).

↑ Section 2.5
Q11

What does peer churn mean in P2P (Peer-to-Peer) systems?

Answer

Peer churn means peers join and leave the system at any time, often without warning (people shut down laptops, close the app, lose connection). P2P systems must cope: data stored at a departing peer must be copied elsewhere, routing structures (like a DHT (Distributed Hash Table) ring) must repair themselves (e.g., by tracking two successors and pinging them), and downloads must continue from other peers.

↑ Section 2.5

Section 2.6: Video Streaming and Content Distribution Networks

25 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20Q21Q22Q23Q24Q25
Q1

What are UDP (User Datagram Protocol) streaming, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) streaming, and Adaptive HTTP streaming?

Answer

  • UDP streaming: the server sends the video over UDP at a steady rate that matches the video's playback rate (e.g., one chunk every fixed interval), usually wrapped in RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) packets. The client keeps only a small buffer (a few seconds) to smooth out jitter.

  • HTTP streaming: the video is an ordinary file on an HTTP server. The client sends an HTTP GET; the server sends the file as fast as TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) allows; the client stores it in a buffer and starts playing once enough has arrived.

  • Adaptive HTTP streaming (DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP)): like HTTP streaming, but the video is encoded in several versions (bit rates) and divided into chunks of a few seconds. The client measures available bandwidth and, chunk by chunk, requests the best version it can handle, adapting as conditions change.

↑ Section 2.6
Q2

Can streaming be done over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)?

Answer

Yes. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) streaming and DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) (used by YouTube and Netflix) run over TCP. TCP's retransmissions and varying rate are handled by client buffering and prefetching: the player downloads ahead, so short slowdowns are absorbed by the buffer. TCP also passes through firewalls and NATs (Network Address Translation) easily and avoids needing special streaming servers. (Very low-delay live/interactive video still often uses UDP (User Datagram Protocol).)

↑ Section 2.6
Q3

What is client buffering? Why is it needed?

Answer

Client buffering means the player stores video data that arrives ahead of the moment it is needed, and starts playback only after a short initial delay (a few seconds of video are buffered).

It's needed because the network's delay and throughput vary (jitter, congestion, TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) slowdowns), while video must be played at a constant rate. The buffer absorbs the variation: when the network slows, playback continues from the buffer; when it speeds up, the buffer refills. Without it the video would freeze whenever a packet was late.

↑ Section 2.6
Q4

How does UDP (User Datagram Protocol) streaming work? What properties does UDP streaming have?

Answer

How it works: the server sends video chunks over UDP at a constant rate equal to the video's consumption rate (e.g., 2 Mbps video → 8,000-bit chunks every 4 ms). Chunks are wrapped in RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) packets (with sequence numbers and timestamps). The client holds a small buffer (2–5 s) and plays; a separate control connection (RTSP (Real Time Streaming Protocol)) carries commands like pause and seek.

Properties:

  • Low overhead and low delay — no congestion control or retransmission holding it back.

  • Push-based at a constant rate; the server keeps state for each client.

  • No reliability — lost packets are simply skipped (the app is loss-tolerant).

  • Not adaptive by default — if bandwidth drops below the video rate, playback freezes or degrades.

  • Needs special media servers and a control channel, and UDP is often blocked by firewalls/NAT (Network Address Translation) — reasons it has lost out to HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) streaming.

↑ Section 2.6
Q5

Why does UDP (User Datagram Protocol) streaming need a parallel control connection?

Answer

Because UDP only carries the media data — it has no way for the client to send commands back to the server. Interactive actions such as pause, resume, play from a new position (seek), fast-forward and stop need a separate, reliable control connection (RTSP, the Real-Time Streaming Protocol, typically over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)) that runs in parallel with the UDP media stream.

↑ Section 2.6
Q6

What protocols are used for UDP (User Datagram Protocol) streaming?

Answer

  • RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) — carries the audio/video chunks over UDP, with sequence numbers, timestamps and payload type.

  • RTCP (RTP Control Protocol) — companion to RTP; sends quality statistics (loss, jitter) between sender and receiver.

  • RTSP (Real-Time Streaming Protocol) — the control channel (play, pause, seek).

  • UDP underneath (and IP (Internet Protocol)). Related: SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) for setting up calls; WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication) (SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) over UDP) for browser video calls.

↑ Section 2.6
Q7

What is HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) streaming? How does it work?

Answer

HTTP streaming stores the video as a regular file on a web server with its own URL (Uniform Resource Locator). The client opens a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection and sends an HTTP GET for the file. The server sends the bytes as fast as TCP allows (not at a fixed rate). The client collects bytes in its application buffer, and once a threshold is reached (a few seconds of video) the player starts, taking frames from the buffer, decompressing and displaying them, while more data keeps arriving. It works through firewalls and NATs (Network Address Translation), uses ordinary web servers and caches (CDNs (Content Distribution Network)), and needs no control channel — seeking uses HTTP byte-range requests.

↑ Section 2.6
Q8

What are multimedia network applications using HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) streaming?

Answer

Examples: YouTube, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, Disney+, Hulu, Apple TV (Television)+, Twitch (live, HLS), TikTok and Instagram video, Spotify and other music streaming, and online courses with recorded lectures. Formats: MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group)-DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP), Apple HLS (HTTP Live Streaming), Microsoft Smooth Streaming.

↑ Section 2.6
Q9

What is prefetching video? Why is it needed?

Answer

Prefetching means the client downloads video faster than it is being watched, storing the future frames in its buffer ahead of time.

Needed because it builds up a reserve: if throughput later drops, playback continues from the prefetched data without freezing. It turns a variable-rate network into smooth, constant-rate playback. (The cost: bandwidth is wasted if the user stops early — see Q11.)

↑ Section 2.6
Q10

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) streaming runs over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and utilizes both the client application buffer and TCP buffers. How do the two collaborate?

Answer

They form a chain:

1. The server writes video bytes into its TCP send buffer; TCP sends them over the network.

2. At the client they arrive in the TCP receive buffer; the application reads them out into its client application buffer.

3. The player takes frames from the application buffer at the video's playback rate.

When the application buffer is full, the app stops reading from the TCP socket → the TCP receive buffer fills → TCP's flow control (the advertised receive window shrinks to zero) tells the server to stop → the server's send buffer fills → the server's writes block. When the player consumes frames, space frees up and the whole chain starts moving again. So the buffers plus TCP flow control automatically match the sending rate to the playback rate once buffers are full.

↑ Section 2.6
Q11

How is early termination handled in HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) streaming?

Answer

When a user stops watching early (or switches video), everything already prefetched but not watched is wasted bandwidth. It is handled by: the client closing the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection (or stopping requests), so the server stops sending; and by limiting how far ahead the client prefetches (keeping a modest buffer size, or using DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) chunks so it downloads only a few chunks at a time). YouTube-style players deliberately limit the buffer for this reason.

↑ Section 2.6
Q12

How is repositioning video handled in HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) streaming?

Answer

Repositioning (jumping to a new point) is done with the HTTP byte-range header: the client sends a new GET with Range: bytes=... indicating the byte offset where the new position begins in the file (or, with DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP), simply requests the chunk for that time from the manifest). The server sends data from that point. Any data already buffered beyond the old position is discarded (wasted), and the player refills its buffer from the new point.

↑ Section 2.6
Q13

What is adaptive HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) streaming? What is dynamic adaptive streaming over HTTP (DASH)

Answer

Adaptive HTTP streaming stores the same video in several encodings at different bit rates (quality levels) and lets the client switch between them during playback according to the bandwidth it's getting.

DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) is the ISO (International Organization for Standardization) standard (MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group)-DASH) for this. The video is cut into short chunks (a few seconds each), each available at several bit rates; a manifest file lists the URL (Uniform Resource Locator) and bit rate of every version of every chunk. The client requests chunks one at a time with ordinary HTTP GETs, choosing the bit rate for each. Apple's HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) works the same way.

↑ Section 2.6
Q14

How does DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) work? What advantages does DASH have?

Answer

How DASH works:

1. The client first downloads the manifest (MPD (Media Presentation Description) file), which lists each version's bit rate and the URLs (Uniform Resource Locator) of its chunks.

2. It requests one chunk at a time with HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) GET.

3. While downloading, it measures the throughput and watches its buffer level.

4. A rate-adaptation algorithm picks the bit rate for the next chunk: high quality when bandwidth is plentiful and the buffer is healthy, lower quality when bandwidth drops or the buffer is draining.

5. It may also choose which server (CDN (Content Distribution Network)) to fetch from.

Advantages: smooth playback with fewer freezes under changing bandwidth; the best quality each user's connection allows (phones on 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) and TVs (Television) on fibre use the same system); runs over ordinary HTTP/TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) — works through firewalls and NATs (Network Address Translation) and can use standard web servers, caches and CDNs; the server is simple and stateless (all intelligence is in the client); easy to switch servers mid-stream.

↑ Section 2.6
Q15

What are content distribution networks (CDNs)?

Answer

A content distribution network (CDN) is a system of many servers spread across many geographic locations that store copies (replicas) of content — videos, web objects, software downloads — and deliver each user's request from a nearby, suitable server instead of one distant origin server. Benefits: lower delay, higher throughput, less long-haul Internet traffic, no single point of failure, and ability to handle huge demand. CDNs can be private (owned by the content provider — Google, Netflix Open Connect) or third-party (Akamai, Cloudflare, Limelight/Edgio, Amazon CloudFront) serving many customers.

↑ Section 2.6
Q16

A CDN (Content Distribution Network) often consists of many servers. How would these servers be placed?

Answer

Servers are placed in clusters at many locations, following one of two philosophies:

  • Enter deep: many small clusters deployed deep inside access ISPs (Internet Service Provider)' networks, very close to users all over the world.

  • Bring home: fewer, larger clusters placed at key points such as Internet Exchange Points (IXPs), "bringing the ISPs home" to them.

Either way the aim is to put copies of popular content near large user populations; content is replicated across clusters (often pulled on demand into a cluster when first requested, like a cache).

↑ Section 2.6
Q17

What is the so-called enter deep philosophy for server placement within content distribution networks? How are servers placed according to enter deep?

Answer

Enter deep means the CDN (Content Distribution Network) goes deep into the access networks of ISPs (Internet Service Provider), placing server clusters inside thousands of access ISPs (and PoPs (Point of Presence)) around the world — as close to end users as possible. Pioneered by Akamai, which has servers in thousands of locations.

Advantage: shortest distance to users → lowest delay and highest throughput, fewer links and routers crossed. Disadvantage: so many small clusters are hard and costly to deploy, maintain and manage.

↑ Section 2.6
Q18

What is the so-called bring home philosophy for server placement within content distribution networks? How are servers placed according to bring home?

Answer

Bring home means the CDN (Content Distribution Network) "brings the ISPs (Internet Service Provider) home" by building fewer but larger clusters (tens rather than thousands) at a smaller number of key sites — typically at IXPs (Internet Exchange Point). Used by Limelight and many others.

Advantage: lower maintenance and management cost, simpler operations. Disadvantage: users are farther away, so somewhat higher delay and lower throughput than enter-deep.

↑ Section 2.6
Q19

How do CDNs (Content Distribution Network) work?

Answer

1. The content provider places (or the CDN pulls in) copies of its content on CDN servers.

2. When a user requests content (e.g., clicks a video URL (Uniform Resource Locator)), the request is intercepted — almost always via DNS (Domain Name System).

3. The CDN chooses a suitable server cluster for that user (nearby, not overloaded, good network path) — the cluster selection strategy.

4. The CDN's DNS returns the IP (Internet Protocol) address of a server in that cluster, and the client fetches the content from it with HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) (often DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP)).

5. If the chosen server doesn't have the object, it fetches it from the origin or another CDN server, caches it and serves it.

↑ Section 2.6
Q20

How do CDNs (Content Distribution Network) take advantage of DNS (Domain Name System) to intercept and redirect requests?

Answer

The content provider's URLs (Uniform Resource Locator) use hostnames that the provider's authoritative DNS server hands off to the CDN. When a user's local DNS server asks for the video's hostname, the provider's DNS returns a CNAME (Canonical Name record) pointing to a CDN hostname (e.g., a342.kingcdn.com). The local DNS then queries the CDN's own DNS, which picks a good CDN server for that user (based on where the user's local DNS server is) and returns that server's IP (Internet Protocol) address. So the "redirect" happens silently inside the ordinary DNS lookup — the browser just connects to the IP it is given.

↑ Section 2.6
Q21

What six steps do CDNs (Content Distribution Network) use to take advantage of DNS (Domain Name System) to intercept and redirect requests?

Answer

The textbook's six steps (NetCinema using the CDN "KingCDN"):

1. The user visits the provider's web page (www.NetCinema.com) and clicks the video link, e.g., http://video.netcinema.com/6Y7B23V.

2. The user's host sends a DNS query for video.netcinema.com to its local DNS server (LDNS (Local Domain Name System server)).

3. The LDNS forwards the query to the provider's authoritative DNS server, which sees the "video" hostname and, instead of an IP (Internet Protocol) address, returns a hostname in the CDN's domain (e.g., a1105.kingcdn.com).

4. The LDNS sends a query for a1105.kingcdn.com; the CDN's DNS system returns the IP address of a chosen CDN content server.

5. The LDNS forwards that IP address to the user's host.

6. The client opens a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection to that CDN server and sends an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) GET for the video (with DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP), first for the manifest).

↑ Section 2.6
Q22

What are the cluster selection strategies for CDNs (Content Distribution Network) to assign a client?

Answer

  • Geographically closest: assign the client to the cluster geographically nearest its LDNS (Local Domain Name System server) (using geo-IP (Internet Protocol) databases). Simple, but the closest by distance may not be closest in network terms, the LDNS may be far from the client, and it ignores current delay and load.

  • Real-time measurements: clusters periodically measure delay and loss to LDNSs (e.g., with pings), and the CDN picks the best-performing cluster.

  • Also consider server load, cost (ISP (Internet Service Provider) delivery/transit contracts) and content availability.

  • IP anycast (let routing pick the nearest), or letting the client choose among several servers (as Netflix and DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) clients can).

↑ Section 2.6
Q23

How do CDNs (Content Distribution Network) measure delay and loss performance for a client?

Answer

  • Active probing: clusters periodically send probes (pings, DNS (Domain Name System) queries) to local DNS servers around the world and measure the round-trip delay and loss. Drawback: many LDNSs (Local Domain Name System server) are configured not to answer probes.

  • Passive measurement: use the characteristics of real traffic between clients and CDN servers — e.g., measure the delay between the SYNACK (Synchronize-Acknowledgement segment) and the ACK (Acknowledgement) in the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) handshake, or throughput and loss of recent transfers.

  • Test the CDN's DNS choices: occasionally send clients to different clusters to see which performs best.

↑ Section 2.6
Q24

How do some CDNs (Content Distribution Network) use IP (Internet Protocol) anycast to match clients with CDN servers?

Answer

With IP anycast, every CDN cluster advertises the same IP address (e.g., via BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) from each location). The CDN's DNS (Domain Name System) returns this one anycast address to all clients. Internet routers, running BGP, send each client's packets to the "closest" cluster in routing terms (the best BGP route from the client's network). So the matching of client to server is done automatically by routing. It is simple and good for short transactions (it's used by DNS root servers and Cloudflare), but a route change mid-session could move a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection to a different server.

↑ Section 2.6
Q25

What strategies are used by Netflix, YouTube, and Kankan, respectively, to assign clients to CDN (Content Distribution Network) servers?

Answer

  • Netflix: runs its own CDN (Open Connect) with servers placed inside ISPs (Internet Service Provider) and at IXPs (Internet Exchange Point), and pushes content to them during off-peak hours (it knows what will be popular). The Netflix app gets a list of servers, measures and chooses the best one, and uses DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP). Sign-up, browsing and billing run in Amazon's cloud.

  • YouTube: uses Google's private CDN with clusters at hundreds of locations (including IXPs and inside ISPs). It uses DNS (Domain Name System) to redirect users to a cluster, typically the one with the lowest RTT (Round-Trip Time), with some load balancing to other clusters; content is pulled into caches on demand; it uses HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) streaming (DASH).

  • Kankan (Chinese video service): uses P2P (Peer-to-Peer) delivery — clients get the video in chunks from other peers that already have it, tracked by a central tracker, with CDN/servers as a fallback when too few peers are available (a hybrid CDN-P2P).

↑ Section 2.6

Textbook Review Questions — Chapter 2

27 questions (Kurose & Ross, 8th edition)

R1R2R3R4R5R6R7R8R9R10R11R12R13R14R15R16R17R18R19R20R21R22R23R24R25R26R27
R1

List five nonproprietary Internet applications and the application-layer protocols that they use.

Answer
Application Application-layer protocol
The Web HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) (RFC (Request for Comments) 9110–9114)
Email sending / reading SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) / IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol), POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3)
File transfer FTP (File Transfer Protocol)
Remote login SSH (Secure Shell) (or Telnet)
Name lookup DNS (Domain Name System)
Streaming video DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) over HTTP
Network time NTP (Network Time Protocol)
↑ Chapter 2 review
R2

What is the difference between network architecture and application architecture?

Answer

Network architecture is the fixed, layered organisation of the network itself (e.g., the five-layer Internet stack) — the application developer cannot change it. Application architecture is chosen by the application developer and says how the application is organised across end systems — usually client-server or peer-to-peer.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R3

For a communication session between a pair of processes, which process is the client and which is the server?

Answer

The process that starts the communication (sends the first message) is the client; the process that waits to be contacted is the server.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R4

For a P2P (Peer-to-Peer) file-sharing application, do you agree with the statement, “There is no notion of client and server sides of a communication session”? Why or why not?

Answer

No, I don't agree. In a P2P file-sharing session, the peer that requests/receives a file is the client for that session and the peer sending the file is the server. A peer can be a client in one session and a server in another, but within any one communication session the two roles still exist.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R5

What information is used by a process running on one host to identify a process running on another host?

Answer

The destination host's IP (Internet Protocol) address and the port number of the destination socket (process).

↑ Chapter 2 review
R6

Suppose you wanted to do a transaction from a remote client to a server as fast as possible. Would you use UDP (User Datagram Protocol) or TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)? Why?

Answer

UDP. With UDP the client can send the request immediately — there is no connection setup — so the transaction can finish in one RTT (Round-Trip Time) (request out, reply back). TCP needs a handshake first, costing at least two RTTs. (The application must then handle any lost message itself.)

↑ Chapter 2 review
R7

Referring to Figure 2.4, we see that none of the applications listed in Figure 2.4 requires both no data loss and timing. Can you conceive of an application that requires no data loss and that is also highly time-sensitive?

Answer

Yes. Examples: remote-controlled surgery or remote control of machinery/vehicles, where every command must arrive (no loss) and quickly; real-time financial trading (every order must arrive, and delay costs money); multiplayer game state updates that must be complete and fast; and real-time collaborative editing.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R8

List the four broad classes of services that a transport protocol can provide. For each of the service classes, indicate if either UDP (User Datagram Protocol) or TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) (or both) provides such a service.

Answer
Service TCP? UDP?
Reliable data transfer Yes No
Throughput guarantee No No
Timing (delay) guarantee No No
Security (encryption, integrity, authentication) Not by itself — added by TLS (Transport Layer Security) on top of TCP No (DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security)/QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) can add it)
↑ Chapter 2 review
R9

Recall that TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) can be enhanced with TLS (Transport Layer Security) to provide process-to-process security services, including encryption. Does TLS operate at the transport layer or the application layer? If the application developer wants TCP to be enhanced with TLS, what does the developer have to do?

Answer

TLS operates at the application layer — it is implemented as a library that sits on top of TCP, inside the application, not in the operating system's transport layer. To use it, the developer must include the TLS library in the application code (e.g., use an SSL (Secure Sockets Layer)/TLS socket API (Application Programming Interface) such as Python's ssl module or .NET's SslStream) instead of a plain TCP socket; the application then passes data to TLS, which encrypts it and hands it to TCP.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R10

What is meant by a handshaking protocol?

Answer

A handshaking protocol is one where the two sides first exchange control messages to set up the communication (agree to talk, exchange parameters) before any real data is sent. Example: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)'s three-way handshake (SYN (Synchronize flag), SYN-ACK (Acknowledgement), ACK); SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol)'s HELO exchange.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R11

Why do HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), and IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) run on top of TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) rather than on UDP (User Datagram Protocol)?

Answer

Because all three need every byte delivered correctly and in order — web pages, emails and mailbox data must not be missing pieces. TCP provides this reliable, in-order data transfer (plus congestion control), so the application protocols don't have to implement retransmission and ordering themselves. UDP gives no such guarantee.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R12

Consider an e-commerce site that wants to keep a purchase record for each of its customers. Describe how this can be done with cookies.

Answer

1. On the customer's first visit, the site creates a unique ID (Identifier) and an entry for it in its back-end database, and sends the browser Set-Cookie: <ID> in the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) response.

2. The browser stores the cookie and includes `Cookie: <ID>` in every later request to that site.

3. Each time the customer buys something, the server looks up the ID in the database and records the purchase against it.

4. On later visits the site uses the ID to show the customer's purchase history, cart and recommendations.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R13

Describe how Web caching can reduce the delay in receiving a requested object. Will Web caching reduce the delay for all objects requested by a user or for only some of the objects? Why?

Answer

A web cache sits close to users (on the same LAN (Local Area Network) or at the ISP (Internet Service Provider)). When a requested object is already in the cache (a hit), it's delivered over the fast local network instead of from a distant server across a congested access link — much lower delay. It also reduces traffic on the access link, lowering its utilisation and therefore the queuing delay for everything else.

It reduces delay only for some objects: those already cached (and still fresh). The first request for an object, objects that change often, personalised or encrypted content, and uncacheable objects must still come from the origin server (although even these benefit indirectly from the less busy access link).

↑ Chapter 2 review
R14

Telnet into a Web server and send a multiline request message. Include in the request message the If-modified-since: header line to force a response message with the 304 Not Modified status code.

Answer

Example session (from a command prompt):

telnet www.example.com 80
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
If-modified-since: Wed, 01 Jan 2025 00:00:00 GMT
(press Enter twice)

If the page has not changed since that date, the server replies HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)/1.1 304 Not Modified with no body. (PowerShell alternative: Invoke-WebRequest https://www.example.com -Headers @{"If-Modified-Since"="Wed, 01 Jan 2025 00:00:00 GMT (Greenwich Mean Time)"} — a 304 appears as a "not modified" response.) Choose a date after the page's Last-Modified date to force the 304.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R15

List several popular messaging apps. Do they use the same protocols as SMS (Short Message Service)?

Answer

Popular messaging apps: WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, iMessage, WeChat, Telegram, Signal, Snapchat. No, they don't use the same protocols as SMS. SMS travels over the cellular network's signalling channels (SS7 (Signalling System No. 7)/SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) in the mobile core). The apps send messages as data over the Internet using their own (often proprietary) protocols on top of TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)/TLS (Transport Layer Security) or UDP (User Datagram Protocol) — e.g., WhatsApp uses a modified XMPP (Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol) with the Signal encryption protocol. (RCS (Rich Communication Services), "Chat", is a newer carrier standard.)

↑ Chapter 2 review
R16

Suppose Alice, with a Web-based e-mail account (such as Hotmail or Gmail), sends a message to Bob, who accesses his mail from his mail server using IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol). Discuss how the message gets from Alice’s host to Bob’s host. Be sure to list the series of application-layer protocols that are used to move the message between the two hosts.

Answer

1. Alice composes the message in her browser and it is sent to her web-mail server (e.g., Gmail) using HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) (HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure)).

2. Alice's mail server sends the message to Bob's mail server using SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) (after a DNS (Domain Name System) MX (Mail Exchanger record) lookup).

3. Bob's user agent retrieves the message from his mail server using IMAP.

Series: HTTP → SMTP → IMAP.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R17

Print out the header of an e-mail message you have recently received. How many Received: header lines are there? Analyze each of the header lines in the message.

Answer

This is a hands-on question — open a recent email and choose "show original / view source". You'll see header lines such as Received: (one added by each mail server the message passed through — count them; typically 2 to 6), From:, To:, Subject:, Date:, Message-ID (Identifier):, Return-Path:, MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions)-Version:, Content-Type:, and authentication headers (DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)-Signature:, Authentication-Results:, ARC (Authenticated Received Chain)-…). Read the Received: lines bottom to top to trace the path from the sender's server to yours; each shows which server received it, from which host/IP (Internet Protocol), with which protocol (ESMTP (Extended Simple Mail Transfer Protocol)/ESMTPS (Extended Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure)) and when.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R18

What is the HOL (Head-of-the-Line) blocking issue in HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)/1.1? How does HTTP/2 attempt to solve it?

Answer

HOL (head-of-line) blocking in HTTP/1.1: over one persistent connection, objects are sent in the order requested, so a large object at the front (e.g., a big video) delays all the small objects behind it, even though they could have been sent quickly. Browsers work around it by opening several parallel TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections.

HTTP/2's solution: it breaks each message into small frames and interleaves frames from different responses on the same connection (multiplexing), so small objects get sent in between pieces of the big one; plus priorities. (HOL blocking at the TCP level — a lost packet stalls everything — remains; HTTP/3 over QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) fixes that.)

↑ Chapter 2 review
R19

Is it possible for an organization’s Web server and mail server to have exactly the same alias for a hostname (for example, foo.com)? What would be the type for the RR (Resource Record) that contains the hostname of the mail server?

Answer

Yes. DNS (Domain Name System) keeps separate record types: the web server's name is found through a CNAME (Canonical Name record)/A record, and the mail server through an MX (Mail Exchanger record) record, both for the alias foo.com. The resource record containing the mail server's hostname has type MX.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R20

Look over your received e-mails, and examine the header of a message sent from a user with a .edu e-mail address. Is it possible to determine from the header the IP (Internet Protocol) address of the host from which the message was sent? Do the same for a message sent from a Gmail account.

Answer

Hands-on. For a message from a .edu address, the bottom Received: header usually shows the IP address of the sending host (or the first server that received it from that host), so it's often possible to determine it. For a message sent from Gmail, Google normally hides the sender's host IP — the earliest Received: header shows a Google server or an internal/private address rather than the user's IP — so it is usually not possible.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R21

In BitTorrent, suppose Alice provides chunks to Bob throughout a 30-second interval. Will Bob necessarily return the favor and provide chunks to Alice in this same interval? Why or why not?

Answer

No, not necessarily. Bob uploads (reciprocates) to the four peers that are currently sending to him at the highest rates. If Alice isn't among Bob's top four uploaders during that interval — because others are sending to Bob faster — Bob won't upload to her (except if she's picked by his random "optimistic unchoke").

↑ Chapter 2 review
R22

Consider a new peer Alice that joins BitTorrent without possessing any chunks. Without any chunks, she cannot become a top-four uploader for any of the other peers, since she has nothing to upload. How then will Alice get her first chunk?

Answer

Through optimistic unchoking: every 30 seconds each peer picks one additional neighbour at random and sends chunks to it. Eventually some peer will randomly choose Alice and send her a chunk. Once she has chunks, she can trade them and join tit-for-tat.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R23

What is an overlay network? Does it include routers? What are the edges in the overlay network?

Answer

An overlay network is a logical network of peers built on top of the physical network. The nodes are the participating peers; the edges are logical links — e.g., TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections between pairs of peers (or knowledge of each other's addresses). It does not include routers — an overlay link may cross many routers, but they aren't part of the overlay.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R24

CDNs (Content Distribution Network) typically adopt one of two different server placement philosophies. Name and briefly describe them.

Answer

  • Enter deep: put many small server clusters deep inside access ISPs (Internet Service Provider) all over the world, close to users (Akamai) — best delay/throughput, but hard to manage.

  • Bring home: build fewer, larger clusters at key locations such as IXPs (Internet Exchange Point) (Limelight) — easier to maintain, but somewhat higher delay/lower throughput for users.

↑ Chapter 2 review
R25

Besides network-related considerations such as delay, loss, and bandwidth performance, there are other important factors that go into designing a CDN (Content Distribution Network) server selection strategy. What are they?

Answer

  • Server load — don't send clients to overloaded clusters (load balancing).

  • Cost — the ISP (Internet Service Provider)/transit delivery costs of each cluster (some paths are cheaper).

  • Content availability — whether the cluster has the content.

  • Business agreements with ISPs, and client-side factors (letting the client choose).

↑ Chapter 2 review
R26

In Section 2.7, the UDP (User Datagram Protocol) server described needed only one socket, whereas the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) server needed two sockets. Why? If the TCP server were to support n simultaneous connections, each from a different client host, how many sockets would the TCP server need?

Answer

The UDP server needs only one socket because UDP is connectionless: all clients send datagrams to that same socket, and each datagram carries the sender's address. The TCP server needs two kinds: a welcoming (listening) socket that accepts new connection requests, and a new connection socket for each client created when the connection is accepted. To support n simultaneous connections, the TCP server needs n + 1 sockets (1 welcoming + n connection sockets).

↑ Chapter 2 review
R27

For the client-server application over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) described in Section 2.7, why must the server program be executed before the client program? For the client-server application over UDP (User Datagram Protocol), why may the client program be executed before the server program?

Answer

TCP: the client starts by trying to set up a TCP connection (handshake) with the server. If the server isn't already running and listening on its welcoming socket, the connection attempt is refused and the client fails. So the server must start first.

UDP: there is no connection setup. The client just sends datagrams when it runs; it doesn't need the server to be ready at that moment (if the server isn't up, the datagram is simply lost, but the client program still runs). So either may start first.

↑ Chapter 2 review

Unit 3: The Transport Layer

3.1 Transport Layer Principles and Services3.2 UDP and TCP3.3 Congestion Control at the Transport Layer and Evolution of Transport-Layer FunctionalityTextbook review questions — Chapter 3

Section 3.1: Transport Layer Principles and Services

16 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16
Q1

What services does the transport layer provide?

Answer

  • Process-to-process (logical) communication — delivering data to the right application process using port numbers (multiplexing/demultiplexing).

  • Error detection — checksums (both UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)).

  • In TCP additionally: reliable data transfer (no loss, no duplicates, in order), connection management (setup/teardown), flow control (don't overflow the receiver) and congestion control (don't overload the network).

  • Segmentation of application data into segments and reassembly.

(No transport protocol on the Internet guarantees delay or bandwidth.)

↑ Section 3.1
Q2

What principles are suggested for use in designing transport layer protocols?

Answer

Key design principles:

  • End-to-end principle: put functions like reliability in the end systems, keep the network core simple.

  • Layering: use the network layer's service and offer a clean service (sockets) to applications.

  • Multiplexing/demultiplexing with port numbers.

  • Reliable data transfer built from: error detection (checksums), receiver feedback (ACKs (Acknowledgement)/NAKs (Negative Acknowledgement)), retransmission, sequence numbers, timers, and pipelining with windows for efficiency.

  • Flow control (match the receiver's speed) and congestion control (be fair to the network — AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease), respond to loss).

  • Connection management (handshake to agree on starting sequence numbers and resources).

↑ Section 3.1
Q3

What is the relationship between the transport layer and the network layer?

Answer

The network layer provides logical communication between hosts; the transport layer provides logical communication between processes running on those hosts. Transport relies on and enhances the network layer's service: it takes IP (Internet Protocol)'s unreliable host-to-host delivery and extends it to process-to-process delivery, optionally adding reliability. However, transport is limited by the network layer — it can't provide delay or bandwidth guarantees if IP doesn't.

↑ Section 3.1
Q4

What are protocol data units (PDUs) called in TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) respectively?

Answer

In TCP the PDU is called a segment. In UDP it is also called a segment in the textbook (the RFCs (Request for Comments) call it a datagram — "user datagram").

↑ Section 3.1
Q5

What is a best-effort delivery service?

Answer

A service that tries its best to deliver packets but makes no guarantees: packets may be lost, corrupted, duplicated, delayed or delivered out of order, and there's no guarantee of bandwidth or delay. The network doesn't tell you when it fails. The Internet's IP (Internet Protocol) is best-effort.

↑ Section 3.1
Q6

What are the multiplexing and demultiplexing applications?

Answer

Multiplexing/demultiplexing lets many applications on one host use the network at the same time over a single IP (Internet Protocol) address — e.g., a browser with several tabs, an email client, Spotify and a Zoom call all running together. Every one of them relies on it; it's needed by every network application (Web, email, DNS (Domain Name System), streaming, games…). It's also how a server handles many clients on one port (e.g., one web server process talking to thousands of browsers).

↑ Section 3.1
Q7

Why is the IP (Internet Protocol) service model called best-effort delivery service?

Answer

Because IP makes its "best effort" to deliver each datagram from source host to destination host but makes no promises: no guarantee that datagrams arrive, arrive in order, or arrive intact, and no guarantees on delay or bandwidth. It doesn't reserve resources or keep per-connection state.

↑ Section 3.1
Q8

Why is IP (Internet Protocol) also called an unreliable service?

Answer

Because IP does not guarantee delivery: it has no acknowledgements, no retransmission and no sequencing. Datagrams can be dropped (full router buffers), corrupted, duplicated or reordered, and IP won't detect or fix it (the IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) header checksum only protects the header, and a bad datagram is just discarded).

↑ Section 3.1
Q9

How does TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provide reliable data transfer?

Answer

TCP builds reliability on top of unreliable IP (Internet Protocol) by combining:

  • Checksums to detect corrupted segments (which are discarded).

  • Sequence numbers on every byte, so the receiver can put data in order and detect duplicates or gaps.

  • Acknowledgements (cumulative ACKs) telling the sender what has arrived ("I've got everything up to byte n−1; send n next").

  • Retransmission timer — if an ACK doesn't arrive in time (timeout based on measured RTT (Round-Trip Time)), resend.

  • Fast retransmit — three duplicate ACKs mean a segment was probably lost; resend it right away without waiting for the timer.

  • Buffering and reordering at the receiver so the application gets an in-order byte stream.

  • Flow control so the receiver's buffer never overflows (which would cause loss).

↑ Section 3.1
Q10

What services do TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provide?

Answer

  • Connection-oriented service (three-way handshake to set up, orderly close).

  • Reliable, in-order byte-stream delivery — no loss, no duplication, correct order.

  • Full-duplex communication (both directions at once) between exactly two endpoints (point-to-point).

  • Flow control (sender won't overflow the receiver's buffer).

  • Congestion control (sender slows down when the network is congested).

  • Multiplexing/demultiplexing via ports and error detection via checksums.

↑ Section 3.1
Q11

What is multiplexing and demultiplexing respectively?

Answer

  • Multiplexing (at the sender): collecting data chunks from different sockets (processes), wrapping each with a transport header (including source and destination port numbers) to make segments, and passing them to the network layer.

  • Demultiplexing (at the receiver): examining the header fields of each arriving segment and delivering the data to the correct socket.

Analogy: in a house, one person collects everyone's outgoing letters (multiplexing) and hands out the incoming letters to the right family member by name (demultiplexing).

↑ Section 3.1
Q12

How are multiplexing and demultiplexing done in TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)?

Answer

A TCP socket is identified by a 4-tuple: (source IP (Internet Protocol) address, source port, destination IP address, destination port).

  • Multiplexing: each TCP segment sent carries its source and destination port numbers; IP adds the IP addresses.

  • Demultiplexing: when a segment arrives, the host uses all four values to find the matching connection socket. Two segments with the same destination port but different source IP or source port go to different sockets.

  • A server has a welcoming socket on a well-known port (e.g., 80). When a client connects, the server creates a new connection socket for that client's 4-tuple. So one server process handles many clients, each on its own socket, all with destination port 80.

↑ Section 3.1
Q13

What are sockets? How are sockets related to ports?

Answer

A socket is the interface (door) between an application process and the transport layer — the program writes data into it and reads data from it, and the operating system handles the rest. A socket is created by the application through the socket API (Application Programming Interface).

Relation to ports: each socket is bound to a port number on the host. For UDP (User Datagram Protocol) a socket is identified by its (IP (Internet Protocol) address, port); for TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) a connection socket is identified by the 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). The port is the address; the socket is the endpoint the program uses at that address.

↑ Section 3.1
Q14

What are some well-known port numbers?

Answer

Port numbers 0–1023 are well-known (reserved for standard services): FTP (File Transfer Protocol) 20/21, SSH (Secure Shell) 22, Telnet 23, SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) 25, DNS (Domain Name System) 53, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) 67/68, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) 80, POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) 110, NTP (Network Time Protocol) 123, IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) 143, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) 161/162, BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) 179, HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) 443, SMTP submission 587, IMAPS (Internet Message Access Protocol Secure) 993, POP3S (Post Office Protocol version 3 Secure) 995. (Registered: 1024–49151, e.g., RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) 3389, MySQL 3306; dynamic/ephemeral: 49152–65535.)

↑ Section 3.1
Q15

What are connectionless multiplexing/demultiplexing and connection-oriented multiplexing/demultiplexing, respectively? What are the differences?

Answer

  • Connectionless (UDP (User Datagram Protocol)) demultiplexing: a UDP socket is identified by just (destination IP (Internet Protocol), destination port). Every segment arriving for that port goes to the same socket, whatever its source. The source port and IP are carried only as a "return address".

  • Connection-oriented (TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)) demultiplexing: a TCP socket is identified by the 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). Segments with the same destination port but from different sources go to different sockets — one per connection.

Difference: UDP uses a 2-tuple and shares one socket among all senders; TCP uses a 4-tuple and gives each connection its own socket (created when the connection is accepted).

↑ Section 3.1
Q16

How are Web servers and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) related?

Answer

A web server (HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)/1.1, HTTP/2) runs on top of TCP, typically on port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure)). The server keeps a welcoming socket listening on port 80. Each browser opens a TCP connection; the server creates a separate connection socket for each (identified by the client's IP (Internet Protocol) and port), all with destination port 80. With non-persistent HTTP a new TCP connection (and socket) is created and closed for every object; with persistent HTTP one connection is reused. High-performance servers use threads or event loops to serve many sockets at once. TCP gives HTTP reliable, in-order delivery.

↑ Section 3.1

Section 3.2: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)

23 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20Q21Q22Q23

Also asked in: Assignment 2 Q1.1, Assignment 2 Q1.2, Assignment 2 Q2.1

Q1

How is a transport layer segment formatted? How is each of the fields created?

Answer

Every transport segment has a header and data. The common fields (both UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)) are the source port and destination port (16 bits each) and a checksum.

  • UDP segment (8-byte header): source port, destination port, length (header + data, in bytes), checksum, then application data.

  • TCP segment (20-byte header without options): source and destination ports, sequence number, acknowledgement number, header length, flags (SYN (Synchronize flag), ACK, FIN (Finish flag), RST (Reset flag), PSH (Push flag), URG (Urgent flag), ECE (ECN-Echo flag), CWR (Congestion Window Reduced flag)), receive window, checksum, urgent pointer, options, then data.

How the fields are created: the application writes data into the socket; the transport layer fills the source port from the sending socket and the destination port from the address the app gave; the length from the data size; sequence number from the byte count sent so far (starting at a random initial number agreed in the handshake); ACK number from the next byte expected from the other side; receive window from free buffer space; flags from the connection state; and finally computes the checksum over the segment (plus a pseudo-header of IP (Internet Protocol) addresses) with the checksum field set to zero.

↑ Section 3.2
Q2

Why is UDP (User Datagram Protocol) called a connectionless transport protocol?

Answer

Because there is no handshaking before data is sent — no connection is set up, no state is kept at sender or receiver, and each segment is handled independently. The sender just addresses a segment and sends it.

↑ Section 3.2
Q3

Why is TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) called a connection-oriented transport protocol?

Answer

Because before sending any data the two processes perform a three-way handshake to establish a connection: they agree on initial sequence numbers and set up buffers and state variables (sequence numbers, windows, timers) at both ends. The connection is then maintained until it's explicitly closed. (The connection exists only in the end systems, not in routers.)

↑ Section 3.2
Q4

What advantages does UDP (User Datagram Protocol) have over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)?

Answer

  • No connection setup delay — data can be sent immediately (good for DNS (Domain Name System): one RTT (Round-Trip Time)).

  • No connection state — a server can support many more clients.

  • Small header — 8 bytes vs TCP's 20+.

  • Finer application control over what is sent and when — no congestion control throttling and no retransmission delays, which suits real-time apps that prefer timeliness over perfection.

  • Supports broadcast/multicast, and lets apps build their own reliability (e.g., QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections)).

↑ Section 3.2
Q5

What transport protocols are used by the following application protocols: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), Telnet, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), FTP (File Transfer Protocol), NFS (Network File System), SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), RIP (Routing Information Protocol), and DNS (Domain Name System)?

Answer
Application protocol Transport
SMTP TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
Telnet TCP
HTTP TCP (HTTP/3: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) over UDP (User Datagram Protocol))
FTP TCP
NFS Traditionally UDP; modern versions (NFSv4 (Network File System version 4)) use TCP
SNMP UDP
RIP UDP (port 520)
DNS UDP normally (TCP for large replies and zone transfers)
↑ Section 3.2
Q6

How is a UDP (User Datagram Protocol) segment formatted?

Answer
|   Source port (16 bits)   |  Destination port (16 bits) |
|   Length (16 bits)        |  Checksum (16 bits)         |
|           Application data (message) ...                |

Header = 8 bytes. Length = header + data in bytes. Checksum covers the header, the data and a "pseudo-header" (IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, protocol, length).

↑ Section 3.2
Q7

What is checksum? How is checksum calculated in UDP (User Datagram Protocol)?

Answer

A checksum is a small value computed from the data so the receiver can detect whether bits were changed in transit.
