UDP's calculation: the sender treats the segment (plus pseudo-header) as a sequence of 16-bit words, adds them all using one's-complement arithmetic (any carry out of the top bit is wrapped around and added to the bottom bit), and then takes the one's complement (flips every bit) of the sum. That result goes in the checksum field. The receiver adds all the 16-bit words including the checksum; if the result is all 1s (1111111111111111), no error is detected; otherwise there's an error and the segment is discarded (or passed up with a warning). See "How the formulas work" above for a worked example.

↑ Section 3.2
Q8

What is reliable data transfer? What is unidirectional data transfer? What is bidirectional data transfer?

Answer

  • Reliable data transfer: delivering data so that no bits are corrupted, nothing is lost, nothing is duplicated, and everything arrives in the order sent — even though the channel underneath may corrupt or lose packets.

  • Unidirectional data transfer: data flows one way only, from sender to receiver (control messages like ACKs (Acknowledgement) still go back). The textbook's rdt protocols assume this for simplicity.

  • Bidirectional data transfer: both sides send data to each other at the same time (full duplex), as TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) does, each acting as sender and receiver.

↑ Section 3.2
Q9

What do the sender and the receiver need to do in order to achieve reliable data transfer over a perfectly reliable channel?

Answer

Nothing extra. Over a perfectly reliable channel (rdt1.0), the sender simply accepts data from above, puts it in a packet and sends it; the receiver simply receives the packet, extracts the data and delivers it up. No feedback, checksums or retransmissions are needed because nothing can go wrong. (Each side's state machine has one state.)

↑ Section 3.2
Q10

How could reliable data transfer be achieved over a channel with bit errors?

Answer

(rdt2.0 and its fixes) Three additions:

  • Error detection — a checksum so the receiver can tell if bits were flipped.

  • Receiver feedback — ACK (Acknowledgement) (received OK) or NAK (Negative Acknowledgement) (received with errors, please resend).

  • Retransmission — the sender resends a packet that was NAKed.

Because the ACK/NAK itself might be corrupted, add sequence numbers (0 and 1 alternate) so the receiver can tell a retransmitted duplicate from a new packet (rdt2.1). rdt2.2 removes NAKs by having the receiver ACK the last correctly received packet (a duplicate ACK then means "resend"). The sender waits for a response before sending the next packet (stop-and-wait).

↑ Section 3.2
Q11

How could reliable data transfer be achieved over a lossy channel with bit errors?

Answer

(rdt3.0) Use everything from rdt2.2 — checksum, sequence numbers, ACKs (Acknowledgement), retransmission — plus a countdown timer. After sending a packet the sender starts a timer. If no ACK arrives before the timer expires, it assumes the packet (or its ACK) was lost and retransmits. If the packet was merely delayed, the duplicate is recognised by its sequence number and discarded (and ACKed again). This is called the "alternating-bit protocol".

↑ Section 3.2
Q12

Protocol rdt3.0 is a stop-and-wait data transfer protocol with poor performance. What techniques can be used to improve its performance?

Answer

Pipelining: let the sender transmit several packets before waiting for ACKs (Acknowledgement) (a window of N unacknowledged packets), so the link isn't idle for an RTT (Round-Trip Time) after each packet. This needs:

  • a larger range of sequence numbers,

  • buffering at the sender (unACKed packets) and possibly at the receiver,

  • a pipelined error-recovery method: Go-Back-N or Selective Repeat.

With a window of N, utilisation rises roughly N-fold (see formula 2 above). Other helps: larger packets, and reducing RTT.

↑ Section 3.2
Q13

What are the two basic approaches to pipelined error recovery?

Answer

Go-Back-N (GBN) and Selective Repeat (SR).

↑ Section 3.2
Q14

What is the key feature of a Go-Back-N (GBN) protocol?

Answer

The sender may have up to N unacknowledged packets in the pipeline (a window of size N), and the receiver only accepts packets in order — it discards out-of-order packets and sends cumulative ACKs (Acknowledgement) (re-ACKing the last in-order packet). There is one timer for the oldest unACKed packet; on a timeout the sender "goes back N" — resends that packet and all later packets already sent.

↑ Section 3.2
Q15

Why is the GBN (Go-Back-N) protocol also called a sliding-window protocol?

Answer

Because the range of sequence numbers the sender is allowed to use — the window of size N — slides forward along the sequence-number space. When the oldest outstanding packet is acknowledged, the window's base moves forward and new packets can be sent. The picture is a window of fixed width sliding along the numbered packets.

↑ Section 3.2
Q16

What is the key feature of the selective repeat protocol? What problem is it intended to solve?

Answer

Key feature: the receiver individually acknowledges each correctly received packet and buffers out-of-order packets; the sender keeps a separate timer for each packet and retransmits only the packets that were lost or corrupted. Both sender and receiver have windows.

Problem it solves: GBN (Go-Back-N)'s wasteful retransmissions — with a large window and a long delay, one lost packet makes GBN resend the whole window, many of which arrived fine. SR (Selective Repeat) resends just the missing one. (Caveat: window must be ≤ half the sequence-number space.)

↑ Section 3.2
Q17

Why is TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) said to be point-to-point?

Answer

Because a TCP connection is always between exactly one sender and one receiver — two endpoints (two sockets). There is no multicast in TCP: you can't send one TCP stream to several receivers.

↑ Section 3.2
Q18

What is a three-way handshake?

Answer

The three-way handshake is how TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sets up a connection:

1. SYN (Synchronize flag): the client sends a segment with the SYN flag = 1 and its randomly chosen initial sequence number (client_isn). No data.

2. SYN-ACK: the server allocates buffers/variables and replies with SYN = 1, ACK = 1, acknowledgement number client_isn + 1, and its own initial sequence number (server_isn).

3. ACK: the client allocates its buffers and sends ACK = 1, acknowledgement server_isn + 1 (this segment may already carry data).

Now both sides agree on starting sequence numbers and the connection is established. It costs about one RTT (Round-Trip Time) before data flows.

↑ Section 3.2
Q19

What fields does a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) segment have, and what role is assigned to each?

Answer
Field Size Role
Source port / Destination port 16 bits each Multiplexing/demultiplexing — which processes
Sequence number 32 bits Number of the first byte of data in this segment (byte-stream numbering)
Acknowledgement number 32 bits Next byte expected from the other side (cumulative ACK (Acknowledgement))
Header length 4 bits Length of the TCP header in 32-bit words (options make it variable)
Flags 6+ bits SYN (Synchronize flag) (set up), ACK (ack number valid), FIN (Finish flag) (close), RST (Reset flag) (reset), PSH (Push flag) (push data up now), URG (Urgent flag) (urgent data), plus ECE (ECN-Echo flag)/CWR (Congestion Window Reduced flag) for congestion notification
Receive window 16 bits Flow control — how many bytes the receiver can still accept (rwnd)
Checksum 16 bits Error detection over header and data
Urgent data pointer 16 bits Where urgent data ends (rarely used)
Options variable MSS (Maximum Segment Size) negotiation, window scaling, timestamps, SACK (Selective Acknowledgement)
Data variable Application bytes
↑ Section 3.2
Q20

The Internet Protocol (IP) is an unreliable best-effort protocol, which runs under TCP (Transmission Control Protocol). How does TCP provide reliable data transfer service over the unreliable IP?

Answer

TCP builds its own reliability at the ends:

  • Checksum detects damaged segments; they're discarded (so damage becomes loss).

  • Sequence numbers (per byte) let the receiver reorder data, detect duplicates and spot gaps.

  • Cumulative ACKs (Acknowledgement) tell the sender what has arrived.

  • Retransmission on timeout — a single timer on the oldest unACKed segment, with an adaptive timeout (EstimatedRTT + 4·DevRTT); the timeout doubles after each expiry.

  • Fast retransmit — on 3 duplicate ACKs, resend the missing segment immediately.

  • Receiver buffering — out-of-order segments are held and delivered to the app in order.

  • Flow control prevents receiver buffer overflow; congestion control reduces loss inside the network.

Result: the application sees a byte stream that is complete, uncorrupted and in order.

↑ Section 3.2
Q21

Why does TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) need flow control?

Answer

Because the receiving application may read data from its buffer more slowly than the sender sends it. The receive buffer is finite; if the sender kept sending at full speed the buffer would overflow and data would be lost. Flow control makes the sender match its rate to the receiver's reading speed: the receiver advertises its free space (rwnd) in every segment, and the sender keeps unacknowledged data ≤ rwnd. (Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network.)

↑ Section 3.2
Q22

How is a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection managed?

Answer

  • Setting up: three-way handshake — SYN (Synchronize flag) → SYN-ACK (Acknowledgement) → ACK; initial sequence numbers exchanged; buffers and variables allocated.

  • Data transfer: full-duplex, with sequence numbers, ACKs, flow and congestion control.

  • Closing: either side sends a segment with FIN (Finish flag) = 1; the other side ACKs it, then sends its own FIN when it's done; the first side ACKs that. (Four segments; a side can close its sending direction while still receiving — "half-close".) The side that closes first waits in TIME_WAIT (typically 30 s–2 min, twice the maximum segment lifetime) before freeing resources, in case the final ACK was lost.

  • Abort: a RST (Reset flag) segment resets a connection immediately (also sent in reply to a SYN for a port with no listening socket).

↑ Section 3.2
Q23

What are the various TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) states?

Answer

TCP states (from RFC (Request for Comments) 793 / 9293):

  • CLOSED — no connection.

  • LISTEN — server waiting for a SYN (Synchronize flag).

  • SYN_SENT — client sent SYN, waiting for SYN-ACK (Acknowledgement).

  • SYN_RCVD — server got SYN, sent SYN-ACK, waiting for ACK.

  • ESTABLISHED — connection open; data flows.

  • FIN_WAIT_1 — this side sent FIN (Finish flag), waiting for its ACK.

  • FIN_WAIT_2 — FIN ACKed, waiting for the other side's FIN.

  • CLOSE_WAIT — received the other side's FIN, waiting for the local app to close.

  • LAST_ACK — sent own FIN after CLOSE_WAIT, waiting for its ACK.

  • CLOSING — both sides sent FIN simultaneously.

  • TIME_WAIT — waiting (2 × maximum segment lifetime) after the final ACK before CLOSED.

Client typical path: CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED. Server: CLOSED → LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED.

↑ Section 3.2

20 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20

Also asked in: Assignment 2 Q2.4

Q1

What is network congestion, and what are its causes?

Answer

Network congestion is when too many sources send too much data too fast for the network to handle — demand at some link or router exceeds its capacity. Symptoms: long queuing delays and lost packets (buffer overflow).

Causes:

  • Total arrival rate at a link approaching or exceeding the link's capacity (traffic intensity near or above 1).

  • Finite buffers — once full, packets are dropped.

  • Retransmissions (including unneeded ones from premature timeouts) adding extra load.

  • Multi-hop paths — a packet dropped at a later router wastes all the capacity used upstream to carry it.

  • Bursty traffic, slow routers (processing), and uncontrolled senders (e.g., UDP (User Datagram Protocol) floods).

↑ Section 3.3
Q2

What are the two approaches to congestion control?

Answer

  • End-to-end congestion control: the network gives no explicit help; end systems infer congestion from what they observe — packet loss (timeouts, duplicate ACKs (Acknowledgement)) and rising delay. Classic TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) uses this.

  • Network-assisted congestion control: routers give explicit feedback to senders — a single congestion bit, or an explicit rate the sender should use; sent directly (a choke packet) or by marking packets that the receiver echoes back. Examples: ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) ABR (Available Bit Rate), ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) in TCP/IP (Internet Protocol), DECbit.

↑ Section 3.3
Q3

How is network congestion controlled in an ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) ABR (Available Bit Rate) service?

Answer

ATM's ABR (Available Bit Rate) service uses network-assisted, rate-based control:

  • The sender interleaves special resource-management (RM) cells with data cells (about 1 RM cell per 32 data cells).

  • Switches along the path can set the EFCI (Explicit Forward Congestion Indication) bit in data cells (congestion indication), and set the CI (congestion indication) and NI (no increase) bits in RM cells, and lower the ER (explicit rate) field in RM cells to the rate they can support.

  • The destination turns RM cells around and sends them back to the sender, setting CI if it saw EFCI-marked cells.

  • The sender adjusts its rate: decrease if CI is set, don't increase if NI is set, and never exceed ER (the minimum rate supported by all switches on the path). ABR guarantees a minimum rate and lets sources use extra bandwidth when available.

↑ Section 3.3
Q4

How is network congestion controlled in TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)? Why does TCP use end-to-end congestion control rather than network-assistant congestion control?

Answer

TCP uses end-to-end congestion control:

  • Each sender keeps a congestion window (cwnd); unACKed data ≤ min(cwnd, rwnd), so rate ≈ cwnd/RTT (Round-Trip Time).

  • Loss = congestion signal: a timeout or 3 duplicate ACKs (Acknowledgement) means a packet was dropped somewhere.

  • AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease): increase cwnd by 1 MSS (Maximum Segment Size) per RTT while ACKs arrive (congestion avoidance); halve it on 3 duplicate ACKs; drop to 1 MSS on a timeout; slow start (doubling) at the beginning and after a timeout, up to ssthresh.

  • ACKs arriving "clock" new transmissions (self-clocking).

Why end-to-end: the IP (Internet Protocol) layer provides no explicit congestion feedback (routers were designed to be simple and stateless); TCP had to work over any network without changing routers; and loss is a reliable enough signal. It also follows the end-to-end principle of keeping the core simple. (Newer ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) adds optional network assistance.)

↑ Section 3.3
Q5

What are the principles for TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)?

Answer

TCP congestion control is guided by these principles:

  • A lost segment implies congestion, so the sender's rate should be decreased when a segment is lost.

  • An acknowledged segment means the network is delivering, so the sender's rate can be increased when ACKs (Acknowledgement) arrive for previously unacknowledged segments (ACKs "clock" the sending).

  • Bandwidth probing: keep increasing the rate while ACKs arrive, back off when loss occurs, then probe again — hence the sawtooth.

  • Each sender acts on local information only (decentralised), yet all together they share the network fairly (AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease)).

↑ Section 3.3
Q6

What is per-connection throughput?

Answer

Per-connection throughput is the rate at which data is actually delivered to the receiving application over one connection (bits per second per connection) — excluding retransmitted duplicates ("goodput"). For example, with N equal TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections on a bottleneck of rate R, each ideally gets R/N. In congestion analysis it's plotted against offered load to show how congestion limits useful throughput.

↑ Section 3.3
Q7

What is offered load to network?

Answer

Offered load (λ'in) is the total rate at which the transport layer sends segments into the network, including original data plus retransmissions — as opposed to λin, the rate of original application data. When retransmissions increase, offered load rises even though no new useful data is being sent.

↑ Section 3.3
Q8

What approaches to congestion control are used in TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)?

Answer

  • End-to-end (loss-based) congestion control — classic TCP (Tahoe, Reno, NewReno, CUBIC).

  • Slow start, congestion avoidance (AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease)) and fast recovery / fast retransmit.

  • Delay-based congestion control (TCP Vegas, and BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time) which models bottleneck bandwidth and RTT (Round-Trip Time)).

  • Network-assisted via ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification): routers mark the IP (Internet Protocol) header; the receiver echoes ECE (ECN-Echo flag); the sender reduces cwnd and replies CWR (Congestion Window Reduced flag).

↑ Section 3.3
Q9

How is ABR (available bit rate) approach used for congestion control in ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) networks?

Answer

(Same mechanism as Q3.) ABR is rate-based and network-assisted: sources send RM (Resource Management) cells among data cells; switches report congestion using the EFCI (Explicit Forward Congestion Indication) bit in data cells, the CI/NI (No Increase) bits in RM cells, and by writing the maximum supportable explicit rate (ER) into RM cells; the destination returns RM cells to the source; the source increases its rate when there's no congestion (up to ER), holds it when NI is set, and decreases it when CI is set. The result is an "elastic" service with a guaranteed minimum cell rate plus a share of spare capacity.

↑ Section 3.3
Q10

What is a choked packet?

Answer

A choke packet (the textbook's term; "choked packet" in the question) is a special control packet that a congested router sends directly back to a source telling it that it is congested and should reduce its sending rate. It's a form of network-assisted congestion control (e.g., the old ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Source Quench message, now deprecated). The alternative is to mark a data packet passing through, and the receiver informs the sender (as in ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification)).

↑ Section 3.3
Q11

How does a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sender coordinate its sending bit rate for congestion control?

Answer

The TCP sender limits unacknowledged data in flight to min(cwnd, rwnd), so its sending rate is about cwnd / RTT (Round-Trip Time). It adjusts cwnd from the feedback it gets:

  • ACKs (Acknowledgement) arriving → increase cwnd (doubling per RTT in slow start; +1 MSS (Maximum Segment Size) per RTT in congestion avoidance). Because new segments are sent as ACKs return, the rate is self-clocking: fast ACKs → fast sending.

  • Loss indication (3 duplicate ACKs, or a timeout) → decrease cwnd (halve, or back to 1 MSS).

  • ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) marks → decrease as if there were a loss.

This way it probes for available bandwidth and backs off when congestion appears.

↑ Section 3.3
Q12

What is the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) slow start state?

Answer

Slow start is the state a TCP connection starts in (and returns to after a timeout). cwnd begins at 1 MSS (Maximum Segment Size) (in practice often 10 MSS) and increases by 1 MSS for every ACK (Acknowledgement) received, which doubles cwnd every RTT (Round-Trip Time) — exponential growth. It ends when: (a) a timeout occurs → ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = 1, restart slow start; (b) cwnd reaches ssthresh → switch to congestion avoidance; (c) 3 duplicate ACKs → fast retransmit and fast recovery.

↑ Section 3.3
Q13

What is congestion avoidance? How does it work?

Answer

Congestion avoidance is the state TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) enters when cwnd reaches ssthresh — near the point where congestion was last seen — so it grows cautiously: cwnd increases by about 1 MSS (Maximum Segment Size) per RTT (Round-Trip Time) (implemented as MSS × MSS/cwnd for each ACK (Acknowledgement)). This is the additive increase. On 3 duplicate ACKs: ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = ssthresh + 3 MSS, go to fast recovery. On a timeout: ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = 1 MSS, go to slow start.

↑ Section 3.3
Q14

How does TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) achieve fast recovery from missing segments?

Answer

With fast retransmit + fast recovery:

  • When the sender gets 3 duplicate ACKs (Acknowledgement) for the same data, it assumes the next segment was lost (but later segments are getting through, so congestion is mild) and retransmits the missing segment immediately, without waiting for the timer (fast retransmit).

  • It sets ssthresh = cwnd/2 and cwnd = ssthresh + 3 MSS (Maximum Segment Size) (the 3 accounts for the segments that left the network), and enters fast recovery: cwnd grows by 1 MSS for each further duplicate ACK, letting new segments keep flowing.

  • When the ACK for the missing segment arrives, cwnd is set to ssthresh and TCP continues in congestion avoidance — it doesn't drop to 1 and slow-start.

↑ Section 3.3
Q15

What are TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) Tahoe and TCP Reno, respectively?

Answer

  • TCP Tahoe (1988, Van Jacobson): slow start, congestion avoidance and fast retransmit. On any loss — timeout or 3 duplicate ACKs (Acknowledgement) — it sets ssthresh = cwnd/2 and cwnd = 1 MSS (Maximum Segment Size), then slow-starts.

  • TCP Reno (1990): adds fast recovery. On 3 duplicate ACKs it halves cwnd (ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = ssthresh + 3) and continues in congestion avoidance; only on a timeout does it drop to 1 MSS. Reno therefore recovers much faster from occasional losses — it produces the classic sawtooth. (NewReno improves handling of multiple losses in one window.)

↑ Section 3.3
Q16

Why is TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) congestion control referred to as an additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease (AIMD)?

Answer

Because, ignoring slow start, TCP increases cwnd additively — by a fixed amount, 1 MSS (Maximum Segment Size) per RTT (Round-Trip Time) — while no loss occurs, and decreases it multiplicatively — cutting it in half (multiplying by 0.5) — whenever a loss (triple duplicate ACK (Acknowledgement)) is detected. The result is the "sawtooth" pattern of window size over time. AIMD is what makes competing TCP flows converge to a fair share.

↑ Section 3.3
Q17

How is TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) throughput measured?

Answer

  • Instantaneous rate: ≈ cwnd / RTT (Round-Trip Time).

  • Average throughput in steady state (ignoring slow start and timeouts), where W is the window when loss occurs: the window swings between W/2 and W, so average throughput ≈ 0.75 × W / RTT (× MSS (Maximum Segment Size) for bytes).

  • In terms of the loss rate L: throughput ≈ 1.22 × MSS / (RTT × √L).

  • Measured in practice by dividing bytes delivered by elapsed time (e.g., with tools like iperf).

See the worked examples above.

↑ Section 3.3
Q18

What is so-called fairness for TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections, especially when they share a single link? How is fairness achieved?

Answer

Fairness: if K TCP connections share one bottleneck link of rate R, each should get about R/K — an equal share.

How it's achieved: AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease). Picture two connections: when the total rate is below R, both increase by the same amount (moving toward the equal-share line at 45°); when loss occurs, both halve their windows — the one with the larger share loses more in absolute terms. Repeated additive increases and multiplicative decreases pull the two rates toward equal shares. (In practice fairness holds only approximately: connections with shorter RTTs (Round-Trip Time) grow faster and get more bandwidth.)

↑ Section 3.3
Q19

How is fairness achieved in UDP (User Datagram Protocol)?

Answer

It isn't — UDP has no congestion control. UDP applications (e.g., video conferencing, some streaming) send at whatever rate they choose, don't back off when the network is congested, and can crowd out TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) flows. Fairness for UDP can only come from outside: the application implementing its own TCP-friendly congestion control (e.g., DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol), TFRC (TCP-Friendly Rate Control), QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections)'s congestion control, WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication)'s rate adaptation), or network mechanisms such as router fair-queuing/policing that limit flows that don't respond.

↑ Section 3.3
Q20

How is fairness achieved in parallel TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections?

Answer

It isn't fully achieved. An application can open several parallel TCP connections (like web browsers or download accelerators), and since TCP shares bandwidth per connection, that application gets more than its fair share. Example: a link of rate R with 9 existing connections; a new app opening 1 connection gets R/10, but opening 11 connections gets 11/20 — more than R/2. Fairness among applications would require per-application or per-host limits (e.g., browsers limiting to ~6 connections per server, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)/2 using one connection, or router fair queuing per host).

↑ Section 3.3

Textbook Review Questions — Chapter 3

19 questions (Kurose & Ross, 8th edition)

R1R2R3R4R5R6R7R8R9R10R11R12R13R14R15R16R17R18R19
R1

Suppose the network layer provides the following service. The network layer in the source host accepts a segment of maximum size 1,200 bytes and a destination host address from the transport layer. The network layer then guarantees to deliver the segment to the transport layer at the destination host. Suppose many network application processes can be running at the destination host.

a. Design the simplest possible transport-layer protocol that will get application data to the desired process at the destination host. Assume the operating system in the destination host has assigned a 4-byte port number to each running application process.

b. Modify this protocol so that it provides a “return address” to the destination process.

c. In your protocols, does the transport layer “have to do anything” in the core of the computer network?

Answer

a. Call it Simple Transport Protocol (STP). Sender side: take up to 1,196 bytes of application data plus the destination process's 4-byte port number; build a segment = [4-byte destination port | data]; hand the segment and the destination host address to the network layer. Receiver side: when the network layer delivers a segment, read the 4-byte port number and pass the data to the process with that port.

b. Add a 4-byte source port field (the sending process's port): segment = [source port | destination port | data] (data ≤ 1,192 bytes). The network layer at the receiver also passes up the source host's address, so the destination process learns both the sending host and the sending process — a "return address" to reply to.

c. No. The transport layer does nothing in the network core; it runs only in the end systems.

↑ Chapter 3 review
R2

Consider a planet where everyone belongs to a family of six, every family lives in its own house, each house has a unique address, and each person in a given house has a unique name. Suppose this planet has a mail service that delivers letters from source house to destination house. The mail service requires that (1) the letter be in an envelope, and that (2) the address of the destination house (and nothing more) be clearly written on the envelope. Suppose each family has a delegate family member who collects and distributes letters for the other family members. The letters do not necessarily provide any indication of the recipients of the letters.

a. Using the solution to Problem R1 above as inspiration, describe a protocol that the delegates can use to deliver letters from a sending family member to a receiving family member.

b. In your protocol, does the mail service ever have to open the envelope and examine the letter in order to provide its service?

Answer

a. Sending: a family member gives the delegate the letter together with the destination house address and the recipient's name. The delegate writes the recipient's name on the letter (or on a label inside/on top of the letter) and puts the letter in an envelope with only the destination house address on the outside, then gives it to the mail service. Receiving: the delegate at the destination house opens the envelope, reads the name on the letter, and hands it to that family member. (Adding the sender's name too gives a return address.)

b. No. The mail service only reads the house address on the envelope; it never opens it. (Just as the network layer never looks inside the segment.)

↑ Chapter 3 review
R3

Consider a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection between Host A and Host B. Suppose that the TCP segments traveling from Host A to Host B have source port number x and destination port number y. What are the source and destination port numbers for the segments traveling from Host B to Host A?

Answer

Source port y, destination port x. (The roles swap for the reply direction.)

↑ Chapter 3 review
R4

Describe why an application developer might choose to run an application over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) rather than TCP (Transmission Control Protocol).

Answer

  • An app may not want TCP's congestion control, which can slow it down when the network is congested — real-time apps (voice, video calls) prefer a steady rate and can tolerate some loss.

  • No connection setup delay (fast one-shot queries such as DNS (Domain Name System)).

  • No connection state — the server can handle more clients.

  • Smaller header (8 vs 20 bytes).

  • The app wants full control over what is sent and when (it may do its own reliability, as QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) does).

↑ Chapter 3 review
R5

Why is it that voice and video traffic is often sent over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) rather than UDP (User Datagram Protocol) in today’s Internet? (Hint: The answer we are looking for has nothing to do with TCP’s congestion-control mechanism.)

Answer

Because many firewalls and NATs (Network Address Translation) block UDP traffic, so running over TCP (usually HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) on port 80/443) gets through to almost every user. TCP-based HTTP streaming also works with ordinary web servers, caches and CDNs (Content Distribution Network); buffering hides TCP's delays.

↑ Chapter 3 review
R6

Is it possible for an application to enjoy reliable data transfer even when the application runs over UDP (User Datagram Protocol)? If so, how?

Answer

Yes. The application itself can build reliability into the application layer — adding sequence numbers, acknowledgements, timers and retransmission (the rdt mechanisms) on top of UDP. Example: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) (HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)/3) does exactly this; so do TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) and some games. It's more work for the developer, and it must be careful not to ignore congestion.

↑ Chapter 3 review
R7

Suppose a process in Host C has a UDP (User Datagram Protocol) socket with port number 6789. Suppose both Host A and Host B each send a UDP segment to Host C with destination port number 6789. Will both of these segments be directed to the same socket at Host C? If so, how will the process at Host C know that these two segments originated from two different hosts?

Answer

Yes, both segments go to the same socket, because a UDP socket is identified only by the destination IP (Internet Protocol) address and destination port. The process tells them apart because the operating system passes up the source IP address and source port of each segment along with the data (e.g., recvfrom() returns the sender's address), so the process knows they came from Host A and Host B.

↑ Chapter 3 review
R8

Suppose that a Web server runs in Host C on port 80. Suppose this Web server uses persistent connections, and is currently receiving requests from two different Hosts, A and B. Are all of the requests being sent through the same socket at Host C? If they are being passed through different sockets, do both of the sockets have port 80? Discuss and explain.

Answer

No, they're sent through different sockets at Host C. For each persistent connection, the server has a separate connection socket, identified by the 4-tuple (source IP (Internet Protocol), source port, destination IP, destination port). A's requests and B's requests have different source IPs (and ports), so they are demultiplexed to different sockets. Yes, both sockets have port 80 as their local (destination) port number — the socket identity includes the client's IP and port, which is what makes them different.

↑ Chapter 3 review
R9

In our rdt protocols, why did we need to introduce sequence numbers?

Answer

To let the receiver tell whether an arriving packet is new data or a retransmission (duplicate). When an ACK (Acknowledgement) or NAK (Negative Acknowledgement) is corrupted, the sender can't know if the packet got through, so it resends; without sequence numbers the receiver couldn't recognise the duplicate and would deliver the same data twice. (With pipelining, sequence numbers also let the receiver detect gaps and reorder.)

↑ Chapter 3 review
R10

In our rdt protocols, why did we need to introduce timers?

Answer

To handle lost packets (data or ACKs (Acknowledgement)). If a packet or its ACK is lost, the sender would wait forever. A timer lets the sender wait a reasonable time and then retransmit if no ACK has arrived.

↑ Chapter 3 review
R11

Suppose that the roundtrip delay between sender and receiver is constant and known to the sender. Would a timer still be necessary in protocol rdt 3.0, assuming that packets can be lost? Explain.

Answer

Yes, a timer is still needed. Knowing the RTT (Round-Trip Time) tells the sender how long to wait, but the sender still needs a timer to measure that wait: if the ACK (Acknowledgement) hasn't come back within the known RTT, the packet (or ACK) must have been lost and should be retransmitted. The only benefit of knowing the RTT exactly is that the timeout can be set tightly (just over one RTT) and a missing ACK can be concluded with certainty.

↑ Chapter 3 review
R12

Visit the Go-Back-N interactive animation at the companion Web site.

a. Have the source send five packets, and then pause the animation before any of the five packets reach the destination. Then kill the first packet and resume the animation. Describe what happens.

b. Repeat the experiment, but now let the first packet reach the destination and kill the first acknowledgment. Describe again what happens.

c. Finally, try sending six packets. What happens?

Answer

(From the Go-Back-N animation.)

a. The first packet is lost, so packets 2–5 arrive out of order. The GBN receiver discards them and keeps re-sending an ACK (Acknowledgement) for the last in-order packet (none yet). When the sender's timer for packet 1 expires, it resends packets 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 ("go back N").

b. Packet 1 arrives and is delivered, but its ACK is lost. Packets 2–5 arrive in order, and the receiver sends ACKs 2–5. Because GBN ACKs are cumulative, ACK 2 (or later) confirms packet 1 too, so the sender doesn't retransmit anything — assuming a later ACK arrives before packet 1's timer expires.

c. The window size in the animation is 5, so the sender can only have 5 unacknowledged packets outstanding; the sixth packet must wait until the first packet's ACK arrives and the window slides forward.

↑ Chapter 3 review
R13

Repeat R12, but now with the Selective Repeat interactive animation. How are Selective Repeat and Go-Back-N different?

Answer

(Selective Repeat animation.)

a. Packet 1 is lost; packets 2–5 arrive, are buffered by the receiver and each individually ACKed. When packet 1's timer expires, the sender resends only packet 1. When it arrives, the receiver delivers packets 1–5 in order.

b. Packet 1's ACK (Acknowledgement) is lost; ACKs 2–5 arrive. SR (Selective Repeat) ACKs are not cumulative, so the sender doesn't know packet 1 arrived; packet 1's timer expires and packet 1 is resent. The receiver recognises the duplicate, discards it and re-ACKs it.

c. As with GBN (Go-Back-N), with a window of 5 the sixth packet can't be sent until the window base (packet 1) is acknowledged.

Differences: SR retransmits only the lost packets, keeps a timer per packet, sends individual ACKs, and the receiver buffers out-of-order packets. GBN retransmits the lost packet and everything after it, uses one timer and cumulative ACKs, and the receiver discards out-of-order packets.

↑ Chapter 3 review
R14

True or false?

Answer

a. Host A is sending Host B a large file over a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection. Assume Host B has no data to send Host A. Host B will not send acknowledgments to Host A because Host B cannot piggyback the acknowledgments on data.

b. The size of the TCP rwnd never changes throughout the duration of the connection.

c. Suppose Host A is sending Host B a large file over a TCP connection. The number of unacknowledged bytes that A sends cannot exceed the size of the receive buffer.

d. Suppose Host A is sending a large file to Host B over a TCP connection. If the sequence number for a segment of this connection is m, then the sequence number for the subsequent segment will necessarily be m + 1.

e. The TCP segment has a field in its header for rwnd.

f. Suppose that the last SampleRTT in a TCP connection is equal to 1 sec. The current value of TimeoutInterval for the connection will necessarily be ≥ 1 sec.

g. Suppose Host A sends one segment with sequence number 38 and 4 bytes of data over a TCP connection to Host B. In this same segment, the acknowledgment number is necessarily 42.

  • a. False. B still sends ACKs (Acknowledgement) to A (in segments with no data); piggybacking is an optimisation, not a requirement.

  • b. False. rwnd changes throughout the connection as the receive buffer fills and empties.

  • c. True. A may never have more unacknowledged bytes than rwnd, which is at most the receive buffer size.

  • d. False. Sequence numbers count bytes, not segments; the next segment's number is m + (number of data bytes in this segment).

  • e. True. The TCP header has a 16-bit receive-window field.

  • f. False. TimeoutInterval = EstimatedRTT + 4·DevRTT depends on the whole history; one sample of 1 s doesn't force it to be ≥ 1 s (EstimatedRTT could be much smaller).

  • g. False. The acknowledgement number in that segment refers to data A has received from B, which has nothing to do with A's own sequence number 38 plus 4 bytes. (42 would be the ACK number B sends back.)

↑ Chapter 3 review
R15

Suppose Host A sends two TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) segments back to back to Host B over a TCP connection. The first segment has sequence number 90; the second has sequence number 110.

a. How much data is in the first segment?

b. Suppose that the first segment is lost but the second segment arrives at B. In the acknowledgment that Host B sends to Host A, what will be the acknowledgment number?

Answer

a. The second segment starts at byte 110, so the first carries 110 − 90 = 20 bytes.

b. B is still waiting for byte 90 (the first segment's data is missing), so the acknowledgement number is 90 (a cumulative ACK — "I still need byte 90").

↑ Chapter 3 review
R16

Consider the Telnet example discussed in Section 3.5. A few seconds after the user types the letter ‘C,’ the user types the letter ‘R.’ After typing the letter ‘R,’ how many segments are sent, and what is put in the sequence number and acknowledgment fields of the segments?

Answer

Three segments are sent (same pattern as for 'C'):

1. Client → server: the letter 'R' — seq = 43, ACK (Acknowledgement) = 80.

2. Server → client: echo of 'R' — seq = 80, ACK = 44.

3. Client → server: ACK of the echo — seq = 44, ACK = 81.

(Following the textbook's example, where the 'C' exchange used seq 42/79 and ACK 79/43/80.)

↑ Chapter 3 review
R17

Suppose two TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections are present over some bottleneck link of rate R bps. Both connections have a huge file to send (in the same direction over the bottleneck link). The transmissions of the files start at the same time. What transmission rate would TCP like to give to each of the connections?

Answer

TCP aims to give each connection an equal share: R/2 bps each.

↑ Chapter 3 review
R18

True or false? Consider congestion control in TCP (Transmission Control Protocol). When the timer expires at the sender, the value of ssthresh is set to one half of its previous value.

Answer

False. On a timeout, ssthresh is set to half of the current congestion window (cwnd) — not half of the previous ssthresh value (and cwnd is set to 1 MSS (Maximum Segment Size)).

↑ Chapter 3 review
R19

In the discussion of TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) splitting in the sidebar in Section 3.7, it was claimed that the response time with TCP splitting is approximately 4 × RTT_FE + RTT_BE + processing time. Justify this claim.

Answer

With TCP splitting, the client connects to a nearby front-end (FE) server, and the FE keeps a persistent connection to the back-end (BE) data centre.

  • 1 RTT_FE for the TCP handshake with the front end.

  • 1 RTT_FE for the client to send the request to the FE (and start the response).

  • The FE forwards the request over its already-open connection to the BE: 1 RTT_BE for request and response (plus BE processing time). No handshake needed there.

  • The response comes back to the client over the client–FE connection; with slow start (small initial window), delivering the response takes about 2 more RTT_FE (the window grows over a couple of round trips).

Total ≈ 4 × RTT_FE + RTT_BE + processing time. Because RTT_FE is small (the FE is close), this is much less than doing everything end to end over a long RTT (Round-Trip Time): without splitting it would be about 4 × RTT (full end-to-end RTT) + processing.

↑ Chapter 3 review

Unit 4: The Network Layer: Data Plane

4.1 Introduction to the Network Layer4.2 Routers4.3 The Internet Protocol (IP): IPv4, Addressing, IPv6, and More4.4 Generalized Forwarding, SDN and MiddleboxesTextbook review questions — Chapter 4

Section 4.1: Introduction to the Network Layer

27 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20Q21Q22Q23Q24Q25Q26Q27
Q1

What services are provided by network layer protocols?

Answer

The network layer's services:

  • Host-to-host delivery of datagrams across multiple networks — every host and router takes part.

  • Addressing — globally unique IP (Internet Protocol) addresses.

  • Forwarding — moving each packet from a router's input to the correct output.

  • Routing — determining the paths packets take from source to destination.

  • Encapsulation/decapsulation of transport segments into datagrams, and fragmentation when needed.

  • Other things a network layer could offer (the Internet's IP does not): guaranteed delivery, bounded delay, in-order delivery, minimum bandwidth, security.

The Internet's IP offers a best-effort service.

↑ Section 4.1
Q2

What are the two important network-layer functions?

Answer

Forwarding and routing.

↑ Section 4.1
Q3

What does forwarding do for a router?

Answer

Forwarding is the router-local action of moving an arriving packet from the input link to the appropriate output link. The router reads the packet's header (destination address), looks it up in its forwarding table, and switches the packet to that output port. It may also drop the packet (e.g., if blocked or buffers are full) or copy it to several ports. It takes nanoseconds and is done in hardware (the data plane).

↑ Section 4.1
Q4

What does routing do for an interconnected network?

Answer

Routing is the network-wide process that determines the end-to-end paths packets take from source to destination. Routing algorithms (e.g., link-state/Dijkstra, distance-vector, BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)) compute the best paths and fill in the forwarding tables of all routers. It works on a timescale of seconds and is usually done in software (the control plane).

↑ Section 4.1
Q5

For packets to be transported from a sending host to a receiving host, what important functions must be performed at the network layer?

Answer

Two main functions: forwarding (at each router, move the packet to the right output link) and routing (compute the paths so forwarding tables are correct). Also: addressing so each host can be identified, encapsulation of segments into datagrams with source/destination addresses, and (in some networks) connection setup for virtual circuits. The packet is then forwarded hop by hop until it reaches the destination host, where the network layer passes the segment up to transport.

↑ Section 4.1
Q6

What is a network-service model?

Answer

A network service model defines the characteristics of end-to-end delivery of packets between sending and receiving hosts — what the network promises. Possible services: guaranteed delivery; guaranteed delivery with bounded delay; in-order delivery; guaranteed minimal bandwidth; security (encryption). The Internet's model is best effort (none of these guaranteed); ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) offered CBR (Constant Bit Rate), VBR (Variable Bit Rate), ABR (Available Bit Rate) and UBR (Unspecified Bit Rate).

↑ Section 4.1
Q7

What are virtual circuits?

Answer

A virtual circuit (VC) is a logical connection set up through the network before data is sent. It consists of (1) a path (series of links and routers) between source and destination, (2) VC numbers, one per link along the path, and (3) entries in the forwarding table of each router on the path. Every packet carries a VC number (not a full destination address); each router looks it up, replaces it with the next link's VC number and forwards it. Routers keep state for each VC. Used in ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode), X.25, frame relay (and MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) is similar).

↑ Section 4.1
Q8

What is the virtual-circuit network service model?

Answer

In the virtual-circuit model, the network provides a connection-oriented service at the network layer: the path is set up in advance and all packets of the connection follow the same path, in order, with routers maintaining per-connection state. Because the network knows about each connection, it can reserve resources (bandwidth, buffers) and give guaranteed services (e.g., constant bit rate, delay bounds). The downside is setup delay, complexity and state in every router.

↑ Section 4.1
Q9

What are the three identifiable phases in a virtual circuit?

Answer

1. VC (Virtual Circuit) setup: the sender contacts the network layer with the receiver's address; the network determines the path, assigns VC numbers for each link, adds entries to each router's forwarding table, and may reserve resources.

2. Data transfer: packets flow along the established VC.

3. VC teardown: when either side ends the call, the network informs the other end and removes the forwarding-table entries (and releases resources) at each router.

↑ Section 4.1
Q10

What is the datagram network service model?

Answer

In the datagram model, there's no connection setup at the network layer. Each packet (datagram) carries the full destination address, and each router forwards it independently using its forwarding table (longest prefix match). Routers keep no per-connection state, packets of the same flow may take different routes and arrive out of order, and there are no guarantees (best effort). The Internet uses this model.

↑ Section 4.1
Q11

What is the constant bit rate (CBR) network service model for ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) networks?

Answer

CBR (Constant Bit Rate) was ATM's first service model, meant to emulate a dedicated circuit (like a telephone line): the flow gets a guaranteed constant rate, and cells are delivered in order with bounded delay, bounded jitter and a guaranteed (small) loss rate. It suits real-time constant-rate traffic like voice and uncompressed video.

↑ Section 4.1
Q12

What is the unspecified bit rate (UBR) network service model for ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) networks?

Answer

UBR (Unspecified Bit Rate) is ATM's best-effort service — like the Internet's: no guarantees of bandwidth, loss, delay or jitter (cells are delivered in order, though). It uses whatever capacity is left over and is suitable for non-critical data such as email and file transfer.

↑ Section 4.1
Q13

What is the variable bit rate (VBR) network service model for ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) networks?

Answer

VBR (Variable Bit Rate) is for traffic whose rate varies over time (e.g., compressed video). The source declares traffic parameters (peak rate, sustained/average rate, maximum burst size) and the network guarantees service within those limits. rt-VBR (real-time) also bounds delay and jitter — for compressed interactive video; nrt-VBR (non-real-time) guarantees low loss but not delay — for bursty data like airline reservation transactions.

↑ Section 4.1
Q14

What are the origins of the datagram and virtual-circuit service models?

Answer

  • Virtual circuits came from the telephone world, where end devices (phones) were "dumb" and the network was complex and connection-oriented; telephone companies carried that idea into X.25, frame relay and ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode), aiming to provide guaranteed service.

  • Datagrams came from the computer/ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network) world, where end devices were powerful computers that could handle reliability and control themselves. The Internet designers kept the network core simple (best effort, no state), putting complexity at the edges (TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), applications). This made it easy to connect many different networks and to deploy new applications.

↑ Section 4.1
Q15

What functions does an input port on a router perform?

Answer

An input port performs:

  • Physical layer termination — receiving the bits from the incoming link.

  • Link-layer processing — decapsulating the frame and error checking (e.g., Ethernet).

  • Lookup and forwarding — using the destination address and the (shadow copy of the) forwarding table to find the output port (longest prefix match), done at "line speed".

  • Other: checking version/checksum, updating TTL (Time-to-Live), collecting statistics, and queuing packets if the switching fabric is busy.

  • Passing control packets (e.g., routing protocol messages) up to the routing processor.

↑ Section 4.1
Q16

In detail, what does the switching fabric do in a router?

Answer

The switching fabric connects the router's input ports to its output ports — it's the network inside the router. It transfers each packet from the input port where it arrived to the output port chosen by the lookup. Its speed determines how fast the whole router can move packets; if it's slower than the combined input rates, packets queue at the input ports. Three kinds: via memory, via a bus, and via an interconnection network (crossbar). Faster fabrics can move several packets in parallel.

↑ Section 4.1
Q17

How does switching via memory work?

Answer

The oldest method: the router is like a computer. An arriving packet raises an interrupt; the routing processor copies it into memory, looks up the output port, then copies it from memory to the output port's buffer. Because every packet crosses the memory bus twice (write then read), with memory bandwidth B the forwarding rate is at most B/2 packets per unit time, and only one packet can be switched at a time. (Modern memory-switched routers have lookup and storage on the line cards, like shared-memory multiprocessors.)

↑ Section 4.1
Q18

How does switching via a bus work?

Answer

The input port sends the packet directly to the output ports over a shared bus, without the routing processor copying it. The input port adds an internal label/header saying which output port it wants; all output ports receive the packet, but only the one matching the label keeps it (the label is then removed). Only one packet can cross the bus at a time, so the switching speed is limited by the bus speed; other packets wait at their input ports.

↑ Section 4.1
Q19

How does stitching via an interconnection network work?

Answer

(The question says "stitching" — it means switching via an interconnection network.) A crossbar switch has 2N buses connecting N input ports to N output ports, in a grid. Each vertical bus meets each horizontal bus at a crosspoint that the fabric controller can open or close. To send a packet from input A to output Y, the controller closes the crosspoint between A's bus and Y's bus. Multiple packets can cross in parallel, as long as they're going to different output ports (it's "non-blocking" in that sense). Packets for the same output must wait. More complex multi-stage networks (e.g., Clos networks, used in Cisco CRS) combine many small switches and can even spread one packet over several paths.

↑ Section 4.1
Q20

What does an output port on a router do?

Answer

An output port: takes packets from the switching fabric, stores them in its buffer/queue, uses a scheduling discipline (FIFO (First In, First Out), priority, round robin, WFQ (Weighted Fair Queuing)) to choose which packet to send next, and performs link-layer (frame encapsulation) and physical-layer functions to transmit the packet onto the outgoing link. It may also drop or mark packets when the buffer is full (packet loss, active queue management).

↑ Section 4.1
Q21

What does the router processor do for a router?

Answer

The routing processor carries out the control-plane functions:

  • In a traditional router: runs the routing protocols (OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)), maintains the routing tables and link-state information, and computes the forwarding table, which it installs into the input ports.

  • In an SDN (Software-Defined Networking) router: communicates with the remote controller, receiving forwarding-table entries and installing them.

  • It also performs network management functions (SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), configuration, logging).

↑ Section 4.1
Q22

What is an SDN (Software-Defined Networking) router?

Answer

An SDN (Software-Defined Networking) router (or switch) is a forwarding device whose control plane is removed from the box: it contains only the data plane (flow tables that match header fields and perform actions) plus a small agent that talks to a remote, logically centralised SDN controller (e.g., via OpenFlow). The controller computes the forwarding rules and installs them in the device. The device is therefore simpler and programmable, and network behaviour is controlled in software.

↑ Section 4.1
Q23

Destination-based forwarding is easy to understand. What is the rationale for generalized forwarding on a router?

Answer

Destination-based forwarding looks only at one field (the destination IP (Internet Protocol) address) and does only one thing (send it out a port). Many modern needs require more: firewalls (block by port or source), load balancing (spread flows across paths or servers), NAT (Network Address Translation) (rewrite addresses), traffic engineering and quality of service (treat flows differently), network virtualisation and slicing. Generalized forwarding ("match plus action") lets a device match on many header fields at several layers and take various actions (forward, drop, modify, copy, send to controller), so one kind of programmable device (e.g., an OpenFlow switch) can act as a router, switch, firewall, NAT or load balancer.

↑ Section 4.1
Q24

What critical questions do router and switch designers face?

Answer

  • Speed: how to do lookups and switching at line rate (billions of packets per second — nanoseconds per packet)?

  • Lookup: how to find the longest prefix match quickly (special memory like TCAM (Ternary Content-Addressable Memory))?

  • Switching fabric: which fabric design to use so it doesn't become the bottleneck?

  • Buffering: how much buffer to provide (too little → loss; too much → bufferbloat)?

  • Scheduling: which packet to send next (FIFO (First In, First Out), priority, fair queuing)?

  • Which packets to drop when buffers fill (drop-tail, RED (Random Early Detection)/active queue management)?

  • Control plane: traditional per-router or SDN (Software-Defined Networking) controller?

  • Cost, power, heat and reliability.

↑ Section 4.1
Q25

What is prefix matching in the context of looking up a forwarding table to decide the destination of a packet? What is the longest prefix matching rule?

Answer

Prefix matching: forwarding-table entries don't list every address; each entry is a prefix (the first k bits of an address, e.g., 11001000 00010111 00010* or 200.23.16.0/21) mapped to an output link. A destination matches an entry if its first k bits equal the prefix**.

Longest prefix matching rule: when an address matches several entries, the router uses the entry with the longest (most specific) matching prefix. Example: with entries 11001000 00010111 00010 → link 0 and 11001000 00010111 00011000 → link 1, a destination starting 11001000 00010111 00011000 matches both, and link 1 (the longer, 24-bit match) wins. A default route (0.0.0.0/0) matches everything and is used only when nothing longer matches.

↑ Section 4.1
Q26

Where does queuing occur inside a router?

Answer

At both the input ports and the output ports:

  • Input port queuing: when the switching fabric can't transfer packets as fast as they arrive at the inputs (fabric slower than the sum of input line rates), or when several inputs want the same output at once — including head-of-line (HOL (Head-of-the-Line)) blocking, where a packet at the front of a queue blocks those behind it even though their outputs are free.

  • Output port queuing: when packets arrive from the fabric for an output faster than the output link can transmit (e.g., several inputs all sending to one output).

↑ Section 4.1
Q27

When does packet-loss occur in a router?

Answer

Packet loss happens when a queue's buffer is full and a new packet arrives — the router has no room, so it drops the arriving packet (drop-tail) or removes an already-queued one (with active queue management like RED (Random Early Detection), packets may be dropped or marked even before the buffer is full). This occurs when arrival rates at an input or output port exceed the fabric or link speed for long enough (traffic intensity near or above 1). Packets can also be dropped if they are corrupted, have TTL (Time-to-Live) reaching 0, or match no forwarding entry/are blocked by a filter.

↑ Section 4.1

Section 4.2: Routers

11 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11

Also asked in: Assignment 2 Q2.3

Q1

What is a router?

Answer

A router is a network-layer (layer 3) packet switch that connects two or more networks and forwards IP (Internet Protocol) datagrams between them, choosing the output link for each packet from its forwarding table based on the destination IP address. It also runs routing protocols to build that table.

↑ Section 4.2
Q2

What are routers used for?

Answer

  • Interconnecting networks — joining LANs (Local Area Network) to each other and to the Internet (e.g., your home router joins your LAN to your ISP (Internet Service Provider)).

  • Forwarding packets toward their destinations and choosing best paths (routing).

  • Separating broadcast domains and subnets.

  • Often also NAT (Network Address Translation), firewall/filtering, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), VPN (Virtual Private Network), quality of service and traffic management.

  • In ISPs, routers form the Internet's backbone.

↑ Section 4.2
Q3

What is inside a router?

Answer

  • Input ports — terminate incoming links, do link-layer processing, perform the forwarding-table lookup, queue packets.

  • Switching fabric — connects input ports to output ports.

  • Output ports — buffer packets, schedule them, and transmit onto outgoing links.

  • Routing processor — runs routing protocols (or talks to an SDN (Software-Defined Networking) controller), computes the forwarding table, handles management.

Plus memory (buffers, forwarding tables — often in TCAM (Ternary Content-Addressable Memory)), power supplies, fans and a management interface.

↑ Section 4.2
Q4

What do the input ports do?

Answer

Input ports: (1) physical layer — receive the bits (line termination); (2) link layer — decapsulate the frame, check it; (3) lookup/forwarding — look up the destination address in the local copy of the forwarding table (longest prefix match) to find the output port; (4) also check the IP (Internet Protocol) header (version, checksum, TTL (Time-to-Live)), update counters; (5) queue packets if the fabric is busy; (6) send routing/control packets to the routing processor. The goal is to process at line speed.

↑ Section 4.2
Q5

How does the switching fabric work inside a router?

Answer

The switching fabric moves packets from input ports to their chosen output ports. After the input port decides the output, it hands the packet (with an internal tag naming the output port) to the fabric, which transfers it by memory, bus or interconnection network. If the fabric is busy (or the output is busy), the packet waits at the input queue. The fabric's speed relative to line rates decides whether packets queue at the inputs.

↑ Section 4.2
Q6

What are the three different switching techniques? How does each of these techniques work?

Answer

  • Switching via memory: the routing processor (or line-card processors) copies the packet into memory, looks up the output, and copies it to the output port. Two memory accesses per packet → at most B/2 throughput; one packet at a time. Used in early routers (like a PC (Personal Computer)).

  • Switching via a bus: the input port puts the packet on a shared bus with a label naming the output port; all outputs see it, only the labelled one keeps it. One packet at a time, limited by bus speed (fine for small/enterprise routers).

  • Switching via an interconnection network (crossbar): a grid of 2N buses with crosspoints; the controller closes the crosspoint joining the input's bus to the output's bus. Several packets can cross simultaneously if they go to different outputs. Multi-stage (Clos) networks scale further. Used in high-end routers.

↑ Section 4.2
Q7

What do the output ports do?

Answer

Output ports: take packets from the fabric, store them in output buffers, schedule them (FIFO (First In, First Out), priority, round robin, WFQ (Weighted Fair Queuing)), perform link-layer encapsulation and physical-layer transmission onto the outgoing link, and drop or mark packets when the buffer is full (buffer management, e.g., RED (Random Early Detection)).

↑ Section 4.2
Q8

Where does queuing occur in a router? How do routing protocols deal with packet queuing?

Answer

Queuing occurs at input ports (fabric slower than combined inputs; head-of-line blocking — the packet at the front waits for its busy output, blocking packets behind it that could go elsewhere) and at output ports (more traffic for an output than its link can send).

Routing protocols don't handle queuing directly — they compute paths based on link costs, and queuing is managed by the router's buffers, scheduling and drop policies (and by TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) congestion control at the ends). Some routing approaches can react indirectly: link costs may reflect congestion/delay (load-sensitive routing, which risks oscillations), and traffic engineering or SDN (Software-Defined Networking) can move flows away from congested links.

↑ Section 4.2
Q9

What is a gateway router?

Answer

A gateway router is a router at the edge of an autonomous system (AS) (or network) that connects it to routers in other ASes. Gateway routers run eBGP (external Border Gateway Protocol) with neighbouring ASes to learn external routes and iBGP (internal Border Gateway Protocol) to spread them inside their own AS. (In everyday use, the "default gateway" is the router that connects a LAN (Local Area Network) to other networks.)

↑ Section 4.2
Q10

What are the fundamental differences between a router and link-layer switch?

Answer
Router Link-layer switch
Layer 3 device — forwards using IP (Internet Protocol) addresses Layer 2 device — forwards using MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses
Connects different networks/subnets Connects devices within one network/LAN (Local Area Network)
Forwarding table built by routing protocols (or SDN (Software-Defined Networking)) Switch table built by self-learning from source MACs
Blocks broadcasts; separates broadcast domains Forwards broadcasts to all ports (one broadcast domain)
Chooses best paths; supports many paths/loops (TTL (Time-to-Live)) Needs a loop-free topology (spanning tree)
Needs configuration (IP addresses) Plug-and-play
Processes layers 1–3 Processes layers 1–2
↑ Section 4.2
Q11

What is the intra-autonomous routing protocol?

Answer

An intra-autonomous-system (intra-AS) routing protocol — also called an interior gateway protocol (IGP) — is a routing protocol used to compute routes within a single AS (one organisation's or ISP (Internet Service Provider)'s network), under one administrative control. All routers in the AS run the same one. Examples: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) (link-state), IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) (link-state), RIP (Routing Information Protocol) (distance-vector), EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) (Cisco). Between ASes, the inter-AS protocol BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is used.

↑ Section 4.2

Section 4.3: The Internet Protocol (IP): IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4), Addressing, IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6), and More

28 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20Q21Q22Q23Q24Q25Q26Q27Q28

Also asked in: Assignment 2 Q1.3, Assignment 2 Q2.3

Q1

What is the role of the network layer routing protocol?

Answer

The routing protocol's role is to determine good (least-cost) paths from senders to receivers through the network of routers, and to build and update the forwarding tables in the routers accordingly — exchanging information between routers so that each knows where to send packets for every destination, and adapting when links fail or change.

↑ Section 4.3
Q2

What is the least-cost path between two hosts in a network? What condition does such a path have to meet?

Answer

The least-cost path is the path between source and destination whose sum of link costs is the smallest among all possible paths. Link costs may represent distance, delay, monetary cost, or inverse of bandwidth. Condition: it must be a valid path — a sequence of nodes where each consecutive pair is directly connected by a link — from source to destination, and there is no other path with a lower total cost.

↑ Section 4.3
Q3

What is the shortest path between two hosts in a network?

Answer

The shortest path is the path with the fewest links (hops) between the two hosts — the least-cost path when every link has the same cost (cost 1).

↑ Section 4.3
Q4

When can the shortest path and the least-cost path be identical?

Answer

When all links have the same cost (e.g., cost = 1 per link), the least-cost path is the one with the fewest hops, so the two are identical.

↑ Section 4.3
Q5

What are routing algorithms used for?

Answer

Routing algorithms compute the least-cost (good) paths through a network, from each router to every destination, given the network graph and link costs. The results fill the routers' forwarding tables, which forwarding uses to move each packet. They also recompute paths when the topology or costs change.

↑ Section 4.3
Q6

What is a global routing algorithm for a network?

Answer

A global (centralized) routing algorithm computes the least-cost path using complete, global knowledge of the network — every node knows the whole topology (all nodes, links and link costs) before calculating. The calculation can run at one site or be repeated at every router. Example: Dijkstra's link-state algorithm (used by OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)).

↑ Section 4.3
Q7

Why is a global routing algorithm referred to as a link-state algorithm?

Answer

Because to gain global knowledge, each node broadcasts "link-state" packets containing the identities and costs of its attached links to all other nodes (link-state broadcast / flooding). Once every node has every node's link states, all have the same complete map and can run Dijkstra. The algorithm is named after the information it uses — the state of the links.

↑ Section 4.3
Q8

What are the differences between distance vector algorithms and link-state algorithms?

Answer
Link-state (LS) Distance-vector (DV)
Global knowledge — every node learns the whole topology Decentralised — each node knows only its neighbours' link costs and their distance vectors
Each node floods its link costs to all nodes Each node sends its distance vector only to its neighbours
Each node runs Dijkstra itself Iterative, distributed Bellman-Ford: D_x(y) = min_v {c(x,v) + D_v(y)}
Message complexity: O(N·E) messages Messages only between neighbours; varies with convergence
Converges quickly, O(N²) computation; may oscillate if costs depend on load Can converge slowly; can have routing loops and count-to-infinity
Robust: each node computes its own table, so a bad node affects only its own advertised links Less robust: a bad node's incorrect vector spreads through the whole network
Used by OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) Used by RIP (Routing Information Protocol), (BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is path-vector)
↑ Section 4.3
Q9

How are link cost changes and link failures handled in the distance-vector algorithm?

Answer

When a node detects a change in the cost of a directly attached link, it updates its distance vector and, if any of its least-cost distances changed, sends its new distance vector to its neighbours, who recompute and pass changes on, until the network converges.

  • Good news travels fast: if a link cost decreases, the improvement spreads in a few iterations.

  • Bad news travels slowly: if a link cost increases or a link fails, nodes may keep using out-of-date routes through each other — a routing loop — increasing their costs a little each round ("count-to-infinity").

Fixes: poisoned reverse (if Z routes to X via Y, Z tells Y its distance to X is infinity), split horizon, hold-down timers, and defining "infinity" as a small number (RIP (Routing Information Protocol) uses 16). Poisoned reverse only fixes loops between two nodes.

↑ Section 4.3
Q10

What is hot potato routing?

Answer

Hot-potato routing means a router passes a packet out of its own network as quickly (cheaply) as possible: among several gateway routers that could reach an external destination, it chooses the gateway with the least intra-AS (Autonomous System) cost from itself — ignoring the rest of the path outside the AS. Like getting rid of a hot potato fast. (Used in BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) route selection.)

↑ Section 4.3
Q11

What is shortest path first routing?

Answer

Shortest path first (SPF (Sender Policy Framework)) routing sends traffic along the path with the lowest total cost computed by Dijkstra's algorithm — the name "Open Shortest Path First" (OSPF) comes from it. The algorithm repeatedly adds the closest not-yet-finalised node to the set of known shortest paths.

↑ Section 4.3
Q12

What is least loaded path routing?

Answer

Least-loaded path routing (used in circuit-switched networks, e.g., telephone) chooses, among possible paths, the one whose most-loaded link (bottleneck) is least busy — i.e., the path with the most spare capacity on its busiest link — to spread load and reduce call blocking.

↑ Section 4.3
Q13

What is maximum free circuit routing?

Answer

Maximum free circuit routing chooses the path that has the largest total number of free (unused) circuits, summed over the links of the path (or the most free circuits available), again to reduce the chance of future calls being blocked in a circuit-switched network. (It differs from least-loaded, which looks at the single busiest link.)

↑ Section 4.3
Q14

What are gateway routers?

Answer

Gateway routers are routers at the edge of an autonomous system with links to routers in other ASes. They exchange routing information with neighbouring ASes (via eBGP (external Border Gateway Protocol)) and forward packets into and out of the AS.

↑ Section 4.3
Q15

What is the intra-autonomous routing protocol?

Answer

It is the routing protocol used inside one autonomous system (an interior gateway protocol) to find least-cost paths among the AS's routers — e.g., OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System), RIP (Routing Information Protocol), EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol). The AS's administrator chooses it, and all routers in that AS run it. (Inter-AS routing uses BGP (Border Gateway Protocol).)

↑ Section 4.3
Q16

Based on the IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) addressing scheme, what is the maximum number of hosts that can be addressed?

Answer

IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, so there are 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 (about 4.3 billion) addresses. The number of usable host addresses is smaller: reserved ranges (private, loopback, multicast, experimental) and the network and broadcast addresses of each subnet are excluded — about 3.7 billion public addresses in practice. NAT (Network Address Translation) and IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) exist because this is not enough.

↑ Section 4.3
Q17

What is a network address? What is a network mask?

Answer

  • Network address: the address that identifies the network (subnet) itself — the prefix with all host bits set to 0, e.g., 192.168.1.0 in 192.168.1.0/24.

  • Network mask (subnet mask): a 32-bit value with 1s in the network-part positions and 0s in the host part, e.g., /24 = 255.255.255.0. ANDing an address with the mask gives its network address: 192.168.1.37 AND 255.255.255.0 = 192.168.1.0.

↑ Section 4.3
Q18

What is classful addressing? What are the differences between class A, B, C, and D addresses?

Answer

Classful addressing (1981–1993) divided the IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) space into fixed-size classes identified by the first bits of the address, so the network part had to be 8, 16 or 24 bits:

Class Leading bits First octet Network / host bits Size
A 0 0–127 8 / 24 126 networks × 16.7 million hosts
B 10 128–191 16 / 16 16,384 networks × 65,534 hosts
C 110 192–223 24 / 8 ~2 million networks × 254 hosts
D 1110 224–239 — multicast group addresses (no hosts)
E 1111 240–255 — reserved/experimental

Differences: the size of the network part and how many hosts each network can have; class D is for multicast, not for individual hosts.

↑ Section 4.3
Q19

Why are the four address classes no longer formally part of the IP (Internet Protocol) addressing architecture?

Answer

Because classes were too rigid and wasteful: an organisation needing 2,000 addresses was too big for a class C (254) and so got a class B (65,534), wasting over 60,000 addresses. This rapidly used up the address space (class B exhaustion) and also made routing tables explode because class C networks couldn't be combined. In 1993 CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) replaced classes with variable-length prefixes (a.b.c.d/x), allowing right-sized allocations and route aggregation.

↑ Section 4.3
Q20

What is classless interdomain routing (CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing))?

Answer

CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) is the Internet's address-assignment strategy that lets the network part of an address be any number of bits x, written a.b.c.d/x (e.g., 200.23.16.0/23). The x leading bits are the prefix. It enables allocating blocks sized to need (any power of two) and route aggregation: many contiguous prefixes can be advertised as one shorter prefix, keeping global routing tables small. Routers forward using longest prefix match.

↑ Section 4.3
Q21

What is subnetting?

Answer

Subnetting is dividing one network (address block) into smaller networks (subnets) by using some of the host bits as extra network bits (a longer prefix). Example: 192.168.10.0/24 split into four /26 subnets (64 addresses each). Benefits: organise networks by department/building, limit broadcast domains, improve security and management, use addresses efficiently. A subnet in the textbook's sense is the group of interfaces that can reach each other without passing through a router.

↑ Section 4.3
Q22

What is the dynamic host configuration protocol (DHCP)?

Answer

DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically gives a host its network configuration when it joins a network — a "plug-and-play" protocol. It supplies an IP (Internet Protocol) address (for a lease period), the subnet mask, the default gateway (first-hop router) and the DNS (Domain Name System) server address. It's a client-server protocol over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) (server port 67, client port 68) with four steps:

1. DHCP Discover — the new host broadcasts (to 255.255.255.255, from 0.0.0.0) "is there a DHCP server?"

2. DHCP Offer — a server replies with an offered address and lease time.

3. DHCP Request — the host broadcasts that it accepts one offer.

4. DHCP ACK (Acknowledgement) — the server confirms.

↑ Section 4.3
Q23

What is route aggregation or route summarization and how does it work?

Answer

Route aggregation (route summarization, supernetting) is combining several contiguous address blocks into one shorter prefix that a router advertises instead of all the individual ones. Example: an ISP (Internet Service Provider) holding 200.23.16.0/20 gives eight customers /23 blocks inside it, but advertises only "send me anything matching 200.23.16.0/20" to the rest of the Internet.

How it works: find the bits that all the blocks share; if the blocks are contiguous and line up on a power-of-two boundary, the common prefix covers exactly them. Routers elsewhere need one entry instead of many (smaller tables, fewer updates). If a customer moves to another ISP, that ISP advertises the more specific prefix, and longest prefix match makes it win.

↑ Section 4.3
Q24

How does an ISP (Internet Service Provider) get a block of addresses?

Answer
