  • Installing and configuring network devices (routers, switches, firewalls, access points, servers) and services (DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), DNS (Domain Name System), VPN (Virtual Private Network)).

  • Monitoring the network's health and performance (utilisation, latency, errors) and troubleshooting/fixing faults.

  • Security — access control, firewalls, patches, monitoring for attacks, user accounts and permissions.

  • Configuration and change management — documentation, backups, keeping inventory of hardware and software.

  • Capacity planning and upgrades; accounting of usage.

  • Meeting SLAs (Service-Level Agreement), supporting users, and keeping disaster-recovery plans.

↑ Section 5.7
Q3

What are the potential benefits of network management tools?

Answer

  • Detecting and diagnosing failures quickly (e.g., an interface going down, a failed card), often before users notice — alarms and traps.

  • Monitoring hosts, traffic and performance — spotting overloaded links, rising error rates, abnormal traffic (attacks, misconfigurations).

  • Detecting rapid changes in routing tables (route flapping) or configuration errors.

  • Service-level monitoring — verifying SLAs (Service-Level Agreement) are met.

  • Intrusion detection — noticing suspicious traffic.

  • Automation — configuring many devices consistently, reducing human errors; capacity planning and accounting reports.

Overall: higher reliability and availability, lower operating cost, better security.

↑ Section 5.7
Q4

What devices can be managed on a network?

Answer

Any device with a management agent: routers, switches, hubs, wireless access points, firewalls, load balancers, modems, servers and hosts (PCs (Personal Computer), workstations), printers, network-attached storage, UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply)/power units, IP (Internet Protocol) phones and cameras, virtual machines and IoT (Internet of Things) devices — plus their components (interfaces, cards) and the software/services running on them.

↑ Section 5.7
Q5

What is a service-level agreement (SLA)?

Answer

A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contract between a service provider (e.g., an ISP (Internet Service Provider), cloud or IT (Information Technology) department) and a customer that defines the level of service expected, with measurable targets — e.g., availability (99.9% uptime), maximum latency or packet loss, throughput, response and repair times for problems — plus how it's measured and the penalties or credits if the provider fails to meet it.

↑ Section 5.7
Q6

What five areas of network management are defined by the ISO (International Organization for Standardization) network management mode? What are the principal components of network management architecture?

Answer

Five areas (FCAPS (Fault, Configuration, Accounting, Performance, Security management)):

  • Fault management — detect, log, isolate and fix problems.

  • Configuration management — track which devices and software are installed and how they are configured; apply changes.

  • Accounting management — record usage per user/device to allocate resources, set quotas and bill.

  • Performance management — measure and report utilisation, throughput, delay, error rates; ensure performance targets.

  • Security management — control access, manage keys and policies, detect intrusions.

Principal components of the architecture:

  • Managing server (the manager application, in the network operations centre, with human operators) that collects, analyses and acts on information.

  • Managed devices containing managed objects (hardware components and software/configuration parameters).

  • MIB (management information base) — the data describing the managed objects' values.

  • Management agent — a process in each managed device that talks to the managing server and acts on its commands.

  • Network management protocol (e.g., SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol)) — the messages exchanged between server and agents.

↑ Section 5.7
Q7

What is the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) CMISE (Common Management Information Service Element)/CMIP (Common Management Information Protocol)?

Answer

CMISE (Common Management Information Service Element) and CMIP (Common Management Information Protocol) are the OSI (ISO (International Organization for Standardization)/ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union – Telecommunication Standardization Sector)) network management standards. CMISE defines the management services (operations such as GET, SET, ACTION, CREATE, DELETE and EVENT-REPORT on managed objects) and CMIP is the protocol that carries them between managers and agents, using an object-oriented information model and ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One). They were more powerful and complex than SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) and were used mainly by telecom carriers (in TMN (Telecommunications Management Network)), but SNMP won in the Internet world because it was simpler and available sooner.

↑ Section 5.7
Q8

What is the Internet simple network management protocol (SNMP)?

Answer

SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is the Internet's standard protocol for carrying management information between a managing server and agents in managed devices. It is a simple request-response protocol running over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) (agents on port 161, traps to port 162). The manager can read (Get) and write (Set) MIB (Management Information Base) values in a device, and agents can send unsolicited Trap messages to report events. Versions: SNMPv1 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 1), v2c, and v3 (secure).

↑ Section 5.7
Q9

What is the Internet management framework?

Answer

The Internet-standard management framework has four parts:

1. MIB (Management Information Base) — the definitions of the network-management data (managed objects) in devices.

2. SMI (Structure of Management Information) — the data-definition language used to define MIB objects.

3. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) — the protocol that carries information and commands between managing entities and agents.

4. Security and administration capabilities (added in SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3)).

↑ Section 5.7
Q10

What is the structure of management information (SMI)?

Answer

SMI (Structure of Management Information) is the data-definition language used to define the managed objects in a MIB (Management Information Base) (the name is a bit misleading — it's a language, not a structure). It is based on a subset of ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) and specifies the basic data types and the higher-level constructs used to describe management information, so that the meaning of the data is unambiguous across devices from different vendors.

↑ Section 5.7
Q11

How is management information defined in SMI (Structure of Management Information)?

Answer

Management information is defined in SMI by:

  • Base data types — e.g., INTEGER, Integer32, Unsigned32, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER, IPaddress, Counter32/Counter64, Gauge32, TimeTicks, Opaque.

  • The OBJECT-TYPE construct, which defines each managed object: its data type, status (current, obsolete…), access (read-only, read-write…), a description, and its object identifier (OID) — its unique position in the global naming tree (e.g., ipInDelivers is 1.3.6.1.2.1.4.9).

  • The MODULE-IDENTITY construct, which groups related objects into a MIB (Management Information Base) module with information about its author, revision and purpose.

  • Objects are named hierarchically in the ISO (International Organization for Standardization) object identifier tree (iso.org.dod.internet.mgmt.mib-2…).

↑ Section 5.7
Q12

What language constructs does SMI (Structure of Management Information) provide?

Answer

SMI provides:

  • OBJECT-TYPE — to define a managed object (type, access, status, description, OID (Object Identifier)).

  • MODULE-IDENTITY — to define a MIB (Management Information Base) module (a group of related objects) with administrative information.

  • NOTIFICATION-TYPE — to define notifications/traps.

  • OBJECT-GROUP / conformance statements — to group objects and specify what implementations must support.

  • Textual conventions (TEXTUAL-CONVENTION) and the base data types (INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER, Counter, Gauge, TimeTicks, IpAddress…), plus the SEQUENCE/table constructs for tables of objects.

↑ Section 5.7
Q13

What is a management information base (MIB)?

Answer

A MIB (Management Information Base) is the collection of managed objects (variables) in a device whose values together reflect the device's current state — e.g., number of packets received on an interface, number of IP (Internet Protocol) datagrams discarded, interface status up/down, routing table entries, system uptime. Related objects are grouped into MIB modules (e.g., MIB-II's system, interfaces, IP, ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), UDP (User Datagram Protocol) groups). Each object is defined in SMI (Structure of Management Information) and identified by an OID (Object Identifier). The managing server reads and writes MIB objects through SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol); it's like a "virtual database" of device information.

↑ Section 5.7
Q14

What is the request response mode of SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol)?

Answer

In request-response mode, the managing server sends a request to an agent in a managed device, and the agent performs the action and replies with a Response message. Requests are:

  • GetRequest — read the value of one or more MIB (Management Information Base) objects;

  • GetNextRequest — read the next object in the MIB tree (used to walk tables);

  • GetBulkRequest — read a large block of data (e.g., a whole table);

  • SetRequest — write (set) values of MIB objects;

  • InformRequest — manager-to-manager information, acknowledged.

The agent answers each with a Response (value, or acknowledgement/error). Because SNMP runs over UDP (User Datagram Protocol), the manager retransmits if no response arrives (request IDs (Identifier) detect duplicates).

↑ Section 5.7
Q15

What is a trap message?

Answer

A trap message is an unsolicited message sent by an agent to the managing server to report an exceptional event without being asked — e.g., a link going down or coming up, a device restart (cold/warm start), authentication failure, a neighbour lost, or a threshold exceeded. It's how devices alert managers immediately instead of waiting to be polled. (SNMPv2 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 2) Trap messages aren't acknowledged; Inform requests are.) Traps go to UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 162.

↑ Section 5.7
Q16

What are SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) applications?

Answer

SNMP applications (from the SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) architecture) are the programs in SNMP entities:

  • Command generator — generates Get/GetNext/GetBulk/Set requests and handles responses (the manager's polling tools).

  • Command responder — in an agent, receives requests, accesses the MIB (Management Information Base) and sends responses.

  • Notification originator — generates traps/informs.

  • Notification receiver — receives and processes traps/informs.

  • Proxy forwarder — forwards requests, notifications and responses between entities.

Examples of tools using them: network monitoring systems (Nagios, Zabbix, PRTG (Paessler Router Traffic Grapher), SolarWinds), snmpget/snmpwalk command-line tools.

↑ Section 5.7
Q17

What does SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) provide?

Answer

SNMPv3 adds security and administration:

  • Authentication (user-based security model, USM) — verifies the message came from an authorised user and wasn't changed, using a shared-key hash (HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code)-MD5 (Message Digest 5)/SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)).

  • Privacy (encryption) — encrypts the message contents (DES (Data Encryption Standard)/AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)).

  • Protection against replay — using timestamps/time windows (nonces).

  • Access control — the view-based access control model (VACM) decides which users can read or write which MIB (Management Information Base) objects.

  • Remote configuration of these settings, and a modular architecture (engines, applications).

(SNMPv1 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 1)/v2c only had a plaintext "community string".)

↑ Section 5.7
Q18

What is ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) and what does it provide?

Answer

ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) is an ISO (International Organization for Standardization)/ITU (International Telecommunication Union) standard, machine-independent language for describing data types and structures. It provides:

  • A way to define data types (INTEGER, BOOLEAN, OCTET STRING, SEQUENCE, CHOICE, OBJECT IDENTIFIER…) independent of any computer's internal representation.

  • Encoding rules — especially BER (Basic Encoding Rules) — which specify exactly how values are transmitted as bytes (using Type-Length-Value, TLV, encoding), so different machines (different byte orders, word sizes) can exchange data and interpret it identically.

This solves the presentation-layer problem. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol)'s SMI (Structure of Management Information) is based on ASN.1, and SNMP messages are encoded with BER. (It's also used in X.509 certificates, LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) and telecom protocols.)

↑ Section 5.7

Textbook Review Questions — Chapter 5

23 questions (Kurose & Ross, 8th edition)

R1R2R3R4R5R6R7R8R9R10R11R12R13R14R15R16R17R18R19R20R21R22R23
R1

What is meant by a control plane that is based on per-router control? In such cases, when we say the network control and data planes are implemented “monolithically,” what do we mean?

Answer

Per-router control means each router has its own routing component (control plane) that runs a routing algorithm and communicates with the routing components in other routers to compute its forwarding table. "Monolithic" means the control plane and the data plane are implemented together in the same box — each router contains both the forwarding hardware and the routing software, sold as one integrated, closed unit.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R2

What is meant by a control plane that is based on logically centralized control? In such cases, are the data plane and the control plane implemented within the same device or in separate devices? Explain.

Answer

Logically centralized control means a single logical controller (often physically replicated for reliability) computes and distributes the forwarding tables to all routers; each router contains a simple control agent that communicates with the controller but doesn't run a routing algorithm or talk to other routers. The data plane and the control plane are implemented in separate devices: the data plane stays in the switches; the control plane runs on the remote controller servers.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R3

Compare and contrast the properties of a centralized and a distributed routing algorithm. Give an example of a routing protocol that takes a centralized and a decentralized approach.

Answer

  • A centralized (global) algorithm computes least-cost paths with complete knowledge of the whole network (all links and costs) — it can run at one site or be replicated at every router. Example: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) (link-state; Dijkstra) — each router gets the full map. (An SDN (Software-Defined Networking) controller computing routes is centralized in the strictest sense.)

  • A decentralized algorithm is iterative and distributed: each node starts knowing only its own link costs and learns least-cost paths through exchanges with neighbours; no node has the full picture. Example: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) (distance-vector); BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is also decentralized (path-vector).

  • Compared: centralized needs full information and more messages to collect it but converges quickly and is robust; decentralized needs less information per node but can converge slowly, loop, and spread errors.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R4

Compare and contrast link-state and distance-vector routing algorithms.

Answer

  • Link-state (LS): each node knows the complete topology (via flooding of link-state advertisements to all nodes) and runs Dijkstra. O(N·E) messages; O(N²) computation; fast convergence; can oscillate if costs are load-dependent; robust — each node computes its own table, so a faulty node can only advertise wrong costs for its own links.

  • Distance-vector (DV): each node knows only its neighbours' costs and distance vectors, exchanges messages only with neighbours, and computes with Bellman-Ford iteratively. Convergence can be slow, with routing loops and the count-to-infinity problem; less robust — a node advertising wrong costs can affect the whole network.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R5

What is the “count to infinity” problem in distance vector routing?

Answer

In distance-vector routing, when a link cost increases (or a link fails), two (or more) nodes can end up routing to a destination through each other (a routing loop). Each keeps advertising an increased but still wrong cost based on the other's out-of-date information, and their costs increase by small steps each iteration, possibly counting up slowly toward "infinity" before converging — "bad news travels slowly". Example: with c(x,y) jumping from 4 to 60, y and z bounce updates for 44 iterations before settling. Poisoned reverse only fixes loops of two nodes.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R6

Is it necessary that every autonomous system use the same intra-AS routing algorithm? Why or why not?

Answer

No. Each AS has administrative autonomy — it can choose whatever intra-AS routing protocol it wants (OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System), RIP (Routing Information Protocol), EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol)), because intra-AS routing only affects routes inside that AS. What connects ASes is the common inter-AS protocol (BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)), which all ASes must run.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R7

Why are different inter-AS (Autonomous System) and intra-AS protocols used in the Internet?

Answer

  • Policy: among ASes, policy issues dominate (which ASes may carry traffic for which others, business relationships); inside one AS, everything is under one control, so policy matters less.

  • Scale: hierarchical routing (intra-AS + inter-AS) keeps table sizes and update traffic manageable; inter-AS routing must handle routing among a huge number of networks.

  • Performance: intra-AS routing can focus on performance (least-cost paths); inter-AS routing often puts policy above performance.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R8

True or false: When an OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) route sends its link state information, it is sent only to those nodes directly attached neighbors. Explain.

Answer

False. OSPF's link-state advertisements are flooded to all routers in the AS (Autonomous System) (or, with hierarchical OSPF, all routers in the same area), not just to directly attached neighbours. (Each router forwards the advertisement to its neighbours, which forward it onward, so it reaches everyone.)

↑ Chapter 5 review
R9

What is meant by an area in an OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) autonomous system? Why was the concept of an area introduced?

Answer

An area is a subset of the routers in an OSPF AS (Autonomous System), configured as a separate routing domain. Each area runs its own OSPF link-state routing: routers flood link-state information only within their area, and each router knows the detailed topology of only its own area. Area border routers connect areas to the backbone area, which routes traffic between areas.

It was introduced for scalability — hierarchy within one AS: it reduces the size of link-state databases, the amount of flooding traffic, and the computation needed, so OSPF can work in large ASes. It also contains the effect of changes within an area.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R10

Define and contrast the following terms: subnet, prefix, and BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) route.

Answer

  • Subnet: a portion of a larger network; a subnet contains no router inside it — its boundaries are defined by router and host interfaces; all its interfaces share a network address, e.g., 223.1.1.0/24.

  • Prefix: the network portion of a CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) address, written a.b.c.d/x — the first x bits. A prefix may cover one subnet or many (an aggregated block).

  • BGP route: a prefix together with its BGP attributes (AS (Autonomous System)-PATH, NEXT-HOP, local preference, etc.) — i.e., an advertisement saying "this prefix is reachable via this path".

Contrast: a subnet is a physical/addressing group of interfaces; a prefix is how that group (or several) is written for routing; a BGP route is a prefix plus the path information needed for inter-AS routing.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R11

How does BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) use the NEXT-HOP attribute? How does it use the AS (Autonomous System)-PATH attribute?

Answer

  • NEXT-HOP: the IP (Internet Protocol) address of the router interface that begins the AS-PATH (the gateway router, often in the neighbouring AS). A router uses it to figure out which of its own interfaces to use: it uses its intra-AS routing to find the least-cost path to the NEXT-HOP address and puts that interface in its forwarding table for the prefix. Also used in hot-potato routing (choose the route with the closest NEXT-HOP).

  • AS-PATH: the list of ASes the advertisement has passed through. Used to detect and prevent routing loops (a router rejects an advertisement that already contains its own AS number), and in route selection (prefer shorter AS-PATHs); also for policy (e.g., reject routes through a certain AS).

↑ Chapter 5 review
R12

Describe how a network administrator of an upper-tier ISP (Internet Service Provider) can implement policy when configuring BGP (Border Gateway Protocol).

Answer

The administrator implements policy through BGP's import and export policies and attributes:

  • Import policy / route filtering: accept or reject advertised routes (e.g., don't accept routes that pass through a certain AS (Autonomous System)), and assign local preference values to prefer certain routes (e.g., prefer routes from customers over peers over providers).

  • Export policy: control which routes are advertised to which neighbours — e.g., a tier-1 ISP advertises its customers' routes to everyone, but does not advertise routes learned from one peer to another peer (so it doesn't carry transit traffic between them for free); a multi-homed customer (stub network) doesn't advertise one provider's routes to another provider, so it never becomes a transit path.

  • Other tools: AS-PATH prepending, MED (Multi-Exit Discriminator), communities, route maps.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R13

True or false: When a BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) router receives an advertised path from its neighbor, it must add its own identity to the received path and then send that new path on to all of its neighbors. Explain.

Answer

False. A BGP router may decide whether (and to which neighbours) to advertise a received path, according to its export policy — it isn't obliged to send it on to all neighbours (e.g., a stub network doesn't re-advertise one provider's routes to another; ISPs (Internet Service Provider) don't advertise peer routes to other peers). Also, a router adds its own AS (Autonomous System) number to the AS-PATH only when advertising to an eBGP (external Border Gateway Protocol) neighbour (another AS), not to iBGP (internal Border Gateway Protocol) neighbours inside its own AS.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R14

Describe the main role of the communication layer, the network-wide statemanagement layer, and the network-control application layer in an SDN (Software-Defined Networking) controller.

Answer

  • Communication layer: handles communication between the controller and the controlled network devices (the southbound side) — e.g., OpenFlow messages to install flow entries and receive events (packet-in, port-status, flow-removed). Includes link/host discovery messages.

  • Network-wide state-management layer: the controller's "brain/database" — keeps up-to-date state of the whole network: hosts, links, switches, topology, flow tables, statistics, and makes it available to applications; implements distributed/replicated state for reliability.

  • Network-control application layer (interface): the northbound API (Application Programming Interface) through which network-control applications (routing, firewall, load balancing, access control) read state and register to be notified of changes, and issue commands; applications "program" the network through this layer.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R15

Suppose you wanted to implement a new routing protocol in the SDN (Software-Defined Networking) control plane. At which layer would you implement that protocol? Explain.

Answer

At the network-control application layer — it would be written as an application running on top of the SDN controller (using the northbound API (Application Programming Interface)). It reads the network topology and link state from the controller's state-management layer, computes the routes (e.g., with Dijkstra), and asks the controller to install the resulting flow entries in the switches through the communication layer. That's the point of SDN: routing is just another program.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R16

What types of messages flow across an SDN (Software-Defined Networking) controller’s northbound and southbound APIs (Application Programming Interface)? Who is the recipient of these messages sent from the controller across the southbound interface, and who sends messages to the controller across the northbound interface?

Answer

  • Southbound API (controller ↔︎ network devices): controller-to-device messages that configure devices, install/modify/delete flow-table entries (modify-state), query statistics (read-state), and send packets out a port (send-packet); device-to-controller messages such as packet-in (packet with no matching rule), port-status changes and flow-removed notifications. The recipients of messages sent across the southbound interface are the controlled devices (SDN switches/routers).

  • Northbound API (network-control applications ↔︎ controller): applications read and write network state and flow tables, and register for notifications of events (e.g., link down). The senders of messages to the controller across the northbound interface are the network-control applications (routing, access control, load balancer…).

↑ Chapter 5 review
R17

Describe the purpose of two types of OpenFlow messages (of your choosing) that are sent from a controlled device to the controller. Describe the purpose of two types of Openflow messages (of your choosing) that are send from the controller to a controlled device.

Answer

Device → controller:

  • Packet-in: sends the controller a packet (or its header) that didn't match any flow-table entry (or whose action says "send to controller"), so the controller can decide what to do and possibly install a rule.

  • Port-status: tells the controller that a port's status changed (e.g., a link went down or came up).

  • (Also Flow-removed: a flow entry was deleted, e.g., because it timed out.)

Controller → device:

  • Modify-state (flow-mod): add, delete or modify entries in the switch's flow table, and set port properties.

  • Send-packet (packet-out): tells the switch to send a specific packet out a specified port (the packet is carried in the message).

  • (Also Configuration — query/set configuration parameters — and Read-state — collect statistics and counters.)

↑ Chapter 5 review
R18

What is the purpose of the service abstraction layer in the OpenDaylight SDN (Software-Defined Networking) controller?

Answer

In OpenDaylight, the Service Abstraction Layer (SAL) decouples network services and applications from the southbound protocols. It lets the controller's components and applications request services in a protocol-independent way and translates them to whichever southbound protocol a device uses (OpenFlow, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol), OVSDB (Open vSwitch Database), etc.) — i.e., it's the plumbing that connects and routes requests between controller modules (a "hub"), so applications don't need to know which protocol a device speaks.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R19

Names four different types of ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) messages

Answer

Four ICMP message types (any four): echo reply (type 0, ping reply), destination unreachable (type 3 — network/host/protocol/port unreachable), source quench (type 4, congestion control, deprecated), echo request (type 8, ping), router advertisement (type 9), router discovery (type 10), TTL (Time-to-Live) expired / time exceeded (type 11), IP (Internet Protocol) header bad (type 12).

↑ Chapter 5 review
R20

What two types of ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) messages are received at the sending host executing the Traceroute program?

Answer

  • ICMP TTL (Time-to-Live)-expired (time exceeded) messages (type 11, code 0) from each router along the path where the probe's TTL reaches 0.

  • ICMP port unreachable message (type 3, code 3) from the destination host, because traceroute's UDP (User Datagram Protocol) probes go to an unlikely port number — this tells the source to stop. (Windows tracert uses ICMP echo requests, so the destination sends an echo reply instead.)

↑ Chapter 5 review
R21

Define the following terms in the context of SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol): managing server, managed device, network management agent and MIB (Management Information Base).

Answer

  • Managing server: the application, typically with a human operator, running in the network operations centre, that controls the collection, processing, analysis and display of management information, and initiates actions to control network behaviour.

  • Managed device: a piece of network equipment (with its software) on a managed network — e.g., a host, router, switch, printer, modem. It contains managed objects (hardware components, configuration parameters).

  • Network management agent: a process running in the managed device that communicates with the managing server and takes local actions (reads/sets values) under the server's command.

  • MIB (Management Information Base): the collection of data (managed objects) in a managed device that describes its state — e.g., counters, status, configuration — defined with SMI (Structure of Management Information) and accessed through the management protocol.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R22

What are the purposes of the SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) GetRequest and SetRequest messages?

Answer

  • GetRequest: sent by the managing server to an agent to read (get) the values of one or more MIB (Management Information Base) objects in the managed device.

  • SetRequest: sent by the managing server to set (write) the values of one or more MIB objects in the device — e.g., change a configuration parameter or disable an interface.

The agent replies to both with a Response message.

↑ Chapter 5 review
R23

What is the purpose of the SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) trap message?

Answer

A Trap message is sent by an agent to the managing server, unsolicited, to notify it of an exceptional situation that has changed MIB (Management Information Base) values — e.g., a link going down or up, a cold/warm restart, authentication failure. It lets the manager learn about important events immediately rather than waiting to poll.

↑ Chapter 5 review

Unit 6: The Link Layer and Local Area Networks

6.1 Introduction to the Link Layer6.2 Error-Detection and Error-Correction at the Link Layer6.3 Link Layer Protocols and Local Area Networks6.4 Link Virtualization and Data Center Networking6.5 Data Flow Across the LayersTextbook review questions — Chapter 6

Section 6.1: Introduction to the Link Layer

8 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8
Q1

What services does the link layer provide?

Answer

  • Framing — encapsulating each network-layer datagram in a frame with a header (addresses) and trailer (error check).

  • Link access — a medium access control (MAC) protocol that decides when a node may transmit, especially on a shared (broadcast) link; MAC addresses identify sender and receiver.

  • Reliable delivery — guaranteeing a datagram crosses the link without error (ACKs (Acknowledgement), retransmission) — used on high-error links like wireless.

  • Error detection and correction — detecting bit errors caused by signal attenuation and noise (and sometimes correcting them).

  • Also flow control between adjacent nodes and half/full-duplex operation.

↑ Section 6.1
Q2

What does a data link layer protocol do?

Answer

A data-link-layer protocol defines the format of the frames exchanged between the two nodes at the ends of a link, and the actions those nodes take when sending and receiving frames — how to put a datagram into a frame, how to address it, when a node may transmit on the medium, how to detect errors, and (if provided) how to acknowledge and retransmit. Examples: Ethernet, Wi-Fi (802.11), PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol).

↑ Section 6.1
Q3

What are frames?

Answer

A frame is the link-layer packet: a network-layer datagram placed in a data field, surrounded by a header (e.g., destination and source MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses, type) and often a trailer (e.g., CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) error-check bits). Each link-layer protocol defines its own frame structure.

↑ Section 6.1
Q4

What are some commonly used link layer protocols?

Answer

Ethernet (IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.3), Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11), PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol), HDLC (High-Level Data Link Control), DOCSIS (Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification) (cable), 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) cellular link layers (PDCP (Packet Data Convergence Protocol)/RLC (Radio Link Control)/MAC (Medium Access Control)), Bluetooth, historically token ring and FDDI (Fiber Distributed Data Interface), Frame Relay, ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode); also MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) (a "layer 2.5") and VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) tagging (802.1Q).

↑ Section 6.1
Q5

What are nodes and links, respectively, in a link layer?

Answer

  • Nodes: any device that runs a link-layer protocol — hosts, routers, switches and Wi-Fi access points.

  • Links: the communication channels that connect adjacent nodes along the communication path — wired (Ethernet cable, fibre) or wireless (radio) — possibly shared by many nodes (broadcast link) or only two (point-to-point).

↑ Section 6.1
Q6

What are the framing, link access, reliable delivery, and error detection and correction services provided by a link layer?

Answer

  • Framing: almost all link-layer protocols encapsulate each datagram in a frame (data field + header fields + possibly trailer) before sending it.

  • Link access: a MAC (Medium Access Control) protocol specifies the rules for transmitting a frame onto the link. On a point-to-point link it's simple (send whenever the link is idle); on a shared broadcast link it coordinates many nodes (the multiple-access problem — CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection), CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance), TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access)…).

  • Reliable delivery: guarantees each datagram moves across the link without error, using acknowledgements and retransmissions (like TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)). Used on high-error links such as wireless to correct errors locally, rather than end to end; often unnecessary on low-error wired links.

  • Error detection and correction: the transmitter adds error-detection bits (parity, checksum, CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check)); the receiver checks them and drops erroneous frames (detection), or, with enough redundancy (FEC (Forward Error Correction)), determines where the error is and corrects it without retransmission. Usually done in hardware.

↑ Section 6.1
Q7

Where is the link layer implemented in a network?

Answer

In every node — every host, router, switch and access point. In a host, the bulk of it is implemented in the network adapter (NIC (Network Interface Card)) — a link-layer controller chip that does framing, link access, error detection and transmission/reception in hardware; the rest (assembling addresses, activating the controller, handling interrupts and passing datagrams up) is software on the host CPU (Central Processing Unit) (device driver). The link layer is where software meets hardware.

↑ Section 6.1
Q8

What do network interface cards (NICs) do in computer networks?

Answer

A network interface card (NIC) / network adapter connects a computer to the network medium and implements the link and physical layers:

  • On sending: takes a datagram from the host, builds the frame (adds MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses, CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check)), follows the MAC protocol (e.g., CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection), CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance)) and transmits the bits as signals.

  • On receiving: receives signals, checks the CRC, checks that the destination MAC address matches its own (or broadcast/multicast), extracts the datagram and passes it up to the network layer.

Each NIC has a unique, permanent 48-bit MAC address. NICs can be wired (Ethernet port) or wireless (Wi-Fi adapter).

↑ Section 6.1

Section 6.2: Error-Detection and Error-Correction at the Link Layer

16 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16

Also asked in: Assignment 3 Q1.5, Assignment 3 Q2.2

Q1

How are errors detected at the link layer?

Answer

The sender computes error-detection bits (EDC (Error-Detection and -Correction bits)) from the data (D) and sends them with the data. The receiver receives D′ and EDC′, recomputes the check from D′, and compares: if they disagree, an error is detected and the frame is typically discarded (or a retransmission is requested). Techniques: parity checks (single or two-dimensional), checksums, and — most commonly in link layers — cyclic redundancy checks (CRC), implemented in the adapter hardware. There's always a small chance of undetected errors, reduced by using more EDC bits.

↑ Section 6.2
Q2

What techniques are commonly used to correct errors?

Answer

  • Two-dimensional parity — corrects any single-bit error by locating it at the intersection of the failing row and column.

  • Forward error correction (FEC) codes — e.g., Hamming codes, Reed-Solomon (CDs (Compact Disc), DVDs (Digital Versatile Disc), satellite), convolutional codes with Viterbi decoding, turbo codes and LDPC (Low-Density Parity-Check code) (Wi-Fi, 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular)) — add enough redundancy for the receiver to correct errors itself.

  • Retransmission (ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest)) — not correction by code, but the most common way to "correct": detect the error, discard, and have the sender resend (e.g., Wi-Fi ACKs (Acknowledgement)).

  • Interleaving — spreads bits so burst errors become scattered single errors that codes can fix.

↑ Section 6.2
Q3

What is a parity check?

Answer

A parity check adds one extra bit (the parity bit) to a block of data so that the total number of 1s is even (even parity) or odd (odd parity). The receiver counts the 1s; if the count has the wrong parity, at least one bit (in fact an odd number of bits) is in error. It detects any odd number of bit errors but misses even numbers of errors.

↑ Section 6.2
Q4

What is two-dimensional parity?

Answer

Two-dimensional parity arranges the d data bits into a grid of i rows and j columns and computes a parity bit for each row and for each column (i + j + 1 bits including the corner). If a single bit flips, one row and one column show parity errors, and the receiver can identify and correct the bit at their intersection. It can also detect (but not correct) any combination of two errors. See the worked example above.

↑ Section 6.2
Q5

What is forward error correction?

Answer

Forward error correction (FEC) is the ability of the receiver to both detect and correct errors itself, using redundant information added by the sender — without asking for a retransmission. It reduces the number of retransmissions needed and gives immediate correction — valuable for real-time applications (audio/video) and links with long delays (satellite, deep space) or high error rates (wireless), where waiting for a resend is too slow. Examples: 2-D parity, Hamming, Reed-Solomon, turbo and LDPC (Low-Density Parity-Check code) codes.

↑ Section 6.2
Q6

What is a checksum in the link layer?

Answer

A checksum treats the data as a sequence of k-bit integers, adds them up (e.g., one's-complement sum of 16-bit words in the Internet checksum), and uses the result (its complement) as the error-detection bits. The receiver recomputes the sum (e.g., sum of all words including the checksum = all 1s) to check. Checksums need little overhead and are fast in software, so they're used at the transport and network layers; but they give weaker protection than CRCs (Cyclic Redundancy Check). The link layer uses CRCs, which are stronger and implemented in hardware.

↑ Section 6.2
Q7

What is a cyclic redundancy check (CRC)?

Answer

A cyclic redundancy check (CRC) — a polynomial code — is an error-detection code widely used in link layers (Ethernet, Wi-Fi). Sender and receiver agree on an (r + 1)-bit generator G. For d data bits D, the sender chooses r extra bits R so that the d + r bit pattern <D,R> is exactly divisible by G using modulo-2 arithmetic; R is the remainder of D × 2^r ÷ G. The receiver divides the received bits by G; a non-zero remainder means an error. Standard 8-, 12-, 16- and 32-bit generators exist (Ethernet uses CRC-32).

↑ Section 6.2
Q8

What techniques are used for error detection in a link layer?

Answer

The three main techniques: parity checks (single-bit and two-dimensional), checksumming methods, and cyclic redundancy checks (CRC) — CRC being the one link layers actually use (in hardware). FEC (Forward Error Correction) codes may also detect errors.

↑ Section 6.2
Q9

How does a cyclic redundancy check (CRC) work for multiple-bit error detection?

Answer

The sender appends r CRC bits R so that <D,R> = D × 2^r XOR (Exclusive OR) R is divisible by G (R = remainder of D × 2^r / G using XOR division). The receiver divides the whole received string by G. Any error pattern E flips bits of the sent string, and the receiver's remainder equals E mod G; the error goes undetected only if E happens to be a multiple of G. With a well-chosen G:

  • All burst errors of length r or less are detected (such a short pattern can't be a multiple of G);

  • a longer burst is detected with probability 1 − 0.5^r;

  • all single-bit errors, all double-bit errors (for suitable G) and all odd numbers of errors (if G has the factor x + 1) are detected.

So CRC detects many multi-bit errors, which parity cannot. See the worked example above.

↑ Section 6.2
Q10

What techniques are used for error correction in the link layer?

Answer

Two-dimensional parity (corrects single-bit errors) and more general forward error correction (FEC) codes (Hamming, Reed-Solomon, convolutional, turbo, LDPC (Low-Density Parity-Check code)). Many link layers instead detect and retransmit (ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest)), e.g., 802.11 with ACKs (Acknowledgement); combined ARQ + FEC (hybrid ARQ) is used in 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular).

↑ Section 6.2
Q11

What are so-called bit-level errors?

Answer

Bit-level errors are errors in which individual bits are changed during transmission — a 1 received as a 0 or a 0 as a 1 — caused by signal attenuation, electromagnetic noise, interference or fading. They may affect single bits or bursts of consecutive bits. The link layer's error-detection and correction mechanisms are designed to catch them.

↑ Section 6.2
Q12

What are parity checks? How can parity checks be used to detect errors?

Answer

Parity checks add a parity bit so that the number of 1s in the data plus parity bit is even (even parity scheme) or odd (odd parity scheme). To detect errors, the receiver counts the 1s in the received bits; if even parity was used and it finds an odd number of 1s, it knows at least one bit error has occurred (an odd number of errors). With two-dimensional parity, the receiver checks every row and every column, which can also locate and correct a single-bit error and detect any two-bit error.

↑ Section 6.2
Q13

What is a parity bit for a given N-bit unit of data?

Answer

For N bits of data, the parity bit is one extra bit whose value makes the total number of 1s in the N + 1 bits even (for even parity) — i.e., parity bit = 1 if the N data bits contain an odd number of 1s, otherwise 0 (and the opposite for odd parity). It's the XOR (Exclusive OR) of all N data bits (for even parity).

↑ Section 6.2
Q14

How is a two-dimension parity checksum calculated for a given data stream?

Answer

1. Choose a grid shape: i rows × j columns with i × j = number of data bits (as square as possible to minimise the checksum length i + j).

2. Write the data stream into the grid row by row.

3. For each row, compute the parity bit (even parity: 1 if the row has an odd number of 1s).

4. For each column, compute the parity bit the same way.

5. Optionally compute the corner bit — the parity of the row-parity bits (which equals the parity of the column-parity bits).

6. The checksum is the row-parity bits + column-parity bits (+ corner); send it with the data.

(See the worked example in "How the formulas work" above and Assignment 3 Q2.2 in Part E.)

↑ Section 6.2
Q15

How can a two-dimension parity checksum be used for 1-bit error correction?

Answer

The receiver recomputes every row parity and column parity from the received data and compares with the received parity bits:

  • No mismatches → no error detected.

  • Exactly one row and one column mismatch → a single data bit is wrong, and it's the bit at the intersection of that row and column → flip it to correct.

  • One row (or column) mismatch only → the error is in that parity bit itself; data is fine.

  • More mismatches → multiple errors, detected but not correctable → discard/retransmit.

This works because every data bit belongs to exactly one row and one column.

↑ Section 6.2
Q16

What is so-called forward error correction (FEC)?

Answer

Forward error correction (FEC) is the technique where the sender adds redundant bits so that the receiver can detect and correct errors on its own, without retransmission. "Forward" means the correction information is sent forward with the data, not requested backward. Benefits: fewer retransmissions, no round-trip delay for correction — important for real-time audio/video, broadcast (where there's no return channel) and long-delay or noisy links. Cost: extra bits always sent. Examples: 2-D parity, Hamming, Reed-Solomon, LDPC (Low-Density Parity-Check code) (Wi-Fi, 5G (Fifth Generation cellular)), turbo codes (4G (Fourth Generation cellular)).

↑ Section 6.2

Section 6.3: Link Layer Protocols and Local Area Networks

57 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20Q21Q22Q23Q24Q25Q26Q27Q28Q29Q30Q31Q32Q33Q34Q35Q36Q37Q38Q39Q40Q41Q42Q43Q44Q45Q46Q47Q48Q49Q50Q51Q52Q53Q54Q55Q56Q57

Also asked in: Assignment 3 Q1.3, Assignment 3 Q2.3

Q1

What is a point-to-point link?

Answer

A point-to-point link connects exactly two nodes — a single sender at one end and a single receiver at the other. There's no sharing, so medium access is simple. Examples: PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) over a dial-up or DSL (Digital Subscriber Line) line, HDLC (High-Level Data Link Control), a full-duplex Ethernet link between a host and a switch port, a fibre link between two routers.

↑ Section 6.3
Q2

What is a multicast link?

Answer

The question means a broadcast (multiple-access) link — a link where many sending and receiving nodes share a single channel, so a frame sent by any node is received by all the other nodes (it can also carry multicast/broadcast frames to many receivers at once). Examples: classic bus Ethernet, Wi-Fi, satellite, cable-modem upstream. Such links need a multiple-access protocol.

↑ Section 6.3
Q3

What is the multiple-access problem? How is it solved?

Answer

The multiple-access problem is how to coordinate the access of multiple sending and receiving nodes to a shared broadcast channel. If two or more nodes transmit at the same time, their signals collide and all the colliding frames are lost (wasted channel time).

It is solved by multiple-access (MAC (Medium Access Control)) protocols — rules that nodes follow to decide when to transmit. Three classes:

  • Channel partitioning (TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access), FDMA (Frequency Division Multiple Access), CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access)): divide the channel into pieces and give each node its own.

  • Random access (ALOHA, slotted ALOHA, CSMA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access), CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection), CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance)): transmit at the full rate; when collisions happen, detect them and retransmit after a random delay.

  • Taking turns (polling, token passing): nodes take turns so there are no collisions.

↑ Section 6.3
Q4

What are channel partitioning protocols? How do they work?

Answer

Channel partitioning protocols divide the broadcast channel's bandwidth among the nodes, giving each node its own dedicated share, so there are no collisions:

  • TDM (Time Division Multiplexing)/TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access): time is divided into frames, each with N slots; node i transmits only in slot i of every frame.

  • FDM (Frequency Division Multiplexing)/FDMA (Frequency Division Multiple Access): the channel's frequency range is divided into N bands; each node transmits only in its own band.

  • CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access): each node gets a unique code and all transmit at once over the whole band; receivers separate the signals using the codes.

Pros: fair, collision-free. Con: a node gets only R/N even when it's the only one with data (idle slots/bands are wasted).

↑ Section 6.3
Q5

What are random access protocols? How do they work?

Answer

Random access protocols: a node always transmits at the full channel rate R. If a collision occurs, each involved node retransmits its frame after waiting a random delay (chosen independently), so hopefully they don't collide again; this repeats until the frame gets through. No coordination beforehand. Examples: ALOHA, slotted ALOHA, CSMA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access) (listen before transmitting), CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) (also stop when a collision is detected — Ethernet), CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance) (avoid collisions — Wi-Fi). Pros: a single active node gets the full rate; decentralised and simple. Con: collisions waste capacity when many nodes are busy.

↑ Section 6.3
Q6

What are taking-turns protocols? How do they work?

Answer

Taking-turns protocols let nodes take turns to transmit so there are no collisions and a node with lots of data can use the full rate when others are idle:

  • Polling: a master node polls each node in turn ("you may send up to N frames now"). Cons: polling delay, and the master is a single point of failure. Used by Bluetooth.

  • Token passing: a special token frame is passed from node to node in a fixed order; only the node holding the token may transmit (up to a maximum), then it passes the token on. Decentralised and efficient, but a node failure or lost token can break the ring. Used by token ring and FDDI (Fiber Distributed Data Interface).

↑ Section 6.3
Q7

What is TDM (Time Division Multiplexing)? What is FDM (Frequency Division Multiplexing)? How do they work?

Answer

  • TDM (time-division multiplexing): the link's time is divided into frames, and each frame into N time slots; each user gets one slot per frame and transmits at the full rate R during its slot — so each gets R/N on average. Like taking turns speaking in fixed order.

  • FDM (frequency-division multiplexing): the link's frequency spectrum is divided into N bands, each of bandwidth R/N; each user transmits continuously in its own band. Like different radio stations on different frequencies.

Both avoid collisions and are fair, but waste capacity when a user has nothing to send.

↑ Section 6.3
Q8

What is code division multiple access (CDMA)? How does it work?

Answer

CDMA (code division multiple access) assigns each sender a unique code (a sequence of M "chips", each +1 or −1); all senders transmit simultaneously over the whole frequency band. How it works:

  • Encoding: to send a data bit d (+1 or −1), the sender transmits its code multiplied by d: Z = d × c (M chips per bit). So a 1 is sent as the code and a 0 (−1) as the inverted code.

  • Channel: signals from all senders add together.

  • Decoding: the receiver multiplies the received chips by the intended sender's code and averages: d = (1/M) × Σ Z_m × c_m. Because codes are chosen to be orthogonal (their products sum to 0), other senders' signals cancel out and the wanted bit is recovered.

Used in 3G (Third Generation cellular) cellular and GPS (Global Positioning System); related spread-spectrum ideas in Wi-Fi.

↑ Section 6.3
Q9

What is the chipping rate?

Answer

The chipping rate is the rate at which the code chips are transmitted in CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access) — the number of chips per second (the "chip rate"). Because each data bit is spread into M chips, the chipping rate is M times the data bit rate. Example: in 3G (Third Generation cellular) WCDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access) the chip rate is 3.84 Mchips/s. A higher chip rate spreads the signal over a wider bandwidth.

↑ Section 6.3
Q10

What are the ALOHA protocols?

Answer

ALOHA protocols are the original random-access protocols, developed at the University of Hawaii (Norman Abramson, 1970, ALOHAnet radio network):

  • Pure (unslotted) ALOHA: when a frame arrives, the node transmits it immediately. If it collides, the node waits one frame time and then retransmits with probability p (or waits another frame time with probability 1 − p). Fully decentralised, no synchronisation, but maximum efficiency is only 1/(2e) ≈ 18% because a frame can collide with frames starting in a window of 2 frame times.

  • Slotted ALOHA: time is divided into slots (see Q11); efficiency doubles to 1/e ≈ 37%.

↑ Section 6.3
Q11

What is the slotted ALOHA protocol?

Answer

Slotted ALOHA assumptions: all frames are L bits; time is divided into slots of L/R seconds (one frame time); nodes transmit only at the start of a slot; nodes are synchronised; if two or more frames collide in a slot, all nodes detect the collision before the slot ends. Operation: when a node has a new frame, it transmits at the start of the next slot. If there's no collision, it's done. If there's a collision, the node retransmits in each later slot with probability p until it succeeds. Pros: a single active node transmits at the full rate; highly decentralised; simple. Cons: collisions and idle slots waste capacity; needs clock synchronisation. Max efficiency = 1/e ≈ 0.37 (as N → ∞, with p = 1/N).

↑ Section 6.3
Q12

What are the carrier sense multiple access (CSMA) protocols?

Answer

CSMA (carrier sense multiple access) protocols have a node listen to the channel before transmitting ("carrier sensing"): if the channel is idle, transmit; if it's busy, wait (defer) until it becomes idle. ("Listen before talking.") Collisions can still happen because of propagation delay: a node may not yet hear another node's transmission that has already begun. Variants: 1-persistent, non-persistent, p-persistent; CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) (adds collision detection — stop when you hear a collision; wired Ethernet) and CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance) (collision avoidance — Wi-Fi).

↑ Section 6.3
Q13

How does the CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) protocol work?

Answer

Ethernet's CSMA/CD algorithm:

1. The adapter gets a datagram from the network layer and builds a frame.

2. Carrier sense: if the channel is idle, start transmitting; if it's busy, wait until it's idle, then transmit.

3. While transmitting, monitor the channel for signals from other adapters (collision detection).

4. If the entire frame is sent without detecting a collision, done.

5. If a collision is detected, stop transmitting immediately and send a 48-bit jam signal so all nodes know there was a collision.

6. Binary exponential backoff: after the m-th collision in a row, choose K at random from {0, 1, …, 2^m − 1} (m up to 10) and wait K × 512 bit times, then return to step 2.

For it to work, frames must be long enough to still be transmitting when a collision from the far end arrives: L/R ≥ 2 × d_prop (see formulas above).

↑ Section 6.3
Q14

What are two desirable properties of a multiple access protocol?

Answer

The textbook lists desirable properties of a multiple-access protocol for a broadcast channel of rate R:

1. When only one node has data to send, it can transmit at the full rate R.

2. When M nodes have data to send, each can transmit at an average rate of R/M (fair sharing).

Plus (the full list of four): 3. it is decentralised — no master node that could fail; 4. it is simple and inexpensive to implement.

↑ Section 6.3
Q15

What is a LAN (Local Area Network) address?

Answer

A LAN address — also called a MAC (Medium Access Control) address, physical address or hardware address — is the link-layer address of a network adapter (interface). For Ethernet and Wi-Fi it's 48 bits (6 bytes), written in hex like 1A-23-F9-CD (Collision Detection)-06-9B. It's assigned by the manufacturer (IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) allocates the first 24 bits, the OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier), to each vendor), is meant to be globally unique and permanent, and is flat (no hierarchy) — it doesn't change when the device moves (unlike an IP (Internet Protocol) address). Used to deliver frames within a LAN.

↑ Section 6.3
Q16

Why does a node in a network have a LAN (Local Area Network) address in addition to a network-layer address?

Answer

Because the two kinds of address do different jobs at different layers:

  • LANs are designed for any network-layer protocol, not just IP (Internet Protocol) (and IPX (Internetwork Packet Exchange), etc., in the past), so adapters need their own addresses independent of the network layer.

  • MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses are flat and permanent (like a social security number); IP addresses are hierarchical and depend on where you're attached (like a postal address), so they're used for routing across the Internet but change when you move.

  • If adapters used IP addresses, they'd have to be reconfigured every time the device moved; and without adapter-level filtering, adapters would have to pass every frame up to the network layer to check the address, interrupting the host constantly.

So IP addresses get a packet across the Internet, and MAC addresses deliver it on each individual link.

↑ Section 6.3
Q17

What is the broadcast address for a LAN (Local Area Network)?

Answer

FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF (48 ones). A frame sent to this address is received and processed by all adapters on the LAN.

↑ Section 6.3
Q18

What is the address resolution protocol (ARP)? Why is it necessary?

Answer

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) translates an IP (Internet Protocol) address into the corresponding MAC (Medium Access Control) address on the same LAN (Local Area Network) (subnet). How: each host and router keeps an ARP table (IP address → MAC address, with a TTL (Time-to-Live), typically ~20 minutes). If the needed MAC isn't in the table, the sender broadcasts an ARP query (to FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF) saying "who has IP address X?"; the node with that IP replies with an ARP response containing its MAC address, sent directly (unicast) to the asker, which caches it. ARP is plug-and-play — tables are built automatically.

Why necessary: IP gives the destination's IP address, but to actually deliver a frame on the LAN, the adapter needs the destination's MAC address. ARP bridges the network layer and the link layer.

↑ Section 6.3
Q19

How does ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) help send a datagram to a node outside the LAN (Local Area Network)?

Answer

To send a datagram to a host on another subnet, the sender puts the destination's IP (Internet Protocol) address in the datagram but addresses the frame to the MAC (Medium Access Control) address of its first-hop router (default gateway):

1. Host A sees (from its subnet mask) that B is on another subnet, so the next hop is its default router R.

2. A uses ARP to get R's MAC address (for R's interface on A's subnet).

3. A sends the frame with destination MAC = R's interface MAC, containing the datagram with destination IP = B's IP.

4. R receives the frame, passes the datagram to its network layer, looks up the forwarding table to choose the output interface, then uses ARP on the next subnet to find the MAC of B (or of the next router), and sends a new frame with that MAC.

So IP addresses stay the same end to end, while the MAC addresses change on every hop.

↑ Section 6.3
Q20

What are the main reasons for the success of Ethernet?

Answer

  • First widely deployed high-speed LAN (Local Area Network) — network administrators knew it, and it was reluctant to be replaced.

  • Simpler and cheaper than competitors (token ring, FDDI (Fiber Distributed Data Interface), ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode)).

  • Kept up with speed demands — 10 Mbps → 100 Mbps → 1 Gbps → 10/40/100/400 Gbps, while keeping the same frame format.

  • Cheap hardware — adapters and switches became commodity items; runs over cheap twisted pair.

  • Moved from shared bus to switched, full-duplex operation without changing the basic protocol, removing collisions.

  • Open IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) standard (802.3) with many vendors.

↑ Section 6.3
Q21

What is the structure of Ethernet frames?

Answer

Ethernet frame (sizes in bytes):

Field Size Purpose
Preamble 8 (7 bytes 10101010 + 1 byte 10101011 start-frame delimiter) "Wakes up" receivers and synchronises their clocks; the last two 1s say "frame starts now"
Destination address 6 MAC (Medium Access Control) address of the receiving adapter (or broadcast/multicast)
Source address 6 MAC address of the sending adapter
Type (EtherType) 2 Which network-layer protocol is inside (e.g., 0x0800 IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4), 0x86DD IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6), 0x0806 ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)) — for demultiplexing
Data (payload) 46–1,500 The IP (Internet Protocol) datagram; padded if shorter than 46 bytes; MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) 1,500
CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) 4 CRC-32 so the receiver can detect bit errors

(An 802.1Q VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) tag of 4 bytes may be inserted after the source address.)

↑ Section 6.3
Q22

Why is Ethernet said to provide unreliable connectionless services?

Answer

  • Connectionless: there's no handshaking between sending and receiving adapters before a frame is sent — the adapter just sends it.

  • Unreliable: the receiving adapter checks the CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) but doesn't send ACKs (Acknowledgement) or NAKs (Negative Acknowledgement). A frame that fails the CRC is simply discarded, and the sender isn't told. Recovery (if needed) is left to higher layers such as TCP (Transmission Control Protocol).

This keeps Ethernet simple and cheap.

↑ Section 6.3
Q23

What band is used for data transmission in Ethernet?

Answer

Ethernet uses baseband transmission: the adapter sends a digital signal directly onto the medium, using the whole bandwidth of the cable for one channel (no modulation onto a carrier frequency or frequency-division multiplexing) — hence the "BASE" in names like 10BASE-T. (Broadband, by contrast, would modulate onto multiple carrier frequencies, as cable TV (Television) does.)

↑ Section 6.3
Q24

Why is Manchester encoding used in Ethernet?

Answer

Manchester encoding (used by 10 Mbps Ethernet) represents each bit with a transition in the middle of the bit period: e.g., 1 = high-to-low, 0 = low-to-high (conventions vary). It's used because:

  • Clock recovery/synchronisation: every bit has a transition, so the receiver can lock its clock onto the signal — no separate clock line is needed, and long runs of 0s or 1s don't cause loss of sync.

  • No DC (Direct Current) component (equal time high and low).

  • Easy detection of an idle line or collision.

The cost is that it needs twice the signalling rate (bandwidth) of the data rate, so faster Ethernets use more efficient codes (4B/5B, 8B/10B, 64B/66B, PAM-5 (Pulse Amplitude Modulation, 5 levels)).

↑ Section 6.3
Q25

What multicast access protocol is used in Ethernet?

Answer

Classic (shared) Ethernet uses CSMA/CD — carrier sense multiple access with collision detection — with binary exponential backoff. (Modern switched full-duplex Ethernet has no shared medium, so it no longer needs it.)

↑ Section 6.3
Q26

Why is a jam signal used in Ethernet?

Answer

When a transmitting adapter detects a collision, it stops sending its frame and transmits a 48-bit jam signal to make sure all the other transmitting adapters become aware of the collision. Without it, a node whose signal only just overlapped might not detect the collision (the colliding energy might be too little); the jam guarantees the collision lasts long enough to be detected everywhere, so everyone discards the corrupted frame and backs off.

↑ Section 6.3
Q27

How is the efficiency of Ethernet defined?

Answer

Ethernet (CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection)) efficiency is the long-run fraction of time that frames are being transmitted on the channel without collisions when there are a large number of active nodes, each with many frames to send. An approximation is:

efficiency = 1 / (1 + 5 × d_prop / d_trans)

where d_prop is the maximum propagation delay between two adapters and d_trans is the time to transmit a maximum-size frame. As d_prop → 0 or d_trans → ∞, efficiency → 1 (much better than ALOHA's 37%).

↑ Section 6.3
Q28

What is a repeater in LANs (Local Area Network)?

Answer

A repeater is a physical-layer device that receives a signal on one port, regenerates (amplifies and retimes) it, and retransmits it bit by bit on its other port(s) — extending the distance a LAN segment can cover beyond the cable's limit. It doesn't understand frames or addresses, and it passes collisions through; all segments joined by repeaters are one collision domain. (A hub is a multi-port repeater.)

↑ Section 6.3
Q29

What is 10BASE2 Ethernet?

Answer

10BASE2 ("Thinnet", "Cheapernet") is an early Ethernet standard: 10 Mbps, BASEband signalling, maximum segment length about 200 m (actually 185 m). It uses a bus topology — computers attach along a single thin coaxial cable with BNC (Bayonet Neill–Concelman connector) T-connectors, with terminators at both ends. Up to 30 nodes per segment; repeaters can join up to 5 segments. Obsolete today.

↑ Section 6.3
Q30

What physical medium is used to network computers in a 10BASE2 Ethernet?

Answer

Thin coaxial cable (RG-58, 50-ohm "thin coax"), connected to each computer with BNC (Bayonet Neill–Concelman connector) T-connectors and terminated with 50-ohm terminators at each end of the bus.

↑ Section 6.3
Q31

What are the main topologies for LAN (Local Area Network) implementation?

Answer

  • Bus — all nodes on one shared cable (10BASE2, 10BASE5).

  • Star — all nodes connect to a central hub or switch (10BASE-T and all modern Ethernet) — the dominant topology.

  • Ring — nodes connected in a loop, passing a token (token ring, FDDI (Fiber Distributed Data Interface)).

  • Tree/hierarchical (extended star) — stars connected by backbone switches.

  • Mesh — multiple interconnections for redundancy (data centres, wireless mesh).

↑ Section 6.3
Q32

What are the important devices used to build 10BASE-T or 100BASE-T Ethernet?

Answer

  • Network adapters (NICs (Network Interface Card)) with RJ-45 (Registered Jack 45) ports in each host.

  • Twisted-pair copper cables — Category 3/5 UTP (Unshielded Twisted Pair) for 10BASE-T; Category 5 (or better) for 100BASE-T — with RJ-45 connectors.

  • A hub (multi-port repeater) or, today, a switch at the centre of the star.

  • (Optionally routers to connect to other networks, and patch panels.) Max node-to-hub distance: 100 m.

↑ Section 6.3
Q33

What is Gigabit Ethernet?

Answer

Gigabit Ethernet is the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.3z (fibre) and 802.3ab (copper, 1000BASE-T) standard that runs Ethernet at 1,000 Mbps (1 Gbps). It:

  • keeps the standard Ethernet frame format (backward compatible with 10/100 Mbps);

  • supports point-to-point links via switches and shared broadcast channels (via hubs/buffered distributors) — in shared mode it uses CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection), with carrier extension (minimum slot 512 bytes) so collision detection works;

  • supports full-duplex operation on point-to-point links (no CSMA/CD needed);

  • runs over Cat 5e/6 copper (100 m) and fibre (up to km).

It's the standard desktop connection today, followed by 10, 40, 100 and 400 Gigabit Ethernet.

↑ Section 6.3
Q34

What are hubs?

Answer

A hub is a physical-layer device — a multi-port repeater — at the centre of a star LAN (Local Area Network). When a bit arrives on one port, the hub regenerates it and sends it out on all its other ports, at the same rate. It doesn't examine frames or addresses, doesn't buffer or filter, and forwards collisions; all attached nodes share one collision domain and the same bandwidth. Hubs have been replaced by switches.

↑ Section 6.3
Q35

What are bridges?

Answer

A bridge is a link-layer (layer 2) device that connects LAN (Local Area Network) segments and forwards frames between them based on MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses. It stores each frame, checks it, looks up the destination MAC in its bridge (forwarding) table, and either forwards it only to the segment where the destination is or filters (drops) it if the destination is on the same segment it came from. It learns addresses automatically (self-learning), separates collision domains, and is transparent to hosts. A switch is essentially a fast multi-port bridge.

↑ Section 6.3
Q36

What are switches?

Answer

A (link-layer) switch is a multi-port layer-2 device that receives link-layer frames and forwards each one only onto the outgoing link(s) leading to its destination MAC (Medium Access Control) address, using a self-learned switch table. Switches are store-and-forward (or cut-through), support full-duplex links, buffer frames, give each port its own collision domain (no collisions in full-duplex), and are transparent and plug-and-play. They're the building block of modern Ethernet LANs (Local Area Network) (and support VLANs (Virtual Local Area Network)).

↑ Section 6.3
Q37

What are the differences between a hub and a bridge?

Answer
Hub Bridge
Physical layer (layer 1) Link layer (layer 2)
Repeats bits to all ports Forwards frames only toward the destination (filtering) using MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses
No buffering, doesn't understand frames Stores and checks whole frames (CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check))
All segments = one collision domain; shared bandwidth Separates collision domains; each segment has its own bandwidth
All ports must run at the same speed/technology Can join segments of different speeds/technologies (10 and 100 Mbps)
Limits on number of nodes and span Removes those limits
Very cheap, simple More complex, more expensive
↑ Section 6.3
Q38

What are the differences between a bridge and a switch?

Answer

Functionally they're the same idea — a switch is a high-performance multi-port bridge. Differences are mostly historical/implementation:

Bridge Switch
Few ports (often 2–4), connecting LAN (Local Area Network) segments Many ports; usually each host has its own port
Forwarding in software — slower Forwarding in hardware (ASICs (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit)) — wire speed on all ports at once
Store-and-forward only Store-and-forward or cut-through
Half-duplex shared segments Full-duplex links, no collisions
— Extra features: VLANs (Virtual Local Area Network), QoS (Quality of Service), link aggregation, management
↑ Section 6.3
Q39

What is a backbone hub?

Answer

A backbone hub is a hub that interconnects other hubs (or LAN (Local Area Network) segments) — e.g., in a university, each department has its own hub, and the department hubs are connected to a central backbone hub, forming a multi-tier (hierarchical) LAN. All segments then share one collision domain.

↑ Section 6.3
Q40

What is a multi-tier hub design? What is a LAN (Local Area Network) segment?

Answer

  • Multi-tier hub design: a hierarchy of hubs — hosts connect to (department) hubs, which connect upward to a backbone hub — extending the LAN across a building or campus, with up to several levels.

  • LAN segment: the part of the LAN attached to one hub (or one cable) — e.g., one department's hub and its hosts. Each department's network is a segment of the larger LAN.

↑ Section 6.3
Q41

Why is it said that all the LAN (Local Area Network) segments are in the same collision domain?

Answer

Because hubs are physical-layer repeaters: they forward every bit to every port, and the backbone hub forwards it to every department hub, so a frame from any host reaches all hosts in all segments. If two hosts in different segments transmit at the same time, their signals meet and collide. There's no device that separates or buffers frames, so the whole interconnected LAN acts as one collision domain.

↑ Section 6.3
Q42

What are the limitations of using a backbone hub as an interconnection device?

Answer

  • One collision domain — the total throughput of the whole LAN (Local Area Network) is limited to that of a single segment (e.g., 10 Mbps shared by everyone), instead of each department having its own 10 Mbps.

  • Can't connect different Ethernet technologies (e.g., 10BASE-T and 100BASE-T) because hubs don't buffer frames.

  • Limits on size — the maximum number of nodes in a collision domain and the maximum distance between hosts (for CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) timing) restrict how big the LAN can grow.

  • No filtering or security (every host sees all traffic), and a failure can affect everyone.

↑ Section 6.3
Q43

What abilities does a bridge have?

Answer

A bridge can:

  • Filter frames — not forward a frame whose destination is on the same segment it came from.

  • Forward frames to the correct segment (interface) using its bridge table.

  • Learn automatically which MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses are on which interface (self-learning) — plug-and-play.

  • Separate collision domains, increasing total throughput (each segment can carry its own traffic).

  • Connect different LAN (Local Area Network) technologies/speeds (e.g., 10 Mbps and 100 Mbps Ethernet), because it buffers frames.

  • Extend LAN size beyond single-segment limits.

  • Run the spanning tree protocol to allow redundant links without loops.

  • Be transparent to hosts.

↑ Section 6.3
Q44

How is the self-learning capability accomplished in bridges?

Answer

The bridge builds its table automatically from the frames it sees:

1. The table starts empty.

2. For each incoming frame, the bridge records (source MAC (Medium Access Control) address, the interface it arrived on, current time) — now it knows that address is reachable via that interface.

3. To forward a frame, it looks up the destination MAC:

  • no entry → flood it out all other interfaces;

  • entry on the same interface the frame came from → filter (drop) it;

  • entry on a different interface → forward it only there.

4. Entries are deleted after an aging time (e.g., 60 min or 300 s) if no frames are seen from that address, so moved/removed hosts are handled.

↑ Section 6.3
Q45

Why are bridges described as transparent?

Answer

Because hosts are unaware of the bridge's existence: they send frames addressed to other hosts' MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses exactly as they would on a single LAN (Local Area Network), and never address frames to the bridge. The bridge doesn't change the frames (no new addresses added), and it needs no configuration by hosts or administrators (plug-and-play). It's "invisible".

↑ Section 6.3
Q46

What are the advantages of pure hierarchical design for interconnected LAN (Local Area Network) segments?

Answer

A pure hierarchical design (a tree — each segment connects upward to a backbone bridge/switch):

  • No loops — only one path between any two segments, so frames don't circulate endlessly and no spanning tree is needed.

  • Simple to design, manage and troubleshoot; easy to add segments.

  • Separate collision domains per segment; local traffic stays local.

  • Bridges' self-learning works straightforwardly.

The drawback: the backbone bridge is a single point of failure — if it (or a link) fails, segments become disconnected.

↑ Section 6.3
Q47

Why are multiple paths between LAN (Local Area Network) segments necessary? What problems are caused by using multiple paths? How is this problem solved by using bridges?

Answer

  • Why necessary: redundancy/reliability — with multiple paths, if one bridge or link fails, traffic can still flow over another path; also for load sharing.

  • Problem: multiple paths create loops (cycles). Broadcast frames and frames for unknown destinations are flooded and circulate forever, multiplying (a broadcast storm) and swamping the network; bridge tables also become confused because a MAC (Medium Access Control) address appears on different interfaces.

  • Solution with bridges: the spanning tree protocol (STP, IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1D) — bridges exchange messages and together choose a loop-free subset of links (a spanning tree), putting redundant ports into a blocking state. Frames are only forwarded along the tree. If a link or bridge fails, the bridges compute a new spanning tree, re-enabling a blocked link.

↑ Section 6.3
Q48

What is the spanning tree protocol?

Answer

The spanning tree protocol (STP, IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1D, invented by Radia Perlman) is a link-layer protocol that lets bridges/switches in a network with redundant links find a loop-free logical topology:

1. Bridges exchange BPDUs (bridge protocol data units) and elect a root bridge (lowest bridge ID (Identifier)).
