2. Each bridge finds its least-cost path to the root and chooses its root port; each segment chooses a designated bridge/port closest to the root.

3. All other ports are set to blocking — they don't forward data frames, removing loops.

4. If a link or bridge fails, the protocol recomputes the tree and unblocks ports as needed.

(Faster variants: RSTP (Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol) 802.1w, MSTP (Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol).)

↑ Section 6.3
Q49

What are the differences between bridges and routers?

Answer
Bridge (switch) Router
Layer 2 — uses MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses Layer 3 — uses IP (Internet Protocol) addresses
Self-learning, plug-and-play Needs configuration (IP addresses, routing protocols)
Forwarding table from observed frames Forwarding table from routing protocols
Topology restricted to a spanning tree (no loops) Can use any topology with multiple active paths; chooses best paths
Forwards broadcasts → one broadcast domain; broadcast storms possible Blocks broadcasts; separates broadcast domains (firewall against storms)
Faster, simpler per-frame processing (layers 1–2) More processing (layers 1–3)
ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) tables and bridge tables grow with the number of hosts → not for huge networks Scales to large networks with hierarchical addressing
↑ Section 6.3
Q50

What are the pros and cons of routers?

Answer

Pros:

  • Any topology is allowed, with multiple active paths — no spanning-tree restriction; routers choose best paths and balance load.

  • No broadcast storms — routers don't forward link-layer broadcasts; they isolate broadcast domains and act as a firewall.

  • Scalability — hierarchical IP (Internet Protocol) addressing and route aggregation allow very large networks.

  • Connect different network technologies; offer security/filtering, NAT (Network Address Translation), QoS (Quality of Service).

Cons:

  • Not plug-and-play — routers and hosts need IP addresses configured (though DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) helps).

  • More processing per packet (up to layer 3) → higher latency than switches and higher cost.

  • More complex to configure and manage.

↑ Section 6.3
Q51

Which IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) standard is used for Ethernet?

Answer

IEEE 802.3 (with its many amendments: 802.3u Fast Ethernet, 802.3z/ab Gigabit, 802.3ae 10 Gigabit, 802.3ba 40/100 Gigabit, 802.3bs 400 Gigabit…).

↑ Section 6.3
Q52

What advantages does a switch have?

Answer

  • Eliminates collisions: each port is its own collision domain; with full-duplex links there's no CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) at all — maximum efficiency.

  • Higher aggregate throughput: many ports can transmit simultaneously (e.g., a 24-port 1 Gbps switch can move many Gbps at once).

  • Heterogeneous links: ports can run different speeds and media (10/100/1000 Mbps, copper and fibre).

  • Plug-and-play self-learning, transparent to hosts.

  • Management and security: filtering, monitoring (port statistics), VLANs (Virtual Local Area Network), port security; traffic only goes where it's needed (less eavesdropping than a hub).

  • Store-and-forward checking of CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check); QoS (Quality of Service), link aggregation.

↑ Section 6.3
Q53

What is cut-through switching?

Answer

Cut-through switching means a switch starts forwarding a frame to its output port as soon as it has read the destination MAC (Medium Access Control) address (the first few bytes), before the entire frame has arrived — instead of storing the whole frame first (store-and-forward). It reduces latency (especially for large frames), but the switch can't check the CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) before forwarding, so corrupted frames may be forwarded. It only helps if the output port is free; otherwise the frame is buffered anyway. (Fragment-free switching waits for the first 64 bytes as a compromise.)

↑ Section 6.3
Q54

What is the PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) protocol and where is it commonly used?

Answer

PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol, RFC (Request for Comments) 1661) is a link-layer protocol for point-to-point links — a single sender and single receiver at each end. It handles framing, error detection, link configuration (LCP (Link Control Protocol)) and negotiation of the network-layer protocol (NCPs (Network Control Protocol) — e.g., IPCP (Internet Protocol Control Protocol) to get an IP (Internet Protocol) address), and optional authentication (PAP (Password Authentication Protocol)/CHAP (Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol)). Commonly used: dial-up connections between a home PC (Personal Computer) and an ISP (Internet Service Provider), DSL (Digital Subscriber Line) and some cable/fibre access as PPPoE (Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet) (PPP over Ethernet), leased lines / SONET (Synchronous Optical Network)/SDH (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy) links between routers (PPP over SONET), and some cellular data and VPN (Virtual Private Network) tunnels.

↑ Section 6.3
Q55

What are the original requirements for the design of PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol)?

Answer

The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force)'s original requirements for PPP (RFC (Request for Comments) 1547):

  • Packet framing — encapsulate a network-layer datagram in a frame so the receiver can find the start and end of the frame and of the datagram.

  • Transparency — carry any bit pattern in the data field (even patterns that look like the flag) — solved by byte stuffing.

  • Multiple network-layer protocols — support several network protocols (IP (Internet Protocol), IPX (Internetwork Packet Exchange), AppleTalk) over the same link, with demultiplexing.

  • Multiple types of links — serial/parallel, synchronous/asynchronous, low/high speed, electrical/optical.

  • Error detection (but not correction).

  • Connection liveness — detect a link failure and tell the network layer.

  • Network-layer address negotiation — let the network layers learn/configure each other's addresses (e.g., get an IP address).

  • Simplicity — the most important requirement.

Not required: error correction/retransmission, flow control, sequencing (in-order delivery), and multipoint links — left to higher layers.

↑ Section 6.3
Q56

What fields are contained in a PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) frame?

Answer

PPP frame (HDLC (High-Level Data Link Control)-like):

Field Size Purpose
Flag 1 byte (01111110) Marks the beginning and end of the frame
Address 1 byte (11111111) Only one possible value — all stations (point-to-point, so unused)
Control 1 byte (00000011) Fixed value (for possible future use)
Protocol 1 or 2 bytes Which upper-layer protocol the data belongs to (e.g., 0x0021 IP (Internet Protocol), LCP (Link Control Protocol), IPCP (Internet Protocol Control Protocol)) — for demultiplexing
Information (data) variable (default max 1,500 bytes) The encapsulated datagram (or control message)
Checksum (FCS (Frame Check Sequence)) 2 or 4 bytes CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) for error detection
Flag 1 byte (01111110) End of frame
↑ Section 6.3
Q57

What is byte stuffing? How is it used in PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) design?

Answer

Byte stuffing is the technique that lets the data field contain any byte values — even the flag pattern 01111110 — without the receiver mistaking it for the end of the frame (the transparency requirement).

How PPP uses it: a special control escape byte, 01111101 (0x7D), is defined.

  • Sender: whenever the data contains a flag byte (0x7E) or an escape byte (0x7D), it inserts ("stuffs") an escape byte before it (and, in PPP, XORs (Exclusive OR) that byte with 0x20 — so 0x7E becomes 0x7D 0x5E and 0x7D becomes 0x7D 0x5D).

  • Receiver: whenever it sees an escape byte, it removes it and treats the next byte as data (restoring it), not as a flag or escape.

  • A single flag byte that is not preceded by an escape means start or end of a frame.

Example: data … 7E … is sent as … 7D 5E …; the receiver turns it back into 7E.

↑ Section 6.3

Section 6.4: Link Virtualization and Data Center Networking

25 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20Q21Q22Q23Q24Q25
Q1

What is a link on a local network such as Ethernet?

Answer

On an Ethernet LAN (Local Area Network), a link is the communication channel that directly connects adjacent nodes — typically a twisted-pair cable (or fibre) between a host's NIC (Network Interface Card) and a switch port, or between two switches (in old shared Ethernet, the shared cable/hub that all nodes attached to). It carries Ethernet frames between neighbouring nodes identified by MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses.

↑ Section 6.4
Q2

What is a link on a wide area network?

Answer

On a WAN (Wide Area Network), a link is typically a long-distance point-to-point connection between two routers (or between a customer router and the provider) — e.g., a leased line (T1/E1, T3), SONET (Synchronous Optical Network)/SDH (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy) optical circuit, fibre/wavelength circuit, Frame Relay/ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) virtual circuit, MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) path, microwave or satellite link. It may itself be built from a carrier's whole network, but IP (Internet Protocol) sees it as one link.

↑ Section 6.4
Q3

What is a link on a dialup network?

Answer

On a dial-up network, the "link" is the telephone connection between the user's modem and the ISP (Internet Service Provider)'s modem — a circuit through the telephone network (many telephone switches and trunks). The PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) protocol runs over it. Even though it crosses an entire telephone network, IP (Internet Protocol) treats the dial-up connection as a single point-to-point link — a clear example of link virtualization.

↑ Section 6.4
Q4

What links might be involved on a VPN (Virtual Private Network) connection?

Answer

A VPN connection involves the ordinary physical links on the path (Wi-Fi/Ethernet at home, the ISP (Internet Service Provider) access link, Internet backbone links, the organisation's access link) plus a virtual link — the encrypted tunnel between the VPN client and the VPN gateway (e.g., IPsec (Internet Protocol Security), SSL (Secure Sockets Layer)/TLS (Transport Layer Security), WireGuard). To the private network, that tunnel looks like one link, even though it runs across many Internet links. (Or, in an MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) VPN, label-switched paths across the provider's network.)

↑ Section 6.4
Q5

What links may exist on an Internet connection?

Answer

A typical Internet connection may involve: the Wi-Fi or Ethernet link from your device to your home router; the access link (DSL (Digital Subscriber Line) line, cable HFC (Hybrid Fiber-Coax), fibre/PON (Passive Optical Network), 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) radio) to the ISP (Internet Service Provider); Ethernet/fibre links inside the ISP between routers; backbone optical links (SONET (Synchronous Optical Network), dense wavelength-division multiplexing), possibly undersea cables, satellite or microwave; links at IXPs (Internet Exchange Point); and data-centre Ethernet links to the server — plus virtual links such as MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) paths or tunnels.

↑ Section 6.4
Q6

What is a virtual link?

Answer

A virtual link is a connection that appears to a higher layer (e.g., IP (Internet Protocol)) as a single direct link between two nodes, but is actually implemented by a whole network or another protocol underneath — e.g., a telephone circuit for dial-up, an MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) label-switched path, an IP tunnel (IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) over IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4), VPN (Virtual Private Network) tunnels), or an ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) virtual circuit. The higher layer is unaware of the intermediate nodes.

↑ Section 6.4
Q7

How can a network become a link layer?

Answer

A network "becomes a link layer" when another network uses it just to carry its packets between two of its nodes, treating it as a single link. For example: the telephone network provides the "link" for dial-up IP (Internet Protocol); an MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) network interconnects IP routers and is treated as their link; with tunnelling, the whole IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) Internet acts as a link between two IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) routers; an Ethernet/ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode)/Frame Relay network can carry IP between routers. The upper network encapsulates its datagrams in the lower network's packets, and the lower network delivers them end to end — just as a link layer delivers frames between adjacent nodes. This is link virtualization.

↑ Section 6.4
Q8

What are multiprotocol label switching (MPLS) networks?

Answer

MPLS networks are packet-switched, virtual-circuit networks (usually within an ISP (Internet Service Provider) backbone) in which routers forward packets based on short, fixed-length labels carried in an MPLS header rather than on the IP (Internet Protocol) destination address. The goal was originally faster forwarding, but MPLS is now used mainly for traffic engineering (routing flows along chosen paths), fast reroute (pre-computed backup paths) and VPNs (Virtual Private Network). It works together with IP ("multiprotocol" — it can carry IP and other protocols).

↑ Section 6.4
Q9

How are MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) networks treated as a link-layer technology?

Answer

The MPLS header sits between the link-layer (e.g., Ethernet or PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol)) header and the IP (Internet Protocol) header ("layer 2.5"). IP routers at the network edge see the MPLS network as a way to deliver datagrams between them — as if it were a link — while inside, label-switched routers forward frames by label, without looking at IP addresses, much like a virtual-circuit link-layer technology (ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode), Frame Relay). So from IP's point of view, an MPLS path is just another link.

↑ Section 6.4
Q10

What is the MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) protocol?

Answer

"The MPLS protocol" refers to the set of mechanisms (RFC (Request for Comments) 3031/3032) by which:

  • an ingress (edge) router classifies incoming IP (Internet Protocol) datagrams, pushes an MPLS header with a label and sends them along a label-switched path (LSP);

  • each label-switched router (LSR) looks up the incoming label (and interface) in its MPLS forwarding table, swaps it for an outgoing label and forwards the frame to the next LSR — no IP lookup;

  • the egress router pops the label and forwards the datagram by normal IP routing.

Labels and paths are distributed by signalling protocols such as LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) or RSVP-TE (Resource Reservation Protocol – Traffic Engineering) (which can reserve bandwidth along explicit paths), using routing information from extended OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)/IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System).

↑ Section 6.4
Q11

What is a MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching)-capable router?

Answer

An MPLS-capable router is a router that understands MPLS labels: it can forward frames based on the MPLS label (label switching) using an MPLS forwarding table, push, swap and pop labels, and participate in the label-distribution/signalling protocols. At the edge it can also classify IP (Internet Protocol) packets into label-switched paths. Also called a label-switched router (LSR).

↑ Section 6.4
Q12

Why is a MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) header needed in a link-layer frame transmitted on MPLS networks?

Answer

Because the MPLS header carries the label that MPLS-capable routers use to forward the frame — they don't examine the IP (Internet Protocol) header. The header must be in the frame so each router can switch the packet by label (and so different packets for the same destination can take different paths, which pure IP destination-based forwarding can't do). An MPLS-enhanced frame can only be sent between MPLS-capable routers; the header is added at the ingress and removed at the egress.

↑ Section 6.4
Q13

What fields does a MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) header contain? What purpose is each field designed for?

Answer

The MPLS header is 32 bits (4 bytes):

Field Bits Purpose
Label 20 The identifier used to look up forwarding — which label-switched path/FEC (Forward Error Correction) this packet belongs to on this link
Exp / Traffic Class (TC) 3 Experimental → now used for quality of service/priority (class of service)
S (bottom of stack) 1 Set to 1 on the last label in a stack of MPLS headers (labels can be stacked, e.g., for VPNs (Virtual Private Network) or tunnels)
TTL (Time-to-Live) 8 Time-to-live, decremented at each LSR (Label-Switched Router), to prevent loops (like IP (Internet Protocol)'s TTL)
↑ Section 6.4
Q14

What is a label-switched router?

Answer

A label-switched router (LSR) is an MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching)-capable router that forwards an MPLS frame by looking up its incoming MPLS label in its forwarding table and immediately passing the datagram to the appropriate output interface (usually swapping the label for the one the next router expects) — without extracting the IP (Internet Protocol) destination address and doing longest-prefix-match. Edge LSRs (ingress/egress) add and remove labels.

↑ Section 6.4
Q15

What is network traffic engineering?

Answer

Traffic engineering is the practice of controlling how traffic flows through a network — deliberately steering flows over particular paths to use capacity efficiently, avoid congestion, meet performance requirements (QoS (Quality of Service)/SLAs (Service-Level Agreement)) and provide fast recovery, rather than letting everything follow the single least-cost path chosen by IP (Internet Protocol) routing. MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) enables it by letting operators set up explicit label-switched paths (e.g., send traffic from one ingress to the same destination over two different paths, or reserve bandwidth), and fast reroute to backup paths within milliseconds of a failure. SDN (Software-Defined Networking) is also used for traffic engineering.

↑ Section 6.4
Q16

How are MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) networks used to implement a VPN (Virtual Private Network)?

Answer

An ISP (Internet Service Provider) uses MPLS to connect a customer's geographically separate sites as if they were on one private network:

  • The ISP sets up label-switched paths between its provider-edge (PE) routers serving the customer's sites.

  • Each customer gets its own VPN routing and forwarding table (VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding)) on the PE routers, so customers can even use overlapping private addresses.

  • Customer packets entering a PE router get two labels (a stack): an inner VPN label identifying the customer's VPN/site, and an outer transport label for the LSP (Label-Switched Path) across the backbone.

  • Core routers switch on the outer label only; the egress PE uses the inner label to deliver to the right customer site.

Traffic of different customers is kept separated (isolation) without encryption, and the ISP can apply QoS (Quality of Service) and traffic engineering. (Layer-2 VPNs — VPLS (Virtual Private LAN Service), pseudowires — work similarly.) This is "MPLS VPN" (RFC (Request for Comments) 4364, BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)/MPLS IP (Internet Protocol) VPNs).

↑ Section 6.4
Q17

What is a data center, and what is a data center network?

Answer

  • A data center is a facility housing a very large number of servers (tens to hundreds of thousands), storage, networking and support systems (power, cooling), used by companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta to provide web search, email, social networks, streaming and cloud computing services.

  • A data center network is the network that interconnects all these servers with each other and with the Internet — racks of hosts, top-of-rack switches, aggregation/spine switches, load balancers and border routers — designed for very high capacity between servers and to the outside.

↑ Section 6.4
Q18

Why are hosts in data centers called blades?

Answer

Because data-centre hosts are typically built as thin "blade" servers — like pizza boxes or blades — stacked in racks (typically 20–40 per rack). Each blade is a complete, generally commodity computer (CPU (Central Processing Unit), memory, disk) designed to slide into a rack or chassis, sharing power and cooling, so thousands can be packed densely.

↑ Section 6.4
Q19

What is the top of rack (TOR) switch?

Answer

A top-of-rack (TOR) switch is the Ethernet switch at the top of each rack of servers, to which all hosts in that rack connect (each host has one or more links to it, e.g., 10–100 Gbps). It is the first-level switch of the data-centre network.

↑ Section 6.4
Q20

What roles does a TOR (Top-of-Rack) switch play in a data center?

Answer

The TOR switch: interconnects the hosts within the rack with each other (intra-rack traffic stays within the rack), and connects the rack to other switches in the data centre (tier-2/aggregation or spine switches), so hosts can reach other racks and, via border routers, the Internet. It aggregates the rack's traffic onto its uplinks; it's also a natural place for access control, VLANs (Virtual Local Area Network), and monitoring.

↑ Section 6.4
Q21

What are border routers?

Answer

Border routers are the routers that connect the data-centre network to the public Internet (or to other networks) — at the boundary between the data centre and the outside world. They handle traffic between external clients and internal hosts (usually via load balancers), and run BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) with ISPs (Internet Service Provider).

↑ Section 6.4
Q22

What is involved in data center network design?

Answer

Data-centre network design involves:

  • Topology/hierarchy — how to interconnect hosts, TOR (Top-of-Rack) switches, aggregation/spine switches and border routers (tree vs Clos/fat-tree/fully connected).

  • Capacity and bandwidth — high host-to-host capacity and minimal oversubscription between tiers (limits on aggregate bandwidth are the main challenge).

  • Load balancing of external requests across servers and of traffic across paths (ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path)).

  • Redundancy and fault tolerance — many parallel paths, no single point of failure.

  • Scalability, cost (commodity switches), power and cooling, cabling.

  • Addressing, routing and management (often SDN (Software-Defined Networking)-based, custom protocols), virtualisation and isolation between tenants, and low latency.

↑ Section 6.4
Q23

What is load balancing and what is a load balancer?

Answer

Load balancing means distributing work (requests or traffic) across many servers (or paths) so no single server is overloaded, improving performance and availability.

A load balancer is the device/software that does this: in a data centre, external requests for a service arrive at the load balancer's public address (a VIP (Virtual IP address)), and the load balancer chooses a host (based on current load, round robin, hashing, health) to handle each request, forwards the request to it (often rewriting the destination IP (Internet Protocol) — acting as a layer-4 NAT (Network Address Translation)), and relays the reply back to the client. It also hides the internal structure and detects failed servers. Layer-7 load balancers can use HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) information (URL (Uniform Resource Locator), cookies).

↑ Section 6.4
Q24

What is a hierarchy of routers and switches?

Answer

The traditional hierarchical data-centre topology: hosts connect to their rack's TOR (Top-of-Rack) switch; TOR switches connect to tier-2 (aggregation) switches; tier-2 switches connect to tier-1 (core) switches; and access routers/border routers connect the core to the Internet. It's a tree (usually with some redundancy — each TOR/tier-2 connected to two switches above). It scales to many hosts but has a bottleneck problem: links near the top are shared by many racks, so host-to-host capacity between racks is limited (oversubscription).

↑ Section 6.4
Q25

What is a fully connected topology? How is it better than the hierarchy of routers and switches?

Answer

A fully connected topology (a Clos / "leaf-spine" design) connects each tier-1 (spine) switch to every tier-2 switch (and each TOR (Top-of-Rack) to several tier-2 switches), so there are many parallel, equal-cost paths between any two racks. Better than the hierarchy because:

  • Much higher host-to-host capacity — traffic between racks is spread over many paths (e.g., with ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path)), removing the bottleneck at the top of the tree.

  • Redundancy/reliability — many alternative paths if a switch or link fails.

  • Scalability with commodity switches — capacity grows by adding switches rather than buying huge, expensive core routers.

  • More uniform latency between any two servers.

↑ Section 6.4

Section 6.5: Data Flow Across the Layers

25 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20Q21Q22Q23Q24Q25
Q1

When you request a Web page with a Web browser, what does the browser do to begin with?

Answer

Before anything else, the browser parses the URL (Uniform Resource Locator) to get the host name (e.g., www.google.com), port and path. If the computer has just joined the network it first needs an IP (Internet Protocol) address (DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)). The browser then needs the IP address of the web server, so it (through the operating system) makes a DNS (Domain Name System) lookup for the host name — unless the address is already in its DNS cache — and only then opens a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection to the server to send the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request.

↑ Section 6.5
Q2

What networking protocols or services are triggered thereafter and in what order?

Answer

In the textbook scenario (a newly connected laptop), in order:

1. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) — obtain the laptop's IP (Internet Protocol) address, mask, default gateway and DNS (Domain Name System) server (DHCP message inside UDP (User Datagram Protocol) inside IP inside Ethernet, broadcast; the switch self-learns the laptop's port).

2. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) — find the MAC (Medium Access Control) address of the default gateway router (broadcast query, unicast reply).

3. DNS — send a query (UDP port 53) for www.google.com to the local DNS server, via the gateway router; routing across the ISP (Internet Service Provider) uses forwarding tables built by intra-domain routing (OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)/RIP (Routing Information Protocol)/IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System)) and inter-domain routing (BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)); the DNS server replies with the IP address.

4. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) — three-way handshake (SYN (Synchronize flag), SYN-ACK (Acknowledgement), ACK) with the web server (port 80, or 443 plus TLS (Transport Layer Security)).

5. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) — the browser sends an HTTP GET; the server replies with an HTTP response containing the page; the browser renders it (and fetches embedded objects).

At every hop, Ethernet/link-layer framing (and switching) and IP forwarding carry these messages.

↑ Section 6.5
Q3

What are DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) request message, UDP (User Datagram Protocol) segment, IP (Internet Protocol) datagram, and Ethernet frame?

Answer

They're the nested layers of one message when the laptop asks for an IP address:

  • DHCP request message — the application-layer message (from the laptop's DHCP client) asking for an IP address and configuration.

  • UDP segment — the transport-layer packet that carries the DHCP message, with source port 68 and destination port 67 (DHCP client/server).

  • IP datagram — the network-layer packet carrying the UDP segment, with broadcast destination IP 255.255.255.255 and source 0.0.0.0 (the laptop has no address yet).

  • Ethernet frame — the link-layer frame carrying the IP datagram, with destination MAC (Medium Access Control) FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF (broadcast) and the laptop's MAC as source, so every device on the LAN (Local Area Network) — including the DHCP server — receives it.

Each is encapsulated inside the next.

↑ Section 6.5
Q4

What does demultiplexing do?

Answer

Demultiplexing means delivering the contents of a received packet to the correct upper-layer protocol or process by examining header fields. At each layer the receiver looks at a field to decide who gets the payload: the Ethernet type field says the payload is IP (Internet Protocol) (or ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)); the IP protocol field says it's UDP (User Datagram Protocol) or TCP (Transmission Control Protocol); the UDP/TCP port numbers say which application process/socket (e.g., the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server on port 67 or a web server on port 80). In the scenario, the DHCP server's frame is demultiplexed up Ethernet → IP → UDP → DHCP server.

↑ Section 6.5
Q5

What is CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)?

Answer

CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) is the Internet's address-allocation and routing scheme in which the network part of an IP (Internet Protocol) address can be any length x, written a.b.c.d/x (e.g., 68.85.2.0/24), instead of fixed classes. It enables right-sized address blocks and route aggregation. In the scenario, the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server allocates Bob an address from the campus's CIDR block 68.85.2.0/24. (See Section 4.3.)

↑ Section 6.5
Q6

What type of information does a DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) ACK (Acknowledgement) message provide?

Answer

A DHCP ACK message provides the client with:

  • its IP (Internet Protocol) address (the "your IP address" field — e.g., 68.85.2.101) and the lease time;

  • the network (subnet) mask (e.g., /24);

  • the IP address of the default gateway (first-hop router);

  • the IP address of the DNS (Domain Name System) server(s) (and often the domain name);

  • plus the DHCP server's identity and possibly other options (NTP (Network Time Protocol) servers, etc.).

↑ Section 6.5
Q7

We say some networking switches can be self-learning. What does that mean?

Answer

A self-learning switch builds its switch (forwarding) table automatically, without any configuration: whenever a frame arrives, the switch records the frame's source MAC (Medium Access Control) address and the port it arrived on, so it learns where each host is. When forwarding, if the destination is in the table it sends the frame only out of that port (or drops it if it's the same port); otherwise it floods the frame to all ports. Entries age out after a while. (In the scenario, the switch learns Bob's laptop's port from the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) request frame.)

↑ Section 6.5
Q8

What information does an IP (Internet Protocol) forwarding table contain?

Answer

An IP forwarding table contains entries mapping destination network prefixes (address/mask, e.g., 68.85.2.0/24) to the outgoing interface (and usually the next-hop router's IP address), plus typically a default route (0.0.0.0/0). Routers also store metrics/costs and the source of the route (OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), static). The router uses longest prefix match on the destination address to pick the entry.

↑ Section 6.5
Q9

What is a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) socket?

Answer

A TCP socket is the endpoint of a TCP connection — the interface through which an application sends and receives the TCP byte stream. It's identified by the 4-tuple (source IP (Internet Protocol), source port, destination IP, destination port). In the scenario, Bob's browser creates a TCP socket to connect to Google's server on port 80 (or 443); the server has a welcoming socket on port 80 and creates a new connection socket for Bob's connection after the three-way handshake.

↑ Section 6.5
Q10

What format or formats does an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request have?

Answer

An HTTP/1.x request is ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) text in this format:

<method> <URL path> <version>          ← request line, e.g., GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
<header-name>: <value>                 ← header lines (Host:, User-Agent:, Accept:, Connection:, Cookie:, ...)
...
                                      ← blank line (CR LF)
<entity body>                          ← optional (e.g., form data for POST)

Methods: GET, POST, HEAD, PUT, DELETE (and others). HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry the same request in binary frames (headers compressed). (See Section 2.2.)

Acronyms: CR = Carriage Return; LF = Line Feed; URL = Uniform Resource Locator

↑ Section 6.5
Q11

What does DNS (Domain Name System) protocol or a DNS server do?

Answer

DNS translates host names into IP (Internet Protocol) addresses (and provides aliases, mail-server records, and load distribution). A DNS server holds resource records and answers queries; a local DNS server also resolves queries on behalf of clients by asking root, TLD (Top-Level Domain) and authoritative servers and caching the answers. In the scenario, the campus DNS server returns the IP address of www.google.com to Bob's laptop. (See Section 2.4.)

↑ Section 6.5
Q12

What information does a DNS (Domain Name System) query message provide?

Answer

A DNS query message contains:

  • a header with a 16-bit identification number (to match the reply), flags (it's a query; recursion desired), and counts;

  • the question section: the name being queried (e.g., www.google.com), the type of record wanted (e.g., A for an IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address, AAAA, MX (Mail Exchanger record)) and the class (IN).

It's sent in a UDP (User Datagram Protocol) segment to port 53 of the DNS server.

↑ Section 6.5
Q13

What does ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) protocol do?

Answer

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps an IP (Internet Protocol) address to a MAC (Medium Access Control) address on the local network. A host that needs to send a frame to an IP address on its subnet (e.g., the default gateway) but doesn't know the MAC address broadcasts an ARP query; the owner of that IP address replies with its MAC address; the sender caches it in its ARP table. (See Section 6.3 Q18.)

↑ Section 6.5
Q14

What information does an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) query message provide?

Answer

An ARP query (request) contains: the sender's MAC (Medium Access Control) address and IP (Internet Protocol) address, and the target IP address (the one whose MAC is wanted), with the target MAC field empty/zero; it also carries the operation code (request), hardware and protocol types and lengths. It's sent in an Ethernet frame with destination MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF (broadcast) so all nodes on the LAN (Local Area Network) receive it.

↑ Section 6.5
Q15

What information does an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) reply message have?

Answer

An ARP reply contains the target's MAC (Medium Access Control) address (the answer) together with its IP (Internet Protocol) address, plus the original requester's MAC and IP addresses as the destination fields, and opcode = reply. It's sent in a unicast Ethernet frame directly to the requester's MAC address. (In the scenario, the gateway router replies with the MAC address of its interface, e.g., 00:22:6B:45:1F:1B.)

↑ Section 6.5
Q16

What are intra-domain routing protocols?

Answer

Intra-domain (intra-AS) routing protocols — interior gateway protocols — compute routes within a single autonomous system/domain under one administration: RIP (Routing Information Protocol), OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) and EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol). They fill the forwarding tables inside the domain (e.g., in the scenario, inside the campus and Comcast networks). (See Section 5.3.)

↑ Section 6.5
Q17

How do RIP (Routing Information Protocol), OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), and IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) work?

Answer

  • RIP — distance-vector: each router exchanges its distance vector (hop counts, max 15) with neighbours every 30 s and applies Bellman-Ford; poisoned reverse; over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 520.

  • OSPF — link-state: each router floods link-state advertisements to all routers in its area, builds the full topology, and runs Dijkstra to compute shortest paths; supports areas, authentication and equal-cost multipath; runs directly over IP (Internet Protocol).

  • IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) — also link-state and very similar to OSPF (flooding + Dijkstra, two-level hierarchy of areas); originally an OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) protocol, runs directly over the link layer; popular in large ISP (Internet Service Provider) backbones.

(See Sections 5.2–5.3.)

↑ Section 6.5
Q18

What are the Internet’s inter-domain routing protocols?

Answer

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, version 4) is the Internet's (only) inter-domain (inter-AS (Autonomous System)) routing protocol, with eBGP (external Border Gateway Protocol) between ASes and iBGP (internal Border Gateway Protocol) within an AS.

↑ Section 6.5
Q19

What does the BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) protocol do?

Answer

BGP lets each AS (Autonomous System) learn which destination prefixes are reachable through its neighbouring ASes (eBGP (external Border Gateway Protocol)), propagate that reachability to all routers inside the AS (iBGP (internal Border Gateway Protocol)), and choose the best routes to each prefix based on policy and path attributes (local preference, AS-PATH length, hot-potato), while detecting loops with the AS-PATH. It is what lets separately run networks form one Internet. In the scenario, the Comcast router learned about Google's prefix via BGP from the AS that connects to Google. (See Section 5.4.)

↑ Section 6.5
Q20

What are DNS (Domain Name System) resource records?

Answer

DNS resource records (RRs) are the entries stored in the DNS distributed database, each a four-tuple (Name, Value, Type, TTL (Time-to-Live)). Types: A (host name → IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address), AAAA (→ IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6)), NS (Name Server record) (domain → authoritative name server), CNAME (Canonical Name record) (alias → canonical name), MX (Mail Exchanger record) (domain → mail server), plus PTR (Pointer record), SOA (Start of Authority record), TXT (Text record). DNS replies carry RRs. (See Section 2.4 Q14.)

↑ Section 6.5
Q21

What is an authoritative DNS (Domain Name System) server?

Answer

An authoritative DNS server is the server that holds the official (authoritative) records for a particular domain — e.g., Google's own DNS servers are authoritative for google.com — and gives definitive answers about hosts in that domain. The local DNS server may contact it (after root and TLD (Top-Level Domain) servers) to get the IP (Internet Protocol) address. (See Section 2.4 Q10.)

↑ Section 6.5
Q22

What information does a DNS (Domain Name System) reply message contain?

Answer

A DNS reply has the same format as the query: a header with the same identification number as the query, flags (it's a reply; whether it's authoritative; recursion available), counts; the question section (repeated); the answer section with the requested resource records (e.g., the A record giving www.google.com's IP (Internet Protocol) address, with its TTL (Time-to-Live)); plus an authority section (records of authoritative servers) and an additional section (extra helpful records, e.g., IP addresses of those servers).

↑ Section 6.5
Q23

How does a Web browser interact with a Web server at the transport and application layer?

Answer

  • Transport layer: the browser first opens a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection to the web server (IP (Internet Protocol) address from DNS (Domain Name System), port 80, or 443 for HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure)) with the three-way handshake: the client's TCP sends a SYN (Synchronize flag) segment, the server replies SYN-ACK (Acknowledgement), the client sends ACK. A connection socket now exists at both ends. (With HTTPS, a TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake follows.)

  • Application layer: the browser sends an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) GET request message into its socket; TCP carries it reliably to the server; the server's HTTP process reads it, finds the object and writes an HTTP response into its socket; TCP delivers it to the browser, which renders the page and then requests the embedded objects (over the same persistent connection in HTTP/1.1, or multiplexed in HTTP/2). Finally the connection is closed (FIN (Finish flag)/ACK) or kept alive.

↑ Section 6.5
Q24

What is an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) response?

Answer

An HTTP response is the message a web server sends back to a client in reply to an HTTP request. It tells the client the result of the request (status code) and, usually, carries the requested object (e.g., the HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) page, an image). In the scenario, Google's server sends an HTTP response containing the web page, which Bob's browser displays.

↑ Section 6.5
Q25

What may an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) response message contain?

Answer

An HTTP response message contains:

  • A status line: protocol version, status code and phrase — e.g., HTTP/1.1 200 OK (others: 301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 505 HTTP Version Not Supported).

  • Header lines — e.g., Date:, Server:, Last-Modified:, Content-Length:, Content-Type: (text/html, image/jpeg…), Connection:, Set-Cookie:, Cache-Control:, ETag (Entity Tag):.

  • A blank line.

  • The entity body — the requested object itself (HTML (Hypertext Markup Language), image, video, JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)…), or empty (e.g., for 304 or HEAD).

↑ Section 6.5

Textbook Review Questions — Chapter 6

16 questions (Kurose & Ross, 8th edition)

R1R2R3R4R5R6R7R8R9R10R11R12R13R14R15R16
R1

Consider the transportation analogy in Section 6.1.1. If the passenger is analagous to a datagram, what is analogous to the link layer frame?

Answer

In the analogy (a travel agent planning a trip from Princeton to Lausanne by limo, plane and train), the passenger = datagram, and the link-layer frame is the transportation vehicle carrying the passenger on each segment — the limousine, the plane, or the train. (Each transport segment = a link; each mode of transport = a link-layer protocol; the travel agent = the routing protocol.)

↑ Chapter 6 review
R2

If all the links in the Internet were to provide reliable delivery service, would the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reliable delivery service be redundant? Why or why not?

Answer

No, TCP would not be redundant. Even if every link were reliable, data could still be lost or corrupted inside routers (e.g., buffer overflow drops, errors in router memory/processing), packets could arrive out of order over different paths, and there are failures and reboots. Link-layer reliability only covers each individual link, not the end-to-end path. TCP also provides in-order delivery, flow control and congestion control end to end. (The end-to-end argument: reliability must ultimately be checked at the ends.)

↑ Chapter 6 review
R3

What are some of the possible services that a link-layer protocol can offer to the network layer? Which of these link-layer services have corresponding services in IP (Internet Protocol)? In TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)?

Answer

Possible link-layer services: framing, link access (MAC (Medium Access Control)), reliable delivery across the link, flow control between adjacent nodes, error detection, error correction, and half-duplex/full-duplex operation.

  • In IP: framing (IP also encapsulates in a datagram) and error detection (the IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) header checksum) have counterparts.

  • In TCP: framing (segments), reliable delivery, flow control and error detection (checksum) all have counterparts (end to end rather than per link); TCP is also full-duplex.

↑ Chapter 6 review
R4

Suppose two nodes start to transmit at the same time a packet of length L over a broadcast channel of rate R. Denote the propagation delay between the two nodes as dprop. Will there be a collision if d_prop < L/R? Why or why not?

Answer

Yes, there will be a collision. If d_prop < L/R, each node is still transmitting when the other node's first bit arrives (the other's signal reaches it after d_prop, before it has finished its own L/R transmission). So the two transmissions overlap at both nodes — a collision — and, because each node is still sending when the other's signal arrives, each can detect it (as CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) requires).

↑ Chapter 6 review
R5

In Section 6.3, we listed four desirable characteristics of a broadcast channel. Which of these characteristics does slotted ALOHA have? Which of these characteristics does token passing have?

Answer

The four desirable characteristics: (1) one active node gets rate R; (2) M active nodes each get R/M on average; (3) decentralised (no master); (4) simple and inexpensive.

  • Slotted ALOHA: has 1, 3 and 4. It doesn't satisfy 2 — with many active nodes, collisions and idle slots mean efficiency is at most 37%, so M nodes don't each get R/M. (It does need slot synchronisation.)

  • Token passing: has 1, 2 and 4. It's not fully decentralised (3) in the sense that the token is a critical element — if the token is lost or a node fails, the whole ring breaks (recovery procedures are needed). (Some add a small delay per node, so condition 1 is only approximately met.)

↑ Chapter 6 review
R6

In CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection), after the fifth collision, what is the probability that a node chooses K = 4? The result K = 4 corresponds to a delay of how many seconds on a 10 Mbps Ethernet?

Answer

After the fifth collision, K is chosen from {0, 1, 2, …, 2^5 − 1} = {0, …, 31} — 32 values. P(K = 4) = 1/32. The delay is K × 512 bit times = 4 × 512 = 2,048 bit times; at 10 Mbps one bit time is 0.1 µs, so the delay is 2,048 × 0.1 µs = 204.8 µs (0.0002048 s).

↑ Chapter 6 review
R7

Describe polling and token-passing protocols using the analogy of cocktail party interactions.

Answer

  • Polling: like a party with a host (moderator) who goes around the room and invites each guest in turn to speak ("Anything to say, Ann? Bob?"). Only the invited guest talks. Orderly, no one talks over another, but time is spent asking, and if the moderator leaves the conversation stops.

  • Token passing: like guests passing a "talking stick" (token) around the circle: only the person holding the stick may speak; when finished (or after a time limit) they pass it to the next person. No moderator is needed, but if someone drops or keeps the stick, the conversation stops.

↑ Chapter 6 review
R8

Why would the token-ring protocol be inefficient if a LAN (Local Area Network) had a very large perimeter?

Answer

Because the token takes a long time to travel around a ring with a large perimeter: when a node finishes sending, the token must propagate all the way to the next node(s), and a node wanting to send must wait for the token to come around. If the ring is long, the propagation delay is large compared with frame transmission times, so the channel is idle a large fraction of the time while the token travels — low efficiency. (A frame also has to travel all the way round before it's removed.)

↑ Chapter 6 review
R9

How big is the MAC (Medium Access Control) address space? The IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) address space? The IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) address space?

Answer

  • MAC address space: 48 bits → 2^48 ≈ 2.8 × 10^14 addresses.

  • IPv4: 32 bits → 2^32 ≈ 4.3 × 10^9 addresses.

  • IPv6: 128 bits → 2^128 ≈ 3.4 × 10^38 addresses.

↑ Chapter 6 review
R10

Suppose nodes A, B, and C each attach to the same broadcast LAN (Local Area Network) (through their adapters). If A sends thousands of IP (Internet Protocol) datagrams to B with each encapsulating frame addressed to the MAC (Medium Access Control) address of B, will C’s adapter process these frames? If so, will C’s adapter pass the IP datagrams in these frames to the network layer C? How would your answers change if A sends frames with the MAC broadcast address?

Answer

C's adapter will process the frames — on a broadcast LAN it receives every frame and examines the destination MAC address — but since the address is B's, not C's, the adapter discards them and does not pass the IP datagrams up to C's network layer.

If A sends frames with the MAC broadcast address (FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF), C's adapter will process them and pass the datagrams up to C's network layer (which will then check the IP address and, if it isn't for C, drop them).

↑ Chapter 6 review
R11

Why is an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) query sent within a broadcast frame? Why is an ARP response sent within a frame with a specific destination MAC (Medium Access Control) address?

Answer

  • ARP query → broadcast frame: the querying host knows only the target's IP (Internet Protocol) address, not its MAC address (that's what it's trying to find) and doesn't know which node on the LAN (Local Area Network) has that IP. So it must send the query to all nodes, using the broadcast MAC address, so the right one sees it.

  • ARP response → specific destination MAC: the responding node knows the MAC address of the node that sent the query (it was in the query), so it can reply directly (unicast) to that node; there's no need to bother every other node on the LAN.

↑ Chapter 6 review
R12

For the network in Figure 6.19, the router has two ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) modules, each with its own ARP table. Is it possible that the same MAC (Medium Access Control) address appears in both tables?

Answer

No. Each ARP module (one per router interface) maps IP (Internet Protocol) addresses to MAC addresses for the hosts on its own subnet — each subnet (LAN (Local Area Network)) has its own distinct set of adapters, each with a unique MAC address. A given MAC address belongs to one adapter on one subnet, so it can't appear in both tables (in normal operation).

↑ Chapter 6 review
R13

Compare the frame structures for 10BASE-T, 100BASE-T, and Gigabit Ethernet. How do they differ?

Answer

They are the same — 10BASE-T, 100BASE-T and Gigabit Ethernet all use the identical Ethernet frame structure (preamble, destination and source MAC (Medium Access Control), type, 46–1,500-byte data, CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check)). That's a key reason Ethernet evolved so smoothly. They differ only at the physical layer (speed, encoding, media), plus Gigabit's carrier extension/frame bursting in shared (half-duplex) mode.

↑ Chapter 6 review
R14

Consider Figure 6.15. How many subnetworks are there, in the addressing sense of Section 4.3?

Answer

Figure 6.15 is a network of four switches connecting three departments, a web server, a mail server and a router to the external Internet. Switches operate at the link layer and don't create new subnets, so in the addressing sense all the hosts, servers and the router's inner interface are in one subnet. (The router's other interface, toward the external Internet, is on a separate subnet — so the router joins two subnets in total, but the institutional network itself is a single subnet.)

↑ Chapter 6 review
R15

What is the maximum number of VLANs (Virtual Local Area Network) that can be configured on a switch supporting the 802.1Q protocol? Why?

Answer

4,094 VLANs. The 802.1Q tag's VLAN identifier field is 12 bits, giving 2^12 = 4,096 values; two values (0 and 4,095, i.e., 0x000 and 0xFFF) are reserved, leaving 4,094 usable VLANs.

↑ Chapter 6 review
R16

Suppose that N switches supporting K VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) groups are to be connected via a trunking protocol. How many ports are needed to connect the switches? Justify your answer.

Answer

Using a trunking protocol, one trunk link between two switches carries all K VLANs (frames are tagged with their VLAN ID (Identifier)), so each inter-switch connection needs just one port on each switch. Connecting N switches (e.g., in a chain or tree) needs N − 1 trunk links, i.e., 2(N − 1) ports in total — independent of K. (Without trunking you'd need a separate link for each VLAN: K(N − 1) links, 2K(N − 1) ports.)

↑ Chapter 6 review

Unit 7: Wireless and Mobile Networks

7.1 Wireless Networking7.2 Cellular Networks: 4G and 5G7.3 Mobility ManagementTextbook review questions — Chapter 7

Section 7.1: Wireless Networking

46 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20Q21Q22Q23Q24Q25Q26Q27Q28Q29Q30Q31Q32Q33Q34Q35Q36Q37Q38Q39Q40Q41Q42Q43Q44Q45Q46

Also asked in: Assignment 3 Q1.4, Assignment 3 Q1.6, Assignment 3 Q2.1, Assignment 3 Q2.4, Assignment 3 Q2.5

Q1

What electronic devices can be wireless hosts in wireless networks?

Answer

Any device with a wireless interface can be a wireless host: laptops, smartphones, tablets, desktop PCs (Personal Computer) with Wi-Fi, smart watches and wearables, smart TVs (Television) and streaming boxes, game consoles, printers, IoT (Internet of Things) devices (thermostats, cameras, smart speakers, sensors), cars, drones, and medical devices. Being wireless doesn't necessarily mean being mobile.

↑ Section 7.1
Q2

What is a wireless communication link?

Answer

A wireless communication link connects a wireless host to a base station (or to another host) using radio (or infrared) signals through the air instead of a cable. Links differ in transmission rate and range (e.g., Wi-Fi: hundreds of Mbps over tens of metres; 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular): tens–hundreds of Mbps over kilometres; Bluetooth: a few Mbps over ~10 m). A multiple-access protocol coordinates access to the shared link. Wireless links also connect base stations to each other or to the wired network in some designs.

↑ Section 7.1
Q3

What are the relationships between base stations and access points?

Answer

A base station is the general term for the device that connects wireless hosts to the larger (wired) network, relaying traffic between them and coordinating the hosts associated with it. An access point (AP) is the 802.11 (Wi-Fi) name for a base station; a cell tower (eNodeB/gNB) is the base station in cellular networks. So an access point is a kind of base station. Hosts associated with a base station are "in its range" and use it to send/receive data; when they move between base stations, a handoff occurs.

↑ Section 7.1
Q4

What are the differences between infrastructure mode wireless networks and ad hoc wireless networks?

Answer

  • Infrastructure mode: hosts connect through a base station/access point that is attached to the wired infrastructure; all traffic goes through the AP, and the network infrastructure provides services such as address assignment (DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)) and routing. Examples: home/office Wi-Fi, cellular.

  • Ad hoc mode: there's no base station and no infrastructure; hosts communicate directly with each other within range and must provide services (routing, addressing, name resolution) themselves. Examples: laptops sharing files directly, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi Direct, and multi-hop MANETs (Mobile Ad hoc Network)/VANETs (Vehicular Ad hoc Network) (mobile ad hoc and vehicular networks) where nodes relay for each other.

↑ Section 7.1
Q5

What are the parts of a wireless network infrastructure?

Answer

  • Wireless hosts (end systems).

  • Wireless links (radio channels).

  • Base stations / access points (Wi-Fi APs, cell towers).

  • The network infrastructure behind them — the wired network (switches, routers, the distribution system connecting APs, cellular core network, Internet connection) plus supporting services (DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), DNS (Domain Name System), authentication, mobility management).

↑ Section 7.1
Q6

Compare and contrast wired networks and wireless networks, emphasizing their differences.

Answer
Wired networks Wireless networks
Signal travels in a cable; little attenuation over short distances Decreasing signal strength (path loss) — the signal weakens quickly with distance and through obstacles
Little interference, very low bit-error rates Interference from other sources (other Wi-Fi, microwaves, Bluetooth, motors) and multipath fading → high bit-error rates
All nodes on a shared cable can hear each other → collision detection works (CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection)) Hidden terminal problem and fading: nodes may not hear each other; a transmitter can't hear collisions → collision avoidance (CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance)) + ACKs (Acknowledgement)
Reliable delivery usually left to TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) Link-layer ACKs/retransmission and error correction needed
Fixed location; physical access needed to tap Mobility, broadcast nature makes eavesdropping easy → encryption needed (WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3))
High, stable rates Rate adapts to channel conditions (SNR (Signal-to-Noise Ratio)); shared capacity
↑ Section 7.1
Q7

How does multipath propagation occur?

Answer

Multipath propagation occurs when a radio signal reflects off objects (walls, buildings, the ground, furniture, vehicles) and reaches the receiver along several paths of different lengths. The copies arrive at slightly different times and phases and combine — sometimes reinforcing, sometimes cancelling — which blurs (distorts) the received signal (fading, inter-symbol interference). Moving objects make it change over time.

↑ Section 7.1
Q8

What is the so-called hidden terminal problem?

Answer

The hidden terminal problem: stations A and C are both within range of B (e.g., an access point), but A and C cannot hear each other — because of an obstacle (a wall or hill) between them, or because they're too far apart (signal fading). A and C may transmit at the same time, both sensing an idle channel, and their frames collide at B without either detecting it. Carrier sensing fails, so 802.11 uses ACKs (Acknowledgement) and optional RTS (Request to Send)/CTS (Clear to Send) reservation to handle it.

↑ Section 7.1
Q9

What is the “chipping rate”?

Answer

The chipping rate is the rate at which chips (the bits of the CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access)/spreading code) are transmitted — M chips per data bit — so it's M times faster than the data rate. (See Section 6.3 Q9 and the formula above.)

↑ Section 7.1
Q10

How does CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access) work in wireless networks?

Answer

In CDMA, all users share the same frequency band at the same time, and each user is given a unique code. Each sender "spreads" its data by multiplying each data bit by its code (a sequence of chips at a much faster rate). The receiver, knowing the sender's code, correlates the combined received signal with that code to recover that sender's bits; if codes are orthogonal (or nearly so), other users' signals look like low-level noise and are filtered out. CDMA gives resistance to interference and jamming, allows many users without strict time or frequency slots, and was used in 3G (Third Generation cellular) cellular (and GPS (Global Positioning System)). In practice it needs power control so near users don't swamp far ones.

↑ Section 7.1
Q11

How does CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access) encode and decode data in wireless networks?

Answer

  • Encoding: a data bit d (+1 for 1, −1 for 0) is transmitted as M chips: Z_m = d × c_m, where c is the sender's M-chip code. So a 1 sends the code and a 0 sends its negative.

  • Channel: with several senders, the received chips are the sum of all senders' chips.

  • Decoding: to recover sender i's bit, multiply the received chips by sender i's code chip by chip, add them up and divide by M: d_i = (1/M) Σ Z*_m × c_i,m. Because codes are orthogonal, the other senders' contributions sum to 0, leaving d_i.

See the full worked example in "How the formulas work" above.

↑ Section 7.1
Q12

What IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) standard is used for wireless networking?

Answer

IEEE 802.11 ("Wi-Fi") for wireless LANs (Local Area Network) — variants 802.11b/a/g/n (Wi-Fi 4)/ac (Wi-Fi 5)/ax (Wi-Fi 6/6E)/be (Wi-Fi 7). Related: IEEE 802.15 for wireless personal area networks (Bluetooth basis, Zigbee 802.15.4), and 802.16 (WiMAX (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access)). Cellular uses 3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project) standards (LTE (Long-Term Evolution), 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) NR (New Radio)).

↑ Section 7.1
Q13

What is a basic service set (BSS)?

Answer

A basic service set (BSS) is the fundamental building block of an 802.11 network: one or more wireless stations plus a central base station — the access point (AP). (Without an AP, a group of stations forms an independent BSS — an ad hoc network.) Several BSSs joined by a distribution system form an extended service set (ESS).

↑ Section 7.1
Q14

What do SSID (Service Set Identifier) and Wi-Fi stand for?

Answer

  • SSID = Service Set Identifier — the network name (up to 32 characters) that an administrator assigns to an access point/BSS (Basic Service Set) (e.g., "HomeWiFi"); it's broadcast in beacon frames so users can choose which network to join.

  • Wi-Fi is a trademark of the Wi-Fi Alliance for products certified to interoperate using the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 standards. It's often said to stand for "Wireless Fidelity" (a marketing play on "Hi-Fi"), but officially it isn't an acronym.

↑ Section 7.1
Q15

What is a distribution system in wireless networking?

Answer

A distribution system (DS) is the network that interconnects the access points (BSSs (Basic Service Set)) of an extended service set — usually the wired Ethernet LAN (Local Area Network) (switches and routers) behind the APs (sometimes a wireless mesh). It carries frames between APs and between the WLAN (Wireless Local Area Network) and the rest of the network (e.g., the router to the Internet), allowing hosts to move between APs within the same subnet.

↑ Section 7.1
Q16

What is CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance)?

Answer

CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance) is 802.11's random-access MAC (Medium Access Control) protocol:

1. If a station senses the channel idle for DIFS (Distributed Inter-Frame Space), it may transmit (in practice it also does step 2).

2. Otherwise it picks a random backoff value and counts down only while the channel is idle (freezes while busy).

3. When the counter reaches zero, it transmits the entire frame (no collision detection) and waits for an ACK (Acknowledgement).

4. The receiver, if the frame's CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) is OK, waits SIFS (Short Inter-Frame Space) and sends an ACK.

5. If no ACK arrives, the sender assumes a collision/error, picks a backoff from a larger range (exponential backoff) and retries.

Optionally, RTS (Request to Send)/CTS (Clear to Send) frames reserve the channel before long frames (collision avoidance, hidden terminals).

↑ Section 7.1
Q17

What are DIFS (Distributed Inter-Frame Space) and SIFS (Short Inter-Frame Space)?

Answer

They are inter-frame spaces (waiting times) in 802.11:

  • DIFS (Distributed Inter-Frame Space): the longer idle time a station must sense before starting a new transmission (e.g., 50 µs in 802.11b; 34 µs in 802.11a/g/n).

  • SIFS (Short Inter-Frame Space): the shorter gap used before responses in an ongoing exchange — ACK (Acknowledgement), CTS (Clear to Send), and the DATA after a CTS (e.g., 10 µs in 802.11b; 16 µs in 802.11a).

Because SIFS < DIFS, the responding station always gets the channel before any new sender can start, so an exchange isn't interrupted.

↑ Section 7.1
Q18

Why doesn’t the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 MAC (Medium Access Control) protocol implement collision detection?

Answer

Two reasons:

  • Detecting collisions needs a station to send and receive at the same time (full duplex). A wireless station's own transmitted signal is far stronger than a weak incoming signal, so it can't hear a collision while transmitting (that would need costly hardware).

  • Even if it could, the hidden terminal problem and fading mean it wouldn't detect all collisions — collisions happen at the receiver, which the sender may not be able to hear.

So 802.11 avoids collisions (CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance), random backoff, RTS (Request to Send)/CTS (Clear to Send)) and uses link-layer ACKs (Acknowledgement) to learn whether a frame got through; once a station starts sending a frame, it sends the whole frame.

↑ Section 7.1
Q19

In an IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 wireless network, why can hidden terminals be problematic? How does the standard deal with the problem? What format does an IEEE 802.11 standard use for its frame?

Answer

Why problematic: hidden stations can't hear each other, so carrier sensing doesn't stop them from transmitting simultaneously; their frames collide at the AP (Access Point), wasting the whole transmission time, and neither sender detects it (they only notice missing ACKs (Acknowledgement)).

How 802.11 deals with it — RTS (Request to Send)/CTS (Clear to Send) reservation (optional):

1. The sender transmits a short RTS (Request to Send) frame to the AP, stating the total time needed.

2. The AP broadcasts a CTS (Clear to Send) frame, which all stations in range of the AP hear — including hidden ones — telling the sender to go ahead and all others to stay quiet for that duration (they set their NAV (Network Allocation Vector)).

3. The sender transmits the data; the AP ACKs.

Collisions can now only happen with the short RTS frames. Because RTS/CTS adds delay, it's used only above an RTS threshold frame length.

802.11 frame format:

Field Size (bytes) Purpose
Frame control 2 Protocol version, type/subtype (data, RTS, CTS, ACK, beacon…), To DS (Distribution System) / From DS, more fragments, retry, power management, more data, protected (WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy)/WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access)), order
Duration 2 Time the channel is reserved (for RTS/CTS/data)
Address 1 6 MAC (Medium Access Control) of the receiving wireless station/AP
Address 2 6 MAC of the transmitting station/AP
Address 3 6 MAC of the router interface (or other device) connected to the AP — needed to bridge to Ethernet
Sequence control 2 Sequence number (to detect duplicate retransmissions) and fragment number
Address 4 6 Used only in ad hoc/mesh or AP-to-AP (wireless distribution) mode
Payload 0–2,312 Usually an IP (Internet Protocol) datagram (or ARP (Address Resolution Protocol))
CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) 4 Error detection
↑ Section 7.1
Q20

In order to accommodate mobile users, what considerations should be taken when designing the network layer?

Answer

  • Addressing: a mobile node should keep a permanent address so others can reach it and ongoing connections (which are identified by IP (Internet Protocol) addresses) don't break; yet IP addresses normally indicate location.

  • Routing/forwarding to the current location: how to find where the mobile is and deliver its datagrams — let routing handle it (advertise the mobile's address — doesn't scale) or let end systems/agents handle it (home agent, foreign agent, care-of addresses — indirect or direct routing).

  • Location management/registration — tracking the mobile's current network.

  • Handoff with minimal disruption and packet loss; transparency to applications and correspondents; scalability (millions of mobiles); efficiency (avoid triangle routing); security (authenticate location updates).

↑ Section 7.1
Q21

From the standpoint of network layers, how mobile is a user?

Answer

From the network layer's viewpoint, mobility is a spectrum:

  • No mobility — a user who moves only within the same access network (e.g., roams among APs (Access Point) in one building on the same subnet) — the IP (Internet Protocol) address doesn't change; the network layer barely notices.

  • Moderate mobility — a user who moves between access networks but switches off while moving (e.g., a laptop used at home, then at a coffee shop) — gets a new address each time; no ongoing connections need to survive.

  • High mobility — a user who moves between access networks while keeping connections alive (e.g., on a phone call or video stream in a moving car or train) — the network layer must support ongoing sessions across changes of network (handoffs).

↑ Section 7.1
Q22

How important is the mobile node’s address?

Answer

Very important: ongoing connections (TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sessions) are identified by IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, so if a mobile's address changed mid-session, the connection would break, and correspondents would no longer know how to reach it. Hence mobility schemes keep a permanent (home) address that stays fixed so the mobile appears to be always at home to correspondents, while a care-of address in the visited network tells the infrastructure where it currently is. Whether the address must be kept depends on the application — for short, restartable sessions (web browsing) a new address is fine.

↑ Section 7.1
Q23

What supporting wired infrastructure is available for supporting wireless connections?

Answer

Supporting wired infrastructure includes: base stations/access points connected to the wired LAN (Local Area Network) or distribution system (Ethernet switches), routers and the Internet backbone, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) and DNS (Domain Name System) servers, authentication servers (RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) for 802.1X), wireless LAN controllers that manage many APs, and for cellular — the radio access network backhaul and the core network (MME (Mobility Management Entity), HSS (Home Subscriber Server), serving and PDN (Packet Data Network) gateways, 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) core functions). For mobility: home agents, foreign agents and location databases (HLR (Home Location Register)/VLR (Visitor Location Register), HSS).

↑ Section 7.1
Q24

What is ad hoc networking?

Answer

Ad hoc networking is wireless networking without any base station or wired infrastructure: hosts communicate directly with each other when in range. If they're out of range, other nodes may relay packets (multi-hop ad hoc networks — MANETs (Mobile Ad hoc Network); vehicular — VANETs (Vehicular Ad hoc Network)). The nodes themselves must provide routing, address assignment and other services. Uses: disaster recovery, military, sensor networks, temporary meetings, device-to-device sharing (Bluetooth, Wi-Fi Direct).

↑ Section 7.1
Q25

What issues are involved in allowing a mobile user to maintain ongoing connections while moving between networks?

Answer

  • Address: keeping an address that correspondents and existing TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections use, even though the node's point of attachment changes.

  • Locating the mobile: registering its current location (care-of address) with a home agent/database.

  • Routing datagrams to it wherever it is — indirect routing (via home agent, triangle routing, inefficient) or direct routing (correspondent learns the care-of address; more complex, needs handling of moves between foreign networks).

  • Handoff — moving between networks quickly with minimal packet loss/delay, forwarding packets from old to new network (anchor).

  • Security — authenticating registrations and preventing hijacking; transparency to applications; scalability; performance (TCP may treat handoff losses as congestion).

↑ Section 7.1
Q26

What do the terms home network, home agent, foreign (or visited) network, foreign agent, and correspondent mean?

Answer

  • Home network: the permanent "home" network of the mobile node (e.g., its ISP (Internet Service Provider) or company network), whose address prefix its permanent address belongs to.

  • Home agent: an entity (usually a router) in the home network that tracks the mobile's current location (care-of address) and forwards datagrams addressed to the mobile's permanent address to it (tunnelling).

  • Foreign (visited) network: the network the mobile is currently in, away from home.

  • Foreign agent: an entity (router) in the foreign network that helps the mobile — provides/creates its care-of address, registers it with the home agent, and delivers forwarded datagrams to it (decapsulating the tunnel).

  • Correspondent: any node that wants to communicate with the mobile node (e.g., a web server or someone calling it).

↑ Section 7.1
Q27

Why should all traffic addressed to a mobile node’s permanent address be routed to the foreign network when the node is a resident of a foreign network? How can this be done?

Answer

Because the mobile node is no longer attached to its home network — traffic delivered to the home network would never reach it. The mobile wants to keep its permanent address (so correspondents and ongoing connections are unaffected), so datagrams sent to that address must be redirected to its current location in the foreign network.

How: the mobile registers a care-of address (COA) with its home agent (via the foreign agent). The home agent intercepts datagrams addressed to the permanent address and encapsulates (tunnels) them in new datagrams addressed to the COA. The foreign agent (or mobile) decapsulates them and delivers them. (Alternatively, direct routing: the correspondent obtains the COA and sends directly.) Another option — letting routing advertise the mobile's address from the foreign network — doesn't scale to millions of mobiles.

↑ Section 7.1
Q28

What roles does a foreign agent play?

Answer

A foreign agent:

  • Advertises its presence (agent advertisements) so mobiles know they're in a foreign network.

  • Provides (or helps obtain) a care-of address (COA) for the mobile — often its own address.

  • Registers the mobile's COA with the mobile's home agent (relaying registration request and reply).

  • Receives the tunnelled (encapsulated) datagrams from the home agent, decapsulates them and forwards them to the mobile node.

  • May act as the mobile's default router for outgoing datagrams.

↑ Section 7.1
Q29

What is a care-of-address?

Answer

A care-of address (COA) is the address that identifies the mobile node's current location in the foreign network — datagrams tunnelled by the home agent are addressed to it. It's typically the foreign agent's address (foreign-agent COA) or an address obtained by the mobile itself in the foreign network (co-located COA, e.g., via DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)). A mobile has a permanent address plus, when away, a COA.

↑ Section 7.1
Q30

What is a home address? What is a foreign address?

Answer

  • Home address (permanent address): the mobile node's long-term IP (Internet Protocol) address in its home network; correspondents always use it to reach the mobile; it doesn't change as the mobile moves.

  • Foreign address: the address associated with the mobile in the foreign (visited) network — i.e., its care-of address (COA), which shows where it currently is. (The textbook uses "permanent address" and "care-of address/foreign address".)

↑ Section 7.1
Q31

How does indirect routing work?

Answer

Indirect routing:

1. The correspondent sends a datagram to the mobile's permanent (home) address as usual — it doesn't need to know the mobile has moved.

2. The datagram is routed to the home network, where the home agent intercepts it.

3. The home agent encapsulates it in a new datagram addressed to the mobile's care-of address and tunnels it to the foreign network.

4. The foreign agent receives it, decapsulates it and delivers the original datagram to the mobile.

5. The mobile replies directly to the correspondent (using its permanent address as the source).

This is transparent to the correspondent, and ongoing connections survive moves (the mobile just registers a new COA (Care-of Address)).

↑ Section 7.1
Q32

How does the mobile node to foreign agent protocol work?

Answer

When a mobile enters a foreign network:

1. Agent discovery: the mobile learns of the foreign agent — via agent advertisements (ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) router advertisements with a mobility extension) or by sending an agent solicitation.

2. Registration: the mobile sends a registration request (over UDP (User Datagram Protocol), port 434) to the foreign agent, containing its permanent address, home agent address, the COA (Care-of Address), requested lifetime and an identification number.

3. The foreign agent relays the request to the home agent, which records the binding (permanent address ↔︎ COA) and sends back a registration reply.

4. The foreign agent relays the reply to the mobile and records it (so it can deliver tunnelled datagrams).

The mobile must re-register before the lifetime expires and when it moves. In the course's general model: the mobile contacts the foreign agent, which informs the home agent of the mobile's location.

↑ Section 7.1
Q33

What problem does the indirect routing approach suffer from?

Answer

Triangle routing inefficiency: every datagram from the correspondent goes first to the home network and then to the foreign network, even when a much more direct path exists between correspondent and mobile — e.g., if both are in the same foreign country and the home network is far away. This adds delay and wastes network resources, and the home agent becomes a bottleneck/single point of failure.

↑ Section 7.1
Q34

How does the direct routing approach work?

Answer

Direct routing:

1. A correspondent agent in the correspondent's network asks the mobile's home agent for the mobile's current care-of address (location query).

2. The home agent replies with the COA (Care-of Address).

3. The correspondent agent tunnels datagrams directly to the COA (to the foreign agent), bypassing the home network.

4. The foreign agent decapsulates and delivers them to the mobile.

It avoids triangle routing, but it's not transparent to the correspondent (which must obtain the COA), and when the mobile moves to another foreign network a mechanism is needed: the first foreign network becomes the anchor foreign agent, which forwards datagrams on to the new foreign network.

↑ Section 7.1
Q35

What is a correspondent agent in the direct routing approach?

Answer

The correspondent agent is the entity in the correspondent's network that (in direct routing) learns the mobile's care-of address by querying the home agent and then tunnels datagrams directly to the mobile's foreign agent. (The correspondent host itself could play this role.)

↑ Section 7.1
Q36

What is mobile IP (Internet Protocol)? Which standard defines mobile IP?

Answer

Mobile IP is the Internet architecture and protocols for supporting mobility of IP hosts — letting a mobile keep its permanent IP address while moving among networks, using home agents, foreign agents, care-of addresses and indirect routing (with optional route optimisation).
