It's defined by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) in RFC (Request for Comments) 5944 (IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4), "IP Mobility Support for IPv4, Revised", updating the original RFC 3344/3220/2002); Mobile IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) is RFC 6275.

↑ Section 7.1
Q37

What are the three main pieces of the mobile IP (Internet Protocol) standard?

Answer

1. Agent discovery — how agents advertise their services to mobiles, and how mobiles solicit agents.

2. Registration with the home agent — how a mobile (via the foreign agent) registers and deregisters its care-of addresses with its home agent.

3. Indirect routing of datagrams — how home agents forward (encapsulate/tunnel) datagrams to mobiles, including forwarding rules, error handling and encapsulation formats.

↑ Section 7.1
Q38

What is done in the process of agent discovery?

Answer

Agent discovery is how a mobile node arriving in a new network learns the identity of the foreign (or home) agent — and thereby whether it has moved to a foreign network and what care-of address to use. It's done in two ways: agent advertisement (agents periodically broadcast their presence) and agent solicitation (the mobile broadcasts a request for agents to announce themselves).

↑ Section 7.1
Q39

What is done in the process of agent advertisement?

Answer

In agent advertisement, a foreign or home agent periodically broadcasts an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) message (type 9, router discovery) with a mobility agent advertisement extension on all links it serves. It contains the agent's IP (Internet Protocol) address, and indicates whether it's a home agent (H bit) and/or foreign agent (F bit), whether registration is required (R bit), the supported encapsulation types (M, G bits), the registration lifetime, and one or more care-of addresses the mobile can use. Mobiles hearing it learn which agent to register with.

↑ Section 7.1
Q40

What does agent solicitation do?

Answer

Agent solicitation: a mobile node that wants to learn about agents without waiting for the next periodic advertisement broadcasts a solicitation message — an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) message of type 10 (router solicitation). Any agent receiving it immediately unicasts an agent advertisement back to the mobile, which can then register.

↑ Section 7.1
Q41

What is the format of an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) router discovery message with mobility agent advertisement?

Answer

An ICMP router discovery message (type 9) with the mobility agent advertisement extension:

  • Standard ICMP router-advertisement part: type = 9, code = 0, checksum, number of addresses, address entry size, lifetime, and the router address(es) (the agent's IP (Internet Protocol) address) with preference levels.

  • Mobility agent advertisement extension: type = 16, length, sequence number (to detect reboots), registration lifetime (maximum time the agent will accept for registration), flag bits — R (registration required), B (busy), H (home agent), F (foreign agent), M (minimal encapsulation), G (GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) encapsulation), plus others — and zero or more care-of addresses (COA 1, COA 2, …) supported by the foreign agent.

↑ Section 7.1
Q42

According to the mobile IP (Internet Protocol) standard, how does a mobile node register its care-of address (COA) with its home agent?

Answer

Registration (via a foreign agent, using UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 434):

1. After agent discovery, the mobile sends a Mobile IP registration request to the foreign agent, including: its home (permanent) address, its home agent's address, the care-of address, the requested registration lifetime, a 64-bit identification (to match replies and prevent replay), and flags (e.g., encapsulation type).

2. The foreign agent records the information and forwards the registration request to the home agent (UDP 434).

3. The home agent checks the request (authentication), binds the mobile's permanent address to the COA, and sends back a registration reply (with the granted lifetime and the identification number).

4. The foreign agent receives the reply and forwards it to the mobile.

Registration must be renewed before the lifetime expires. (With a co-located COA the mobile registers directly with the home agent.)

↑ Section 7.1
Q43

How do wireless stations move seamlessly from one BBS to another while maintaining ongoing TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sessions?

Answer

If the BSSs (Basic Service Set) are in the same IP (Internet Protocol) subnet (APs (Access Point) connected to the same Ethernet switch/router interface), the station can keep its IP address, so TCP sessions continue:

1. As the signal from the old AP weakens, the station scans and associates with a new AP in the new BSS (authentication and association frames).

2. The switch must learn the station's new location: after association, the new AP sends an Ethernet broadcast frame with the station's source MAC (Medium Access Control) address (it "spoofs" the station's MAC), so the self-learning switch updates its table — frames for the station now go out the port toward the new AP.

3. Traffic flows through the new AP; the IP address and TCP connection are unchanged.

(Enterprise networks use controllers and 802.11r fast roaming to speed this up. Moving between different subnets requires Mobile IP or similar.)

↑ Section 7.1
Q44

What are the main features of 802.15 wireless networks?

Answer

IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.15 covers wireless personal area networks (WPANs) — short range (~10 m, up to ~100 m for some classes), low power, low cost, cable replacement between devices such as phones, headsets, keyboards, mice, sensors. Features: operates in the 2.4 GHz unlicensed band; ad hoc — no infrastructure needed; master-slave (controller/peripheral) organisation in piconets (one master + up to 7 active slaves, and up to 255 parked); TDM (Time Division Multiplexing) with 625 µs slots; frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) over 79 channels, 1,600 hops/s; data rates from ~1 to 3 Mbps (classic Bluetooth). 802.15.4 (basis of Zigbee and Thread) targets even lower-power, lower-rate sensor/IoT (Internet of Things) networks.

↑ Section 7.1
Q45

How is a Bluetooth network related to 802.15 wireless networks?

Answer

Bluetooth is the technology that IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.15.1 was based on — the IEEE standardised the Bluetooth (v1.1) physical and MAC (Medium Access Control) layers as 802.15.1. Today Bluetooth is maintained by the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) rather than the IEEE, but it is the best-known 802.15 WPAN (Wireless Personal Area Network) technology (802.15.4 covers Zigbee-style networks).

↑ Section 7.1
Q46

What do FHSS (Frequency-Hopping Spread Spectrum) and PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) stand for?

Answer

  • FHSS = Frequency-Hopping Spread Spectrum — the transmitter rapidly hops among many frequency channels in a pseudo-random sequence known to the receiver (Bluetooth: 79 channels, 1,600 hops/s), reducing interference and eavesdropping.

  • PSTN = Public Switched Telephone Network — the traditional circuit-switched telephone network.

↑ Section 7.1

Section 7.2: Cellular Networks: 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) and 5G (Fifth Generation cellular)

27 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20Q21Q22Q23Q24Q25Q26Q27

Also asked in: Assignment 3 Q1.2

Q1

How do TDM (Time Division Multiplexing) and FDM (Frequency Division Multiplexing) work?

Answer

  • TDM (time-division multiplexing): time is divided into repeating frames, each split into slots; each user/call is given one slot per frame and uses the whole channel bandwidth during its slot. Users take turns very quickly, so each gets a fraction (1/N) of the rate.

  • FDM (frequency-division multiplexing): the channel's frequency spectrum is divided into separate bands; each user gets its own band and transmits continuously in it (like radio stations).

In cellular (e.g., GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications)), both are combined: the spectrum is split into frequency channels (FDM), and each channel is split into time slots (TDM) — each call gets one slot in one frequency channel.

↑ Section 7.2
Q2

What are the main features of GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) networks?

Answer

GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) — the main 2G (Second Generation cellular) standard:

  • Digital, circuit-switched voice (plus SMS (Short Message Service) and low-rate data).

  • Combined FDMA (Frequency Division Multiple Access)/TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access) radio: 200 kHz frequency channels, each with 8 time slots (8 simultaneous calls per channel).

  • Architecture: mobile station with a SIM (Subscriber Identity Module) card; BTS (base transceiver station, in each cell); BSC (base station controller, managing several BTSs — allocating channels, paging, handoffs); together the BSS (base station system); MSC (Mobile Switching Center) (mobile switching centre — call setup/teardown, mobility, connects to the PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network), gateway MSC); databases HLR (home location register — permanent subscriber info and current location) and VLR (visitor location register — users currently in the MSC's area), AuC (Authentication Center) (authentication).

  • Authentication and encryption of the radio link, international roaming, handoffs between cells (with an anchor MSC).

↑ Section 7.2
Q3

What are the main features of GPRS (General Packet Radio Service) networks?

Answer

GPRS (General Packet Radio Service) — 2.5G (Second-and-a-half Generation cellular) — added packet-switched data to GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications):

  • Packet switching over the GSM radio network: time slots are allocated on demand to data users (several slots can be combined), instead of dedicating a circuit.

  • "Always-on" Internet connection; billing by data volume rather than connection time.

  • Data rates of roughly tens of kbps (up to ~100+ kbps); EDGE (Enhanced Data rates for GSM Evolution) later improved this (~200–400 kbps).

  • New core nodes: SGSN (serving GPRS support node — delivers packets to mobiles in its area, mobility, authentication) and GGSN (gateway GPRS support node — gateway to the Internet/IP (Internet Protocol) networks), with GTP (GPRS Tunnelling Protocol) tunnels between them — the ancestor of 3G (Third Generation cellular)/4G (Fourth Generation cellular) data cores.

↑ Section 7.2
Q4

What is the triangle routing problem?

Answer

The triangle routing problem is the inefficiency of indirect routing to a mobile node: datagrams from a correspondent must go first to the mobile's home network (home agent) and then be tunnelled to the mobile's current (foreign) network, even when the correspondent and the mobile are close together — forming a triangle (correspondent → home → mobile, with replies going straight back). It adds delay and load. Direct routing avoids it. (See Section 7.1 Q33.)

↑ Section 7.2
Q5

How do mobile user location protocols work?

Answer

Mobile user location protocols keep track of where each mobile currently is so calls/datagrams can be delivered:

  • The home network keeps a database of its subscribers and their current location (GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) HLR (Home Location Register), 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) HSS (Home Subscriber Server), Mobile IP (Internet Protocol) home agent).

  • When a mobile enters a visited network, it registers there (visited network's VLR (Visitor Location Register)/MME (Mobility Management Entity) or foreign agent), and the visited network informs the home network of the mobile's location (e.g., the address of the visited MSC (Mobile Switching Center), or the care-of address). The home network may tell the old visited network to delete its record.

  • To reach the mobile, a caller's network queries the home network for the current location (e.g., an MSRN — mobile station roaming number — in GSM), then routes the call/datagrams to the visited network, which pages the mobile within its location area.

  • Mobiles also send periodic location/tracking-area updates as they move within a network.

↑ Section 7.2
Q6

How do handoffs happen in GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) networks?

Answer

GSM handoff (within the area of one MSC (Mobile Switching Center)):

1. The mobile continuously measures the signal strength of beacons from its current BSS (Base Station System) and neighbouring BSSs and reports to its current BSS.

2. The old BSS decides to hand off (e.g., the signal is getting weak or the cell is overloaded) and informs the MSC, listing candidate BSSs.

3. The MSC sets up a path (allocates resources) to the new BSS.

4. The new BSS allocates a radio channel for the mobile and signals the MSC and the old BSS that it's ready.

5. The old BSS tells the mobile to switch to the new BSS (the new channel).

6. The mobile activates the new channel and signals the new BSS.

7. The mobile signals the MSC via the new BSS that handoff is complete; the MSC reroutes the call.

8. Resources along the old path are released.

When moving between MSCs, the anchor MSC (the first MSC of the call) stays in the path, and the call is extended from it to the new MSC, so only the last leg changes.

↑ Section 7.2
Q7

How can calls be routed to a mobile user in mobile networks?

Answer

Calls to a mobile use indirect routing through the home network:

1. The correspondent dials the mobile's phone number; the call reaches the home network (gateway MSC (Mobile Switching Center)).

2. The home MSC looks up the HLR (Home Location Register) to find the mobile's current location — the HLR returns a roaming number (MSRN (Mobile Station Roaming Number)) obtained from the visited network's VLR (Visitor Location Register).

3. The home MSC sets up the second leg of the call to the visited network's MSC using the roaming number.

4. The visited MSC pages the mobile in its area and completes the call through the base station serving it.

The home network is always the first point of contact (like indirect routing in Mobile IP (Internet Protocol)), and later legs can change with handoffs (anchor MSC).

↑ Section 7.2
Q8

What are the main components of cellular network architecture?

Answer

Main components (4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/LTE (Long-Term Evolution) in textbook terms):

  • Mobile device (UE (User Equipment)) with a SIM (Subscriber Identity Module) storing the IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity) and keys.

  • Base stations (eNodeB in 4G, gNB in 5G (Fifth Generation cellular)) — radio access; manage the radio resources of their cells; handover.

  • Radio access network (base stations and backhaul).

  • Core network: MME (Mobility Management Entity) (mobility management, authentication, tracking, tunnel setup), HSS (Home Subscriber Server) (subscriber database), S-GW (serving gateway — data-plane anchor for mobility within the network) and P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway) (PDN gateway — gateway to the Internet, assigns IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, NAT (Network Address Translation)/policy).

  • Connection to the Internet and to other carriers' networks (roaming).

(In 2G (Second Generation cellular)/3G (Third Generation cellular): BTS (Base Transceiver Station)/NodeB, BSC (Base Station Controller)/RNC (Radio Network Controller), MSC (Mobile Switching Center), HLR (Home Location Register)/VLR (Visitor Location Register), SGSN (Serving GPRS Support Node)/GGSN (Gateway GPRS Support Node).)

↑ Section 7.2
Q9

What are some important standards and technologies for cellular networks?

Answer

  • 2G (Second Generation cellular): GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) (TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access)/FDMA (Frequency Division Multiple Access)), IS-136 (Interim Standard 136) (TDMA), IS-95 (Interim Standard 95) cdmaOne (CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access)).

  • 2.5G (Second-and-a-half Generation cellular): GPRS (General Packet Radio Service), EDGE (Enhanced Data rates for GSM Evolution).

  • 3G (Third Generation cellular): UMTS (Universal Mobile Telecommunications System)/WCDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access) (3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project)), CDMA2000/EV-DO (Evolution-Data Optimized) (3GPP2 (3rd Generation Partnership Project 2)), HSPA (High Speed Packet Access)/HSPA+.

  • 4G (Fourth Generation cellular): LTE (Long-Term Evolution) / LTE-Advanced (3GPP), (WiMAX (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access) 802.16).

  • 5G (Fifth Generation cellular): 5G NR (New Radio) and the 5G Core (3GPP Release 15 onward), including mmWave.

Technologies: FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, OFDM (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing)/OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access), MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output) and beamforming, carrier aggregation, VoLTE (Voice over Long-Term Evolution)/IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem). Standards bodies: 3GPP, ITU (International Telecommunication Union) (IMT (International Mobile Telecommunications)-2000, IMT-Advanced, IMT-2020).

↑ Section 7.2
Q10

What role or roles does a Radio Network Controller (RNC) play on a 3G (Third Generation cellular) cellular network?

Answer

In 3G (UMTS (Universal Mobile Telecommunications System)), the Radio Network Controller (RNC) controls a group of base stations (Node Bs) — like GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications)'s BSC (Base Station Controller). It:

  • manages radio resources — channel allocation, power control, admission control;

  • controls handoffs/handovers between cells (including soft handover in CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access));

  • performs mobility management within its area and paging;

  • handles encryption of the radio link;

  • connects the radio access network to the core network — to the MSC (Mobile Switching Center) for circuit-switched voice and to the SGSN (Serving GPRS Support Node) for packet data.

↑ Section 7.2
Q11

What are the differences between 3G (Third Generation cellular) cellular network and 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) LTE (Long-Term Evolution) cellular network?

Answer
3G 4G LTE
Radio: WCDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access)/CDMA2000 (code division) Radio: OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access) downlink, SC-FDMA (Single-Carrier Frequency Division Multiple Access) uplink — combined frequency + time slots; MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output)
Separate circuit-switched core for voice and packet core for data All-IP (Internet Protocol) — a single packet core (EPC (Evolved Packet Core)); voice is just IP data (VoLTE (Voice over Long-Term Evolution))
Hierarchical: Node B + RNC (Radio Network Controller) controller Flatter: eNodeB does the RNC's job; no RNC
Data rates: hundreds of kbps to a few/tens of Mbps (HSPA (High Speed Packet Access)+) Tens to hundreds of Mbps (LTE-A (Long-Term Evolution Advanced) >1 Gbps peak); lower latency
Core nodes SGSN (Serving GPRS Support Node)/GGSN (Gateway GPRS Support Node), MSC (Mobile Switching Center) MME (Mobility Management Entity), HSS (Home Subscriber Server), S-GW (Serving Gateway), P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway) — separate control plane and data plane
↑ Section 7.2
Q12

What are the three sublayers of the mobile device’s link layer on a 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) LTE (Long-Term Evolution) cellular network? What role does each sublayer play?

Answer

The mobile device's link layer in LTE has three sublayers:

  • PDCP (Packet Data Convergence Protocol): IP (Internet Protocol) header compression (to save radio bandwidth) and encryption/decryption of the IP datagram (security), plus sequencing/duplicate removal during handover.

  • RLC (Radio Link Control): fragmentation and reassembly of IP datagrams that are too large for the radio frames, and link-layer reliable data transfer with an ACK (Acknowledgement)/NAK (Negative Acknowledgement)-based ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest) protocol.

  • MAC (Medium Access Control): requests and uses radio transmission slots (the base station schedules them), handles HARQ (Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest) (hybrid ARQ with error correction/retransmission), and multiplexing of logical channels.

↑ Section 7.2
Q13

What is the 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) Core network?

Answer

The 4G core network — the Evolved Packet Core (EPC) — is the all-IP (Internet Protocol) core of an LTE (Long-Term Evolution) network that sits between the radio access network (base stations) and the Internet/other networks. It consists mainly of the MME (Mobility Management Entity), HSS (Home Subscriber Server), Serving Gateway (S-GW) and PDN (Packet Data Network) Gateway (P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway)) (plus the PCRF (Policy and Charging Rules Function) for policy), with separate control plane (MME, HSS) and data plane (S-GW, P-GW).

↑ Section 7.2
Q14

What does the 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) Core network do?

Answer

The 4G core network:

  • Authenticates devices and the network (MME (Mobility Management Entity) with HSS (Home Subscriber Server)) and handles security (keys).

  • Manages mobility — tracking where devices are (tracking areas), paging, and coordinating handovers (MME).

  • Sets up data paths — tunnels (GTP (GPRS Tunnelling Protocol)) from the base station through the S-GW (Serving Gateway) to the P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway) for each device's traffic.

  • Assigns IP (Internet Protocol) addresses to devices and acts as the gateway to the Internet (P-GW), including NAT (Network Address Translation), filtering, QoS (Quality of Service) and policy enforcement, and charging/billing.

  • Anchors mobility (S-GW for moves between base stations; P-GW as the stable IP anchor) and supports roaming with the home network.

↑ Section 7.2
Q15

On an LTE (Long-Term Evolution) cellular network, what is network attachment?

Answer

Network attachment is the process by which a mobile device connects to (joins) the LTE network when switched on or arriving:

1. The device listens for the primary synchronisation signals broadcast by base stations on all frequencies, finds them, then reads each base station's system information (bandwidth, configuration, operator).

2. It selects a base station (typically the strongest signal of its home/allowed carrier) and associates with it.

3. Mutual authentication: the device and network authenticate each other — the MME (Mobility Management Entity) consults the HSS (Home Subscriber Server) (in the home network) and creates keys; encryption keys for the radio link are derived.

4. The MME configures the data-plane path: tunnels are set up base station ↔︎ S-GW (Serving Gateway) ↔︎ P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway), and the device gets an IP (Internet Protocol) address (from the P-GW).

The device is now attached and can send/receive data (and is tracked by the MME).

↑ Section 7.2
Q16

On an LTE (Long-Term Evolution) cellular network, what does power management do?

Answer

Power management saves the mobile device's battery — since radio transmit/receive use lots of energy — by letting the device turn its radio off ("sleep") when there's nothing to send or receive, and wake up periodically (or when paged). The network coordinates this (discontinuous reception, DRX) so the device doesn't miss incoming data; also transmit power control to use only as much power as needed.

↑ Section 7.2
Q17

What are sleep modes of wireless devices on an LTE (Long-Term Evolution) cellular network?

Answer

LTE devices have two sleep modes:

  • Light sleep (connected DRX (Discontinuous Reception)): after a few hundred milliseconds of inactivity, the device sleeps but wakes up periodically (e.g., every ~100 ms) to check for downstream transmissions; it stays associated with the same base station and connected to the network.

  • Deep sleep (idle mode): after 5–10 seconds of inactivity, the device sleeps longer and releases its connection. It may move to a new cell while asleep, so on waking it may need to re-establish association with a (possibly new) base station; the network only knows its location to within a tracking area and must page all base stations in that area to reach it.

↑ Section 7.2
Q18

What is the global cellular network? How does it work?

Answer

The global cellular network is the "network of networks" formed by the world's many mobile carriers (operators), interconnected so users can roam internationally and communicate across carriers. Each carrier runs its own radio and core network; carriers interconnect via roaming agreements, gateways and the IPX (Internetwork Packet Exchange) (IP (Internet Protocol) exchange) or the public Internet. When a device is in a visited network, the visited network contacts the device's home network (HSS (Home Subscriber Server)) to authenticate it and set up service; the data may be tunnelled back to the home network's P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway) (home routing) or leave from the visited network (local breakout). Voice calls and SMS (Short Message Service) are routed between carriers similarly. So, like the Internet, it works through interconnected, independently operated networks with standard protocols (3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project)).

↑ Section 7.2
Q19

What defines the ultimate wide-area data service?

Answer

The textbook's vision of the ultimate wide-area data service: fast, ubiquitous, affordable Internet access everywhere, reliable enough for any application — i.e., high data rates (Gbps), very low latency, seamless mobility and coverage (anywhere, on the move), huge device density, reliability, low energy use, and low cost — the goals that 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) (and beyond) pursue, so that "wireless is just as good as wired".

↑ Section 7.2
Q20

What services are 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) cellular networks expected to provide?

Answer

5G (3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project)/ITU (International Telecommunication Union) IMT (International Mobile Telecommunications)-2020) targets three service classes:

  • eMBB (enhanced mobile broadband): much higher data rates (peak up to ~10–20 Gbps; typical hundreds of Mbps), for HD (High Definition)/4K/8K video, AR (Augmented Reality)/VR (Virtual Reality), fixed wireless home broadband.

  • URLLC (Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communications) (ultra-reliable low-latency communication): latency down to ~1 ms and very high reliability, for autonomous vehicles, industrial automation, remote surgery, smart grids.

  • mMTC (massive machine-type communication): massive IoT (Internet of Things) — up to ~1 million devices per km², low power, low cost sensors.

Also: network slicing (customised virtual networks), better mobility and energy efficiency.

↑ Section 7.2
Q21

What are the two major drawbacks of FR2 (Frequency Range 2, millimetre wave) frequencies (millimeter wave frequencies) used some 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) networks?

Answer

The two major drawbacks of mmWave (FR2, roughly 24–52 GHz+) frequencies:

1. Short range — high path loss; signals travel only about 100–200 m or less (they attenuate quickly, including through rain and foliage).

2. Poor penetration / blockage — they're easily blocked by walls, buildings, trees, even people and hands; line of sight is often needed.

Consequently far more base stations (small cells) and beamforming are required.

↑ Section 7.2
Q22

What are the priorities for the design of 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) networks?

Answer

Design priorities for 5G:

  • Much higher throughput (up to 10+ Gbps peak, 100× 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) capacity) — via new spectrum (mmWave), massive MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output), beamforming.

  • Very low latency (~1 ms) and high reliability.

  • Massive connectivity — huge numbers of devices (IoT (Internet of Things)).

  • Energy efficiency and low cost per bit.

  • Flexibility — network slicing, virtualisation/software-based core (SDN (Software-Defined Networking)/NFV (Network Function Virtualization)), support for diverse services, backward compatibility with 4G (non-standalone deployment).

  • Mobility support at high speeds and seamless coverage.

↑ Section 7.2
Q23

Why are small cell stations needed for 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) networks using FR2 (Frequency Range 2, millimetre wave) frequencies?

Answer

Because mmWave signals have short range and are easily blocked, a single tall macro tower can't cover a large area at these frequencies. Small cells — low-power base stations mounted on lamp posts, buildings and indoors, spaced ~100–200 m apart — are needed to provide coverage and to reuse the huge mmWave bandwidth densely, delivering high capacity to many users in hotspots (city centres, stadiums).

↑ Section 7.2
Q24

What is the 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) Core network?

Answer

The 5G Core (5GC (Fifth Generation Core network)) is the core network of 5G, defined by 3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project) as a service-based architecture (SBA): a set of software network functions (running on cloud/virtualised infrastructure) that talk to each other through standard APIs (Application Programming Interface) (HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)/2-based). Main functions: AMF (Access and Mobility Management Function) (access and mobility management), SMF (Session Management Function) (session management), UPF (user plane function — data forwarding), AUSF (Authentication Server Function) (authentication server), UDM (unified data management — subscriber data, like HSS (Home Subscriber Server)), PCF (Policy Control Function) (policy control), NRF (Network Repository Function) (function registry), NSSF (Network Slice Selection Function) (slice selection), NEF (Network Exposure Function) (network exposure).

↑ Section 7.2
Q25

What does the 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) Core network do?

Answer

Like the 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) core, the 5G Core connects devices to data networks (the Internet) and manages them: it handles registration and authentication, mobility management (tracking, paging, handovers), session management (setting up data sessions/tunnels, assigning IP (Internet Protocol) addresses), forwarding user data (UPF (User Plane Function)), QoS (Quality of Service) and policy enforcement, charging, roaming, and — new in 5G — network slicing (running several virtual, isolated networks with different characteristics on the same infrastructure) and exposing network capabilities to applications.

↑ Section 7.2
Q26

What are the main functions of the 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) Core network? Compared to 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) Core network, what are new in 5G Core network?

Answer

Main functions: access and mobility management (AMF (Access and Mobility Management Function)), session management (SMF (Session Management Function)), user-plane forwarding (UPF (User Plane Function)), authentication (AUSF (Authentication Server Function)), subscriber data (UDM (Unified Data Management)), policy (PCF (Policy Control Function)), plus network repository (NRF (Network Repository Function)), slice selection (NSSF (Network Slice Selection Function)), network exposure (NEF (Network Exposure Function)).

What's new compared with the 4G core:

  • Service-based architecture — network functions are cloud-native software services communicating via APIs (Application Programming Interface), instead of fixed point-to-point boxes (MME (Mobility Management Entity), S-GW (Serving Gateway), P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway)).

  • Complete control-plane / user-plane separation (CUPS (Control and User Plane Separation)) — the UPF can be placed anywhere (e.g., at the edge, near users, for low latency — edge computing).

  • Network slicing — multiple logical networks tailored for eMBB, URLLC (Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communications), mMTC.

  • The 4G MME's functions are split (AMF for mobility, SMF for sessions); HSS (Home Subscriber Server) → UDM/AUSF.

  • Designed for virtualisation (NFV (Network Function Virtualization)/SDN (Software-Defined Networking)), better scalability, flexibility, stronger security (e.g., encrypted subscriber identity — SUCI (Subscription Concealed Identifier)), and support for non-3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project) access.

↑ Section 7.2
Q27

What are differences and similarities between 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) Core network and 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) Core network?

Answer

Similarities: both are all-IP (Internet Protocol) packet cores that sit between the radio access network and the Internet; both separate control plane and data plane; both perform authentication (with a home subscriber database), mobility management (tracking, paging, handover), session/bearer setup, IP address allocation, tunnelling of user data (GTP (GPRS Tunnelling Protocol)-U), QoS (Quality of Service)/policy, charging and roaming; both keep the home-network/visited-network model.

Differences: 4G's EPC (Evolved Packet Core) uses dedicated network elements (MME (Mobility Management Entity), S-GW (Serving Gateway), P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway), HSS (Home Subscriber Server), PCRF (Policy and Charging Rules Function)) connected by point-to-point interfaces; 5GC (Fifth Generation Core network) uses a service-based architecture of virtualised network functions (AMF (Access and Mobility Management Function), SMF (Session Management Function), UPF (User Plane Function), AUSF (Authentication Server Function), UDM (Unified Data Management), PCF (Policy Control Function)…) with API (Application Programming Interface)-based communication; 5GC has full CUPS (Control and User Plane Separation) allowing flexible/edge UPF placement, native network slicing, better support for low latency, massive IoT (Internet of Things) and cloud deployment, and enhanced security/privacy.

↑ Section 7.2

Section 7.3: Mobility Management

37 questions

Q1Q2Q3Q4Q5Q6Q7Q8Q9Q10Q11Q12Q13Q14Q15Q16Q17Q18Q19Q20Q21Q22Q23Q24Q25Q26Q27Q28Q29Q30Q31Q32Q33Q34Q35Q36Q37

Also asked in: Assignment 3 Q1.1

Q1

In order to accommodate mobile users, what considerations should be taken when designing the network layer?

Answer

Keep a permanent address so correspondents and ongoing connections aren't disrupted; provide a way to locate the mobile (registration with a home agent/database); route datagrams to its current location (indirect via tunnelling, or direct); support fast handoffs with minimal loss; ensure transparency, scalability (millions of mobiles — don't put per-mobile routes in the global routing tables), efficiency (avoid triangle routing) and security (authenticate location updates). (See Section 7.1 Q20.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q2

From the standpoint of the network layers, what defines mobility of a network device?

Answer

Mobility is defined by whether the device changes its point of attachment (access network/IP (Internet Protocol) subnet) and whether it must keep its connections while doing so: from no mobility (moving within one access network, same IP address), to moving between networks with the device off/disconnected (gets a new address; nothing to preserve), to high mobility (moving between networks while maintaining ongoing connections — the hard case the network layer must support). (See Section 7.1 Q21.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q3

How important is the mobile node’s address?

Answer

Very important — ongoing connections and correspondents identify the mobile by its IP (Internet Protocol) address, so mobility schemes keep a permanent (home) address fixed and use a care-of address to indicate the current location. (See Section 7.1 Q22.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q4

What supporting wired infrastructure is available for supporting wireless connections?

Answer

Base stations/APs (Access Point), the wired LAN (Local Area Network)/distribution system, routers, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)/DNS (Domain Name System)/authentication servers, WLAN (Wireless Local Area Network) controllers, and in cellular the backhaul and core network (MME (Mobility Management Entity), HSS (Home Subscriber Server), gateways); for mobility, home/foreign agents and location databases. (See Section 7.1 Q23.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q5

What is ad hoc networking?

Answer

Wireless networking without base stations or infrastructure: nodes talk directly and may relay for each other (MANETs (Mobile Ad hoc Network), VANETs (Vehicular Ad hoc Network), Bluetooth, Wi-Fi Direct). (See Section 7.1 Q24.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q6

What issues are involved in allowing a mobile user to maintain ongoing connections while moving between networks?

Answer

Keeping the address used by correspondents/TCP (Transmission Control Protocol); locating the mobile; routing to it (indirect vs direct); fast handoff with little loss; security; transparency; scalability; TCP performance during handoffs. (See Section 7.1 Q25.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q7

What do the terms home network, home agent, foreign (or visited) network, foreign agent, and correspondent mean?

Answer

Home network = the mobile's permanent network; home agent = entity there that tracks it and forwards its datagrams; foreign/visited network = where it currently is; foreign agent = entity there that assists it (COA (Care-of Address), registration, decapsulation); correspondent = the node communicating with it. (See Section 7.1 Q26.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q8

Why should all traffic addressed to a mobile node’s permanent address be routed to the foreign network when the node is resident of a foreign network? How can this be done?

Answer

Because the mobile isn't at home; datagrams to its permanent address must be redirected to where it is — done by the home agent intercepting them and tunnelling them to the care-of address (or by direct routing). (See Section 7.1 Q27.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q9

What roles does a foreign agent play?

Answer

Advertises itself, provides a care-of address, registers the mobile with its home agent, receives and decapsulates tunnelled datagrams and delivers them to the mobile. (See Section 7.1 Q28.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q10

What is a care-of-address?

Answer

The address that identifies the mobile's current location in the foreign network (often the foreign agent's address). (See Section 7.1 Q29.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q11

What is a home address? What is a foreign address?

Answer

Home (permanent) address = fixed address in the home network; foreign address = the care-of address in the visited network. (See Section 7.1 Q30.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q12

How does indirect routing work?

Answer

Correspondent → permanent address → home agent intercepts → encapsulates and tunnels to the care-of address → foreign agent decapsulates → mobile; replies go directly. (See Section 7.1 Q31.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q13

Suppose a mobile user is watching a streamed HD (High Definition) video on a smartphone connected to a visited 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) network. What major steps are taken when the mobile user moves from one cell to another?

Answer

When the phone moves from one cell to another in the visited 4G/5G network, a handover happens (textbook steps):

1. Measurement and decision: the phone continuously measures signal strength from its current and nearby base stations and reports them; the current (source) base station decides to hand over and chooses the target base station, and sends it a handover request.

2. Preparation: the target base station checks it has resources, pre-allocates radio channels (and timing) for the phone, and replies with a handover request acknowledgement containing the information the phone needs.

3. Command: the source base station tells the phone the new base station's details and to switch. The phone leaves the old base station and joins the new one (synchronising and gaining access to the new cell). From the phone's view the handover is done.

4. Forwarding: meanwhile, the source base station stops sending to the phone and forwards any datagrams still arriving (buffered video data) to the target base station by tunnel, which delivers them to the phone once it arrives — so little or no video data is lost.

5. Path switch: the target base station informs the MME (Mobility Management Entity) that it is now serving the phone; the MME instructs the Serving Gateway to re-route the tunnel endpoint from the source base station to the target base station.

6. Release: the target base station confirms to the source, which releases the resources it used for the phone.

The phone's IP (Internet Protocol) address and the tunnels S-GW (Serving Gateway) ↔︎ P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway) (and to the home network, if home-routed while roaming) stay the same, so the streaming TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)/QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) connection continues; the phone's video buffer covers the brief interruption.

↑ Section 7.3
Q14

How does the mobile node-to-foreign agent protocol work?

Answer

The mobile learns of the foreign agent (agent advertisement/solicitation), sends it a registration request (permanent address, home agent, COA (Care-of Address), lifetime, ID (Identifier); UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 434), the foreign agent relays it to the home agent, which binds the COA and replies; the foreign agent relays the reply to the mobile. (See Section 7.1 Q32 and Q42.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q15

What problem does the indirect routing approach suffer from?

Answer

Triangle routing — all traffic detours via the home network, adding delay and load. (See Section 7.1 Q33.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q16

How does the direct routing approach work?

Answer

A correspondent agent obtains the mobile's care-of address from the home agent and tunnels datagrams directly to it; an anchor foreign agent forwards datagrams if the mobile moves on. (See Section 7.1 Q34.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q17

What is a correspondent agent in the direct routing approach?

Answer

The entity in the correspondent's network that learns the COA (Care-of Address) and tunnels directly to the mobile. (See Section 7.1 Q35.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q18

What is mobile IP (Internet Protocol)? Which standard defines mobile IP?

Answer

The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) architecture/protocols letting IP hosts keep their address while moving: RFC (Request for Comments) 5944 (IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4); earlier RFC 3344/2002); Mobile IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) RFC 6275. (See Section 7.1 Q36.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q19

What are the three main pieces of the mobile IP (Internet Protocol) standard?

Answer

Agent discovery, registration with the home agent, and indirect routing of datagrams. (See Section 7.1 Q37.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q20

What is done in the process of agent discovery?

Answer

The mobile learns which agent(s) serve the network — and thus whether it's home or away and what COA (Care-of Address) to use — through agent advertisements or solicitations. (See Section 7.1 Q38.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q21

What is done in the process of agent advertisement?

Answer

Agents periodically broadcast ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) type-9 messages with a mobility extension (H/F/R bits, lifetime, care-of addresses). (See Section 7.1 Q39.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q22

What does agent solicitation do?

Answer

The mobile broadcasts an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) type-10 solicitation to prompt agents to advertise immediately. (See Section 7.1 Q40.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q23

What is the format of an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) router discovery message with mobility agent advertisement?

Answer

ICMP router advertisement (type 9, code 0, checksum, addresses, lifetime, router address) + mobility agent advertisement extension (type 16, length, sequence number, registration lifetime, R/B/H/F/M/G bits, care-of addresses). (See Section 7.1 Q41.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q24

According to the mobile IP (Internet Protocol) standard, how does a mobile node register its care-of address (COA) with its home agent?

Answer

Registration request (home address, home agent, COA, lifetime, identification) to the foreign agent → relayed to the home agent (UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 434) → home agent binds and sends a registration reply → relayed to the mobile; renewed before expiry. (See Section 7.1 Q42.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q25

How do wireless stations move seamlessly from one BBS to another while maintaining ongoing TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sessions?

Answer

Within one subnet the station re-associates with a new AP (Access Point) and keeps its IP (Internet Protocol) address; the new AP sends a broadcast frame with the station's MAC (Medium Access Control) so the self-learning switch updates its table; TCP continues. (See Section 7.1 Q43.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q26

What are the main features of 802.15 wireless networks?

Answer

Short-range, low-power, low-cost WPAN (Wireless Personal Area Network); 2.4 GHz; ad hoc piconets with one controller and up to 7 active devices; TDM (Time Division Multiplexing) slots, FHSS (Frequency-Hopping Spread Spectrum); ~1–3 Mbps (Bluetooth); 802.15.4 for Zigbee/IoT (Internet of Things). (See Section 7.1 Q44.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q27

How is Bluetooth network related to 802.15 wireless networks?

Answer

Bluetooth's radio and MAC (Medium Access Control) were standardised as IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.15.1; it's the best-known 802.15 WPAN (Wireless Personal Area Network). (See Section 7.1 Q45.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q28

What do FHSS (Frequency-Hopping Spread Spectrum) and PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) stand for?

Answer

FHSS = Frequency-Hopping Spread Spectrum; PSTN = Public Switched Telephone Network. (See Section 7.1 Q46.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q29

What are the main components of cellular network architecture?

Answer

Mobile device (SIM (Subscriber Identity Module)/IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity)), base stations (eNodeB/gNB), radio access network, core network (MME (Mobility Management Entity), HSS (Home Subscriber Server), S-GW (Serving Gateway), P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway) — or 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) AMF (Access and Mobility Management Function), SMF (Session Management Function), UPF (User Plane Function), UDM (Unified Data Management)), Internet connection. (See Section 7.2 Q8.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q30

What are some important standards and technologies for cellular networks?

Answer

GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications), GPRS (General Packet Radio Service)/EDGE (Enhanced Data rates for GSM Evolution), UMTS (Universal Mobile Telecommunications System)/WCDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access), CDMA2000, HSPA (High Speed Packet Access), LTE (Long-Term Evolution)/LTE-A (Long-Term Evolution Advanced), 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) NR (New Radio); technologies FDMA (Frequency Division Multiple Access)/TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access)/CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access)/OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access), MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output); bodies 3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project)/ITU (International Telecommunication Union). (See Section 7.2 Q9.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q31

How do TDM (Time Division Multiplexing) and FDM (Frequency Division Multiplexing) work?

Answer

TDM gives each user a recurring time slot using the whole bandwidth; FDM gives each user its own frequency band continuously; cellular systems combine them. (See Section 7.2 Q1.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q32

What are the main features of GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) networks?

Answer

2G (Second Generation cellular) digital circuit-switched voice; FDMA (Frequency Division Multiple Access)/TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access) (8 slots per 200 kHz channel); SIM (Subscriber Identity Module), BTS (Base Transceiver Station), BSC (Base Station Controller), MSC (Mobile Switching Center), HLR (Home Location Register)/VLR (Visitor Location Register), AuC (Authentication Center); authentication/encryption; roaming; handoffs with an anchor MSC. (See Section 7.2 Q2.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q33

What are the main features of GPRS (General Packet Radio Service) networks?

Answer

2.5G (Second-and-a-half Generation cellular) packet data over GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications): on-demand slots, always-on, volume billing, SGSN (Serving GPRS Support Node)/GGSN (Gateway GPRS Support Node) with tunnels, tens–100+ kbps. (See Section 7.2 Q3.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q34

What is the triangle routing problem?

Answer

Traffic to a mobile goes via its home network before reaching it, even if the direct path is shorter. (See Section 7.1 Q33.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q35

How do mobile user location protocols work?

Answer

The home network (HLR (Home Location Register)/HSS (Home Subscriber Server)/home agent) keeps each subscriber's current location; visited networks register mobiles (VLR (Visitor Location Register)/MME (Mobility Management Entity)/foreign agent) and inform the home network; callers' networks query the home network, then the visited network pages the mobile. (See Section 7.2 Q5.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q36

How do handoffs happen in GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) networks?

Answer

Mobile measures signals; old BSS (Base Station System) decides and informs the MSC (Mobile Switching Center); MSC sets up a path to the new BSS; new BSS allocates a channel; old BSS tells the mobile to switch; mobile joins new BSS; MSC reroutes; old resources released; anchor MSC stays in the path across MSCs. (See Section 7.2 Q6.)

↑ Section 7.3
Q37

How can calls be routed to a mobile user in mobile networks?

Answer

Via the home network: the home MSC (Mobile Switching Center) queries the HLR (Home Location Register) for a roaming number, routes the call to the visited MSC, which pages the mobile. (See Section 7.2 Q7.)

↑ Section 7.3

Textbook Review Questions — Chapter 7

31 questions (Kurose & Ross, 8th edition)

R1R2R3R4R5R6R7R8R9R10R11R12R13R14R15R16R17R18R19R20R21R22R23R24R25R26R27R28R29R30R31
R1

What does it mean for a wireless network to be operating in “infrastructure mode”? If the network is not in infrastructure mode, what mode of operation is it in, and what is the difference between that mode of operation and infrastructure mode?

Answer

Infrastructure mode: wireless hosts are associated with a base station/access point that connects them to the larger wired network; all communication goes through the base station, and the infrastructure provides services such as addressing and routing.

If not in infrastructure mode, the network is in ad hoc mode: there is no base station and no connection to a larger network; hosts communicate directly with each other (and must provide routing, addressing, etc. themselves).

↑ Chapter 7 review
R2

What are the four types of wireless networks identified in our taxonomy in Section 7.1? Which of these types of wireless networks have you used?

Answer

The four types (by number of wireless hops and whether there's infrastructure):

1. Single-hop, infrastructure-based — hosts connect to a base station one hop away (Wi-Fi at home, 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) cellular).

2. Single-hop, infrastructure-less — no base station; one node coordinates the others (Bluetooth piconets, ad hoc 802.11).

3. Multi-hop, infrastructure-based — a base station is present, but some nodes relay through other wireless nodes to reach it (wireless mesh networks, some sensor networks).

4. Multi-hop, infrastructure-less — no base station; nodes relay through other nodes (MANETs (Mobile Ad hoc Network), VANETs (Vehicular Ad hoc Network)).

Commonly used personally: types 1 (home Wi-Fi, cellular) and 2 (Bluetooth headphones).

↑ Chapter 7 review
R3

What are the differences between the following types of wireless channel impairments: path loss, multipath propagation, interference from other sources?

Answer

  • Path loss: the signal weakens (attenuates) as it travels — with distance (it spreads out) and when passing through obstacles (walls).

  • Multipath propagation: the signal reflects off objects and reaches the receiver by several paths of different lengths, arriving at slightly different times, which blurs the received signal.

  • Interference from other sources: other transmitters on the same frequency band (other Wi-Fi networks, Bluetooth, cordless phones) and electromagnetic noise (microwave ovens, motors) add to the signal and corrupt it.

Path loss is about the signal itself fading; multipath is about the signal interfering with copies of itself; interference is about other signals/noise.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R4

As a mobile node gets farther and farther away from a base station, what are two actions that a base station could take to ensure that the loss probability of a transmitted frame does not increase?

Answer

1. Increase the transmission power (so the SNR (Signal-to-Noise Ratio) stays high enough).

2. Reduce the transmission (data) rate — switch to a more robust modulation scheme (fewer bits per symbol), which has a lower bit-error rate at a given SNR (rate adaptation).

(Also possible: stronger error-correcting codes.)

↑ Chapter 7 review
R5

Describe the role of the beacon frames in 802.11.

Answer

Beacon frames are sent periodically by each access point (e.g., every ~100 ms). Each contains the AP's SSID (Service Set Identifier) and MAC (Medium Access Control) address, plus capability information. They let wireless stations discover which APs (networks) are in range — the station scans channels, listening for beacons (passive scanning), and then chooses an AP to associate with. They also carry timing synchronisation and power-save information.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R6

True or false: Before an 802.11 station transmits a data frame, it must first send an RTS (Request to Send) frame and receive a corresponding CTS (Clear to Send) frame.

Answer

False. RTS/CTS is optional. A station can send a data frame directly (using CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance)) without an RTS/CTS exchange; RTS/CTS is typically used only for frames longer than the configured RTS threshold.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R7

Why are acknowledgments used in 802.11 but not in wired Ethernet?

Answer

Because in wireless networks a sender can't detect collisions (it can't hear others while transmitting; hidden terminals and fading mean collisions happen at the receiver), and wireless links have high bit-error rates (fading, interference). The sender therefore needs an ACK (Acknowledgement) to know the frame arrived correctly; if no ACK comes back, it retransmits. In wired Ethernet, collisions are detected by CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) and bit errors are rare, so link-level ACKs aren't needed (TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) handles the rare losses).

↑ Chapter 7 review
R8

True or false: Ethernet and 802.11 use the same frame structure.

Answer

False. The frame structures are different. For example, an 802.11 frame has four address fields (Ethernet has two), a frame control field, a duration field for channel reservation, a sequence number (for retransmissions), and a larger payload (up to 2,312 bytes); Ethernet has a preamble and a type field. (An AP (Access Point) converts between them.)

↑ Chapter 7 review
R9

Describe how the RTS (Request to Send) threshold works.

Answer

The RTS threshold is a configurable frame-length value: a station uses the RTS/CTS (Clear to Send) exchange only when the data frame is longer than the threshold; frames shorter than the threshold are sent directly (DIFS (Distributed Inter-Frame Space), data, SIFS (Short Inter-Frame Space), ACK (Acknowledgement)) without RTS/CTS. This way the overhead of RTS/CTS is paid only for long frames, where a collision would waste a lot of channel time. (If the threshold is larger than the maximum frame size, RTS/CTS is never used.)

↑ Chapter 7 review
R10

Suppose the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 RTS (Request to Send) and CTS (Clear to Send) frames were as long as the standard DATA and ACK (Acknowledgement) frames. Would there be any advantage to using the CTS and RTS frames? Why or why not?

Answer

No, there would be no advantage. RTS/CTS helps because RTS and CTS are short, so a collision involving them wastes little time, and they then protect the long DATA frame. If RTS and CTS were as long as DATA and ACK frames, a collision between RTS frames would waste as much time as a collision between DATA frames, and the RTS/CTS exchange would add extra delay and overhead on every successful transmission — no benefit, only cost.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R11

Section 7.3.4 discusses 802.11 mobility, in which a wireless station moves from one BSS (Basic Service Set) to another within the same subnet. When the APs (Access Point) are interconnected with a switch, an AP may need to send a frame with a spoofed MAC (Medium Access Control) address to get the switch to forward the frame properly. Why?

Answer

Because the switch uses self-learning based on the source MAC address of frames it receives. When a station moves from AP1's BSS to AP2's BSS (same subnet), the switch's table still says the station is reachable via AP1's port, so frames for it would go to the wrong AP. To fix this, after association AP2 sends an Ethernet broadcast frame with the station's MAC address as the source (a "spoofed" source address). The switch sees this frame and updates its table: the station is now reached via AP2's port.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R12

What are the differences between a master device in a Bluetooth network and a base station in an 802.11 network?

Answer

  • A Bluetooth master (controller) controls its piconet: it sets the clock and frequency-hopping pattern, and polls each slave — slaves may transmit only when the master allows (in the slot after the master addressed them). There's no carrier sensing or contention. Up to 7 active slaves; communication is typically master ↔︎ slave. It is itself one of the peer devices (ad hoc; no link to wired infrastructure is required).

  • An 802.11 base station (AP (Access Point)) connects stations to the wired network; stations contend for the channel using CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance) (random access) — the AP doesn't poll (in the usual DCF (Distributed Coordination Function) mode) — and it supports many stations. The AP forwards frames between stations and between the WLAN (Wireless Local Area Network) and the wired network.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R13

What is the role of the base station in 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) cellular architecture? With which other 4G/5G network elements (mobile device, MME (Mobility Management Entity), HSS (Home Subscriber Server), Serving Gateway Router, PDN (Packet Data Network) Gateway Router) does it directly communicate with in the control plane? In the data plane?

Answer

The base station (eNodeB in 4G, gNB in 5G) is the network-side end of the wireless link: it manages the radio resources in its cell (scheduling of time-frequency slots for each device), handles device authentication/association with the network (relaying to the MME) and handovers, and forwards data between devices and the core (via tunnels).

  • Control plane: it communicates directly with the mobile device and the MME.

  • Data plane: it communicates directly with the mobile device and the Serving Gateway (S-GW) (via a GTP (GPRS Tunnelling Protocol) tunnel).

↑ Chapter 7 review
R14

What is an International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI)?

Answer

The IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity) is a globally unique identifier of a cellular subscriber, stored on the device's SIM (Subscriber Identity Module) card. It consists of the mobile country code (MCC), the mobile network code (MNC) (the home carrier) and the subscriber number within that network (up to 15 digits). The network uses it to identify and authenticate the subscriber and to locate their home network (it's kept confidential and replaced with temporary identities where possible).

↑ Chapter 7 review
R15

What is the role of the Home Subscriber Service (HSS (Home Subscriber Server)) in 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) cellular architecture? With which other 4G/5G network elements (mobile device, base station, MME (Mobility Management Entity), Serving Gateway Router, PDN (Packet Data Network) Gateway Router) does it directly communicate with in the control plane? In the data plane?

Answer

The HSS (Home Subscriber Server) is a database in the device's home network holding subscriber information — identity (IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity)), service profile, and authentication keys/credentials — and the device's current location (which MME is serving it). It works with the MME to authenticate devices (including when roaming) and to authorise services.

  • Control plane: it communicates directly with the MME (not the device or base station).

  • Data plane: none — the HSS doesn't carry user data.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R16

What is the role of the Mobility Management Entity (MME) in 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) cellular architecture? With which other 4G/5G network elements (mobile device, base station, HSS (Home Subscriber Server), Serving Gateway Router, PDN (Packet Data Network) Gateway Router) does it directly communicate with in the control plane? In the data plane?

Answer

The MME (Mobility Management Entity) performs the control-plane functions for devices: authentication (with the HSS), tracking the device's location (tracking areas), paging, handover coordination between base stations, and setting up the data-plane tunnels (bearers) between base station, S-GW (Serving Gateway) and P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway).

  • Control plane: it communicates directly with the mobile device (via the base station — NAS (Non-Access Stratum) signalling), the base station, the HSS and the Serving Gateway.

  • Data plane: none — it doesn't handle user data.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R17

Describe the purpose of two tunnels in the data plane of the 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) cellular architecture. When a mobile device is attached to its own home network, at which 4G/5G network element (mobile device, base station, HSS (Home Subscriber Server), MME (Mobility Management Entity), Serving Gateway Router, PDN (Packet Data Network) Gateway Router) does each end of each of the two tunnels terminate?

Answer

Two tunnels (GTP (GPRS Tunnelling Protocol) tunnels) carry each device's data in the 4G data plane:

1. Base station ↔︎ Serving Gateway (S-GW) tunnel — carries the device's datagrams between its current base station and the S-GW; when the device moves to another base station, only this tunnel's base-station end is changed — so the S-GW is the mobility anchor within the network.

2. Serving Gateway ↔︎ PDN Gateway (P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway)) tunnel — carries datagrams between the S-GW and the P-GW, the gateway to the Internet that gives the device its IP (Internet Protocol) address (and stays fixed).

When the device is in its home network: tunnel 1 terminates at the base station and the Serving Gateway; tunnel 2 terminates at the Serving Gateway and the PDN Gateway.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R18

What are the three sublayers in the link layer in the LTE (Long-Term Evolution) protocol stack? Briefly describe their functions.

Answer

  • PDCP (Packet Data Convergence Protocol): IP (Internet Protocol) header compression and encryption/decryption.

  • RLC (Radio Link Control): fragmentation/reassembly of datagrams to fit radio frames, and reliable data transfer (ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest) with ACK (Acknowledgement)/NAK (Negative Acknowledgement)).

  • MAC (Medium Access Control): requesting and using transmission slots scheduled by the base station, and HARQ (Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest) error recovery.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R19

Does the LTE (Long-Term Evolution) wireless access network use FDMA (Frequency Division Multiple Access), TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access), or both? Explain your answer.

Answer

Both. LTE's downlink uses OFDM (orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing), a combination of FDM and TDM (Time Division Multiplexing): the channel is divided into many frequency sub-carriers (FDMA), and time is divided into slots (0.5 ms slots in 10 ms frames) (TDMA). The base station allocates time-frequency resource blocks — particular sub-carriers in particular time slots — to each device. So LTE uses both FDMA and TDMA.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R20

Describe the two possible sleep modes of a 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) mobile device. In each of these sleep modes, will the mobile device remain associated with the same base station between the time it goes to sleep and the time it wakes up and first sends/receives a new datagram?

Answer

  • Light sleep: after a few hundred milliseconds of inactivity; the device wakes up periodically (e.g., every ~100 ms) to check for downlink data. It remains associated with the same base station.

  • Deep sleep: after 5–10 s of inactivity; the device sleeps longer. Because it may move to a different cell while asleep, it may not be associated with the same base station when it wakes; it may need to re-associate (re-establish a connection with the base station it's now near), and the network must page it across a tracking area to reach it.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R21

What is meant by a “visited network” and a “home network” in 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) cellular architecture?

Answer

  • Home network: the cellular network of the carrier you subscribe to (whose SIM (Subscriber Identity Module) you have); it holds your subscriber information (in the HSS (Home Subscriber Server)) and authenticates you.

  • Visited network: a network operated by another carrier (or another region) that your device is currently attached to while roaming; it provides service to you by contacting your home network (HSS) for authentication and authorisation, and may tunnel your traffic back to your home network.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R22

List three important differences between 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) and 5G (Fifth Generation cellular) cellular networks.

Answer

1. Higher data rates / capacity — peak ~10–20 Gbps vs ~1 Gbps in 4G (new spectrum including mmWave FR2 (Frequency Range 2, millimetre wave) bands, wider channels, massive MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output), beamforming).

2. Much lower latency — ~1 ms (URLLC (Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communications)) vs ~10+ ms in 4G.

3. Massive device density — up to ~1 million devices per km² (IoT (Internet of Things), mMTC) vs far fewer in 4G.

Also: a new service-based core (5GC (Fifth Generation Core network)) with network slicing and full control/user-plane separation; many more small cells; improved energy efficiency.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R23

What does it mean that a mobile device is said to be “roaming?”

Answer

A mobile device is roaming when it's attached to a visited network — a network other than its home network (e.g., another carrier's network, often in another country) — while still being served (authenticated through its home network).

↑ Chapter 7 review
R24

What is meant by “hand over” of a network device?

Answer

Handover (handoff) is the process of transferring a mobile device's connection from one base station (or access point/network) to another as it moves (or as signal conditions change), so that its ongoing communication continues with minimal interruption. The new base station takes over the radio link, and the network's data path (tunnels) is redirected to it.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R25

What is the difference between direct and indirect routing of datagrams to/ from a roaming mobile host?

Answer

  • Indirect routing: the correspondent sends datagrams to the mobile's permanent (home) address; they go to the home network, whose home agent (or P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway)) forwards/tunnels them to the mobile's current location in the visited network. Transparent to the correspondent, handles mobility easily, but can be inefficient (triangle routing).

  • Direct routing: the correspondent (a correspondent agent) learns the mobile's current care-of address from the home network and sends datagrams directly to the visited network, avoiding the detour. More efficient, but not transparent (the correspondent must get the address) and needs extra mechanisms when the mobile moves again (an anchor).

↑ Chapter 7 review
R26

What does “triangle routing” mean?

Answer

Triangle routing refers to the inefficient path in indirect routing: datagrams from the correspondent to the mobile go via the mobile's home network (correspondent → home agent → mobile), even when a much more direct route exists between the correspondent and the mobile (replies go directly, completing the triangle).

↑ Chapter 7 review
R27

Describe the similarity and differences in tunnel configuration when a mobile device is resident in its home network, versus when it is roaming in a visited network.

Answer

Similarity: in both cases the device's traffic is carried by the same two kinds of tunnels — base station ↔︎ Serving Gateway and Serving Gateway ↔︎ PDN (Packet Data Network) Gateway — and the device keeps an IP (Internet Protocol) address assigned by the P-GW. Difference: when at home, all elements (base station, S-GW, P-GW) are in the home network. When roaming, the base station and S-GW are in the visited network, and the P-GW is typically in the home network (home-routed roaming), so the S-GW ↔︎ P-GW tunnel crosses from the visited network to the home network (over the inter-carrier interconnection); alternatively a P-GW in the visited network may be used (local breakout).

↑ Chapter 7 review
R28

When a mobile device is handed over from one base station to another in a 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) network, which network element makes the decision to initiate that handover? Which network element chooses the target base station to which the mobile device will be handed over?

Answer

The source (current) base station makes the decision to initiate the handover (based on signal-strength measurement reports from the device, and load). The source base station also chooses the target base station to which the device will be handed over.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R29

Describe how and when the forwarding path of datagrams entering the visited network and destined to the mobile device changes before, during, and after hand over.

Answer

  • Before handover: datagrams entering the visited network go P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway) → S-GW (Serving Gateway) → (tunnel) → source base station → device.

  • During handover: the source base station tells the device to switch and stops sending to it; datagrams arriving at the source base station are forwarded (tunnelled) to the target base station, which buffers them and delivers them to the device once it has joined. (Path: S-GW → source BS → target BS → device.)

  • After handover: the target base station tells the MME (Mobility Management Entity), which tells the S-GW to change the tunnel endpoint from the source to the target base station; datagrams now go P-GW → S-GW → target base station → device, and the source releases its resources.

↑ Chapter 7 review
R30

Consider the following elements of the Mobile IP (Internet Protocol) architecture: the home network, foreign network permanent IP address, home agent, foreign agent, data plane forwarding, Access Point (AP), and WLANs (Wireless Local Area Network) at the network edge. What are the closest equivalent elements in the 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) cellular network architecture?

Answer
Mobile IP element Closest 4G/5G equivalent
Home network Home network (the subscriber's own carrier network)
Foreign network Visited network
Permanent IP address IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity) (permanent identity) — and in the data plane, the IP address assigned by the (home) P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway)
Home agent HSS (Home Subscriber Server) (knows location, authenticates) together with the home PDN (Packet Data Network) Gateway (data-plane anchor that forwards traffic)
Foreign agent MME (Mobility Management Entity) (control) and Serving Gateway (data) in the visited network
Data-plane forwarding (tunnelling) GTP (GPRS Tunnelling Protocol) tunnels base station ↔︎ S-GW (Serving Gateway) ↔︎ P-GW
Access point (AP) Base station (eNodeB/gNB)
WLANs at the network edge Radio access network (the cells served by base stations)
↑ Chapter 7 review
R31

What are three approaches that can be used to avoid having a single wireless link degrade the performance of an end-to-end transport-layer TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection?

Answer

1. Local recovery — recover from bit errors on the wireless link itself (e.g., 802.11 ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest) retransmissions, or FEC (Forward Error Correction)), so TCP never sees the loss.

2. TCP sender awareness of wireless links — let the TCP sender distinguish wireless (corruption) losses from congestion losses (e.g., explicit loss notification) so it doesn't cut its window unnecessarily.

3. Split-connection approaches — split the end-to-end TCP connection into two at the base station/gateway: one connection over the wired part and one over the wireless hop (e.g., I-TCP, or a performance-enhancing proxy), so wireless losses are handled locally.
