Part 1: Short Answer Questions (30%)

Q1.1Q1.2Q1.3Q1.4Q1.5Q1.6
Q1.1 (5%)

Run Traceroute/TRACERT (Trace Route, a Windows command) between a source and a destination in your country at three different times of day. Summarise the average and standard deviation of the round-trip delays and the number of routers in the path at each time, and explain your findings.

Unit 1 · Section 1.1
Answer

What traceroute does, in plain words: it sends test packets with a "hop limit" (TTL (Time-to-Live)) of 1, 2, 3, … Each router that sees the limit run out sends back an "expired" message, so you learn every router on the path and how long the round trip to it took (three tries per hop).

Your measured data (evening run, 21:48 EDT (Eastern Daylight Time), to www.mit.edu):

Run Routers in path Replied / silent RTT (Round-Trip Time) at destination (3 TRACERT probes) 30 extra pings
Morning not enough info — not yet measured — — —
Afternoon not enough info — not yet measured — — —
Evening 22 19 replied, 4 silent mean 35.00 ms, sd 0.00 ms mean 50.60 ms, sd 36.61 ms (min 28, max 167)

How to compute the statistics (show this in your answer): mean = sum of RTTs ÷ number of samples; standard deviation = square root of the average squared distance from the mean. Example with the three probes 35, 35, 35 ms: mean = 105/3 = 35 ms; every value equals the mean, so sd = 0 ms.

Explaining the findings in plain English:

  • Number of routers: 23 hops were listed; the last is MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology)'s server itself, so 22 routers sit in between. The 4 silent hops ("* * *") are routers that don't answer traceroute (common in Akamai/AWS (Amazon Web Services) networks) — they still exist and forward your packets.

  • Why three probes gave sd = 0: three samples taken a few milliseconds apart are too few to show variation. The 30-ping test is more honest: mean 50.6 ms but sd 36.6 ms, with a few very slow replies (up to 167 ms).

  • Where the variation comes from: propagation delay (distance ÷ speed of light in fibre) and transmission delay (packet size ÷ link speed) are fixed. The only delay that changes from packet to packet is queuing — waiting in router buffers. So the spread is caused by busy links, mostly the home Wi-Fi and the shared cable network in the evening.

  • What to expect across the day: the minimum RTT should stay about the same (distance doesn't change), but the evening (peak streaming time, about 7–11 pm) should show a higher mean and larger sd than morning or afternoon because queues are longer. The router count should stay the same; a change would mean a route change, not a load change.

To finish the morning and afternoon rows (your script already does this — scripting option first):

# PowerShell — run once in the morning and once in the afternoon
pwsh -File .\evidence\collect-tracert.ps1 -Target www.mit.edu -Label Morning
pwsh -File .\evidence\collect-tracert.ps1 -Target www.mit.edu -Label Afternoon
# Quick manual alternative:
tracert -d www.mit.edu
$r  = 1..30 | ForEach-Object { (Test-Connection www.mit.edu -Count 1).Latency }   # PowerShell 7 (.ResponseTime in 5.1)
$m  = ($r | Measure-Object -Average).Average
$sd = [math]::Sqrt((($r | ForEach-Object { ($_ - $m) * ($_ - $m) }) | Measure-Object -Sum).Sum / $r.Count)
"{0:N2} ms mean, {1:N2} ms sd" -f $m, $sd

("Clicking" option: open Command Prompt, type tracert www.mit.edu, copy the output into a spreadsheet and use AVERAGE() and STDEV.P().)

How to approach it

Topic: Traceroute, RTT statistics

Method / formula: Run tracert three times at different times of day; report mean and standard deviation of RTTs and the hop count; explain differences by queuing (load varies by time of day)

Practice: Tutorials: Genre 01 (Family 9)

↑ Assignment 1 Part 1
Q1.2 (5%)

What are the five layers in the Internet protocol stack? Develop a table to summarise what each layer does.

Unit 1 · Section 1.2
Answer

Think of sending a parcel: the application writes the letter, transport makes sure it reaches the right person in the house, network finds the route to the house, link moves it one road at a time, physical is the road surface itself.

Layer What it does (plain English) Data unit Address used Examples Runs on
5 Application Gives the user the service; defines the messages two programs exchange Message Host names, URLs (Uniform Resource Locator) HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol), DNS (Domain Name System) End hosts only
4 Transport Delivers data to the right program; TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) adds reliability, ordering, flow and congestion control Segment Port numbers TCP, UDP (User Datagram Protocol) End hosts only
3 Network Moves datagrams from any host to any other across many networks; routing and forwarding; best effort Datagram IP (Internet Protocol) addresses IP, ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) Hosts and routers
2 Link Moves a frame across one hop to the next device; shared-medium access; error detection Frame MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses Ethernet, Wi-Fi, DOCSIS (Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification) Hosts, switches, routers
1 Physical Turns bits into signals (voltage, light, radio) and back Bit — Copper, fibre, radio Every device

Two points worth adding: each layer uses the service of the one below and serves the one above, so one can change without affecting the others (Wi-Fi on one hop, fibre on the next); and routers only go up to layer 3, switches to layer 2 — only the two end hosts run transport and application (the end-to-end principle). OSI (Open Systems Interconnection)'s 7-layer model adds presentation and session layers, which the Internet leaves inside the application.

How to approach it

Topic: Five-layer stack

Method / formula: Table: layer, job, PDU (Protocol Data Unit) name, protocols, address

Practice: Part D, Unit 1 Section 2 table

↑ Assignment 1 Part 1
Q1.3 (5%)

What are a packet-switched network and a circuit-switched network? Develop a table to summarise their features, pros and cons.

Unit 1 · Section 1.1
Answer

  • Circuit-switched (the old phone network): before talking, a path with a fixed share of every link is reserved for the whole call, like booking a private lane. Shared using FDM (Frequency Division Multiplexing) (frequency slices) or TDM (Time Division Multiplexing) (time slots).

  • Packet-switched (the Internet): nothing is reserved; data is cut into packets with addresses, and each is forwarded hop by hop, waiting in a queue if the link is busy — like cars sharing public roads.

Feature Circuit-switched Packet-switched
Resources Reserved in advance for the whole session Shared on demand, per packet
Setup Call setup needed before data None — send immediately
Bandwidth / delay Guaranteed, constant, predictable Varies with other traffic (queuing)
When idle Reserved capacity wasted Capacity used by others
Overload New calls blocked; existing calls fine Queues grow, delay rises, packets dropped
State in switches Per-call state Only a forwarding table
Order / loss In order, no loss once set up May reorder or lose; TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) repairs
Pros Guaranteed quality; no congestion once connected; little header overhead Efficient sharing; many more users for bursty traffic; no setup delay; simple, robust core
Cons Wasteful for bursty data; setup delay; calls refused when full; doesn't scale No guarantees; jitter hurts real-time media; loss; header overhead; needs congestion control

Why the Internet chose packets (statistical multiplexing): a 1 Mbps link and users who need 100 kbps but are active only 10% of the time. Circuit switching: 1 Mbps ÷ 100 kbps = 10 users. Packet switching: with 35 users, the chance that more than 10 are active at once is under 0.04%, so ~3.5× as many users share the same link almost always without problems.

How to approach it

Topic: Packet vs circuit switching

Method / formula: Table of features, pros, cons; mention statistical multiplexing and reserved resources

↑ Assignment 1 Part 1
Q1.4 (5%)

What are processing, queuing, transmission and propagation delay? Where does each occur? What is traffic intensity? Why should it be no greater than 1 when designing a network?

Unit 1 · Section 1.1
Answer
Delay Plain meaning Where it happens Formula Depends on
Processing Router reads the header, checks for errors, picks the output link Inside the router, before the output queue — (microseconds) Router hardware
Queuing Waiting in line behind other packets In the router's output buffer No simple formula; grows with traffic intensity Traffic load — the only delay that varies
Transmission Pushing all the packet's bits onto the link At the output interface L / R Packet size L, link rate R
Propagation One bit travelling the length of the wire Along the link d / s Distance d, signal speed s (~2×10^8 m/s)

Total at one hop: d_nodal = d_proc + d_queue + d_trans + d_prop. Toll-booth picture: transmission = how long a whole convoy takes to pass the booth; propagation = how long one car takes to drive to the next booth.

Traffic intensity I = L·a / R: L·a is how many bits per second arrive (a packets/s of L bits); R is how many bits per second the link can send. It's demand ÷ capacity — the fraction of time the link is busy.

Why I ≤ 1 (and in practice well below 1):

1. If I > 1, bits arrive faster than they can leave forever: the queue grows without limit, and since buffers are finite, packets are dropped. More buffer only adds delay; it can't create capacity.

2. Waiting time explodes as I approaches 1 — roughly like I/(1 − I): about 1 packet-time at I = 0.5, 9 at 0.9, 99 at 0.99.

3. Traffic comes in bursts; an average of 0.9 means frequent moments above 1. Engineers aim for about 0.7 or less to leave headroom.

How to approach it

Topic: Four delays, traffic intensity

Method / formula: Define each delay and where it occurs; I = La/R; explain why I > 1 makes the queue grow without bound

Practice: Genre 01, Genre 04

↑ Assignment 1 Part 1
Q1.5 (5%)

What is Web caching? When may it be more useful in a university? What problem does the conditional GET solve?

Unit 2 · Section 2.2
Answer

Web caching: a proxy server near the users keeps copies of recently fetched web objects. Browsers send requests to it. If it has the object (a hit), it answers immediately over the fast campus network. If not (a miss), it fetches the object from the real server, keeps a copy and passes it on. Benefits: faster responses for hits, less traffic on the campus's Internet link (so even misses get faster), and less load on origin servers.

When it's most useful at a university:

  • Many people request the same content (a class of 300 downloading the same slides, readings or videos) → high hit rate.

  • The campus Internet link is the bottleneck (campus LAN (Local Area Network) 1–100 Gbps, outside link much smaller) — a cache is a one-time purchase versus a monthly bill for a bigger link.

  • Peaks (before deadlines, right after a lecture recording is posted) push the link's traffic intensity toward 1; the cache absorbs them.

  • Large, rarely changing files (videos, PDFs (Portable Document Format)). It helps least with personal pages (grades, LMS (Learning Management System) pages) and encrypted HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) traffic it can't open.

Conditional GET: caching creates a risk of serving stale (out-of-date) copies. The cache sends an ordinary GET with an If-Modified-Since: <date of my copy> header. If the object hasn't changed, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body (a few hundred bytes) and the cache serves its copy; if it has changed, the server sends 200 OK with the new object. So the cache stays correct without re-downloading unchanged objects.

How to approach it

Topic: Web caching, conditional GET

Method / formula: Explain the cache, when a university benefits (many users, shared popular content, limited access link), what problem conditional GET solves (stale copies)

Q1.6 (5%)

You send an email from a Web-based account (e.g., Gmail) on your smartphone to Alice, who reads mail with IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) on her smartphone; both are on home Wi-Fi. List all protocols involved and describe how the message travels through all layers on each device (ignore everything between the two ISPs (Internet Service Provider)).

Unit 1 · Section 1.2 · Unit 2 · Section 2.3
Answer

Protocols by layer:

Layer Protocols Role
Application HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)/HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), IMAP, DNS (Domain Name System), DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) HTTP: your phone → Gmail; SMTP: Gmail → Alice's mail server; IMAP: Alice's server → Alice's phone; DNS: names and MX (Mail Exchanger record) records; DHCP: each phone gets its address
(Security) TLS (Transport Layer Security) Encrypts each leg
Transport TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) (HTTP, SMTP, IMAP); UDP (User Datagram Protocol) (DNS, DHCP) Reliable streams for mail; quick one-shot queries for DNS/DHCP
Network IP (Internet Protocol), ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol); NAT (Network Address Translation) at home routers Host-to-host delivery
Link 802.11 Wi-Fi, Ethernet, DOCSIS (Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification)/fibre access, ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) One hop at a time; ARP finds next-hop MAC (Medium Access Control) addresses
Physical Wi-Fi radio, copper, fibre Bits as signals

Step by step:

1. Joining the network: your phone associates with your Wi-Fi access point, gets an IP address, gateway and DNS server via DHCP (UDP broadcast), and uses ARP to learn the router's MAC address.

2. Your phone → Gmail (HTTP): you tap Send. The app looks up Gmail's server with DNS (UDP). It opens a TCP connection (SYN (Synchronize flag), SYN-ACK (Acknowledgement), ACK) to port 443, sets up TLS, and sends an HTTP POST with the message. Going down your phone's stack: HTTP message → TLS encrypts → TCP segments with ports and sequence numbers → IP datagrams with addresses → Wi-Fi frames with MAC addresses and CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) → radio signals.

3. Your home router: receives the frame (layers 1–2), looks at the IP header (layer 3), decrements TTL (Time-to-Live), does NAT (replaces your private address/port with its public address and a new port), and re-wraps the datagram in a new frame for the cable/fibre link. It never looks at TCP or HTTP.

4. ISP routers: each strips the frame, looks up the destination IP, builds a new frame for the next link — layers 1–3 only.

5. Gmail server: the datagram goes up the stack: frame → IP → TCP (reassembled in order) → TLS decrypts → HTTP → the mail system queues the message.

6. Gmail → Alice's mail server (SMTP): Gmail asks DNS for the MX record of Alice's domain, opens a TCP connection to port 25 (usually with STARTTLS), and pushes the message with SMTP commands: HELO/EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, the message, ".", QUIT. Alice's server stores it in her mailbox.

7. Alice's phone (IMAP): her phone joined its Wi-Fi the same way (DHCP, ARP, NAT at her router). Her mail app opens a TCP/TLS connection to port 993, logs in, and uses IMAP commands (SELECT INBOX, FETCH) to pull the message, which climbs her phone's stack (radio → Wi-Fi → IP → TCP → TLS → IMAP → mail app).

Key idea: three application protocols, none end to end — HTTP (you → provider), SMTP (provider → provider, push), IMAP (provider → Alice, pull). Only end hosts look above layer 3.

How to approach it

Topic: Email path through all layers

Method / formula: Trace the message: phone → Wi-Fi AP (Access Point) → your ISP → Gmail servers (HTTP/HTTPS or SMTP submission) → SMTP → Alice's server → IMAP → Alice's phone; name the protocols at each layer on each device

Part 2: Long Answer Questions (70%)

Q2.1Q2.2Q2.3Q2.4
Q2.1 (20%)

You upload a 10 MB (Megabytes) assignment to the university server. Packets are 10,000 bits including 100 bits of header. (a) How many packets? (b) How many links does TRACERT (Trace Route, a Windows command) show, and what are they? (c) The speed of each link? (d) If upload starts at t0, when is the last packet pushed into the first link? (e) When does the last packet arrive at the server?

Unit 1 · Section 1.1
Answer

(a) Number of packets.

  • Useful data per packet = 10,000 − 100 = 9,900 bits (the header carries no file data).

  • File size = 10 MB = 10 × 10^6 bytes × 8 = 80,000,000 bits (network "MB" = 10^6 bytes; state this).

  • Packets = 80,000,000 ÷ 9,900 = 8,080.8 → round up (a part-packet still needs a packet) = 8,081 packets.

  • (If 10 MB meant 10 × 2^20 bytes = 83,886,080 bits → 8,474 packets. Say which you use.)

(b) Links. Your TRACERT to login.athabascau.ca (54.184.188.222, AWS (Amazon Web Services) Oregon) listed 17 hops = 17 links (each hop is one more link, starting with the one leaving your computer):

Link From → to What it is
1 your PC (Personal Computer) → 192.168.86.1 Home Wi-Fi (802.11ac, 5 GHz)
2 router → 10.27.184.114 Cable (DOCSIS (Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification)) access link — the bottleneck
3–8 Comcast Richmond → Charlottesville routers (rur, tcr, ccr, asbr) Comcast aggregation/core network
9–10 Comcast backbone, Ashburn VA (Virginia) Backbone and hand-off to AWS
11–16 six silent hops AWS internal backbone to Oregon (routers don't reply)
17 → EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) server Data-centre link to the server

(c) Link speeds. Traceroute measures delay, not speed, so speeds must be measured or estimated separately:

  • Link 1: 877.5 Mbps transmit rate (from netsh wlan show interfaces).

  • Link 2: 47.4 Mbps upstream = average of your three 25 MB uploads (49.6 + 53.0 + 39.6) ÷ 3 = 142.2 ÷ 3 = 47.4 Mbps.

  • Links 3–16: about 100 Gbps (estimated — carrier backbone links); link 17: about 10 Gbps (estimated — typical cloud server link).

The estimates barely matter: at 100 Gbps a packet takes 0.0001 ms, versus 0.21 ms on the 47.4 Mbps link.

(d) Last packet into the first link. Your PC sends all packets back-to-back at R1:

time = N × L / R1 = 8,081 × 10,000 / 877,500,000 = 80,810,000 / 877,500,000 = 0.0921 s

t = t0 + 0.0921 s (92.1 ms).

(e) Last packet arrives at the server. Because link 2 (47.4 Mbps) is far slower than link 1, packets pile up at the home router and link 2 sets the pace. The last packet arrives at:

t = L/R1  +  N × L/R2  +  (L/R of each faster link after the bottleneck)  +  total propagation
 = 0.0000114 s + (80,810,000 / 47,400,000) + 0.0000024 s + d_prop
 = 0.0000114 + 1.7049 + 0.0000024 + 0.0263 s  ≈  1.731 s

t ≈ t0 + 1.73 s. In words: the first packet needs a moment to reach the bottleneck, then the bottleneck needs 1.705 s to push all 8,081 packets through, then the last packet crosses the fast links (almost no time) and travels the distance (26.3 ms one-way propagation from Q2.2).

A correction to note in your submission: your answer used 0.0530 s for propagation, which gives 1.758 s. But 0.0530 s is about twice the one-way propagation delay from your own Q2.2(b) (26.32 ms) — it is close to the round-trip value (52.6 ms). For a one-way arrival time the propagation term should be 0.0263 s, giving ≈ 1.731 s. (If you intended to include measured queuing/processing delay, say so explicitly.)

Why not just add everything to (d)? The "first link paces everything" formula gives about 0.145 s — about 12 times too fast. Lesson: the slowest link decides how long a big transfer takes.

How to approach it

Topic: Packetised transfer timing

Method / formula: packets = file bits / (packet − header bits); identify links with traceroute; estimate link rates; last packet into first link = P x L/R₁; arrival = pipelined formula over all links with the bottleneck

Q2.2 (20%)

(a) Total distance your data travels to the server? (b) Propagation delay with s = 2×10^8 m/s? (c) With all links at R bps, the bandwidth-delay product R × Tprop? (d) Sending the file continuously, the maximum bits in the links at any time? (e) What does the bandwidth-delay product imply?

Unit 1 · Section 1.1
Answer

(a) Distance. The router names in your trace reveal the route: Mechanicsville → Richmond (9.4 km) → Charlottesville (106.4 km) → Ashburn (141.9 km) → AWS (Amazon Web Services) Oregon (3,502.6 km). Straight-line total = 3,760.2 km. Real fibre doesn't run in straight lines (it follows roads and railways), so multiply by a typical route factor of 1.4:

d = 3,760.2 km × 1.4 = 5,264.3 km = 5.264 × 10^6 m

(b) Propagation delay.

Tprop = d / s = 5,264,280 m / (2 × 10^8 m/s) = 0.02632 s = 26.32 ms (one way)

Sanity check: your measured round trip to Oregon was 105 ms (≈ 52.5 ms one way); propagation explains about half, and the rest is transmission, processing and queuing — reasonable for home cable.

(c) Bandwidth-delay product.

BDP = R × Tprop = 47,400,000 × 0.02632 ≈ 1.25 × 10^6 bits  (about 156 KB)   (upload rate)
     113,400,000 × 0.02632 ≈ 2.98 × 10^6 bits                             (download rate)

(d) Maximum bits in the links. Sending continuously, the sender puts R bits into the path each second, and each bit stays in the "pipe" for Tprop seconds, so the pipe holds R × Tprop ≈ 1.25 × 10^6 bits at once — the same as (c). (This is the maximum only if the file is at least that big; 80,000,000 bits is.)

(e) What it means. Picture the path as a pipe: R is its width, Tprop its length, and BDP (Bandwidth-Delay Product) its volume in bits. It tells you:

1. How much data is "in the air" (sent but not yet received) at any moment.

2. How big a sender's window must be to keep the link busy — a protocol that stops to wait for ACKs (Acknowledgement) needs a window of at least one BDP; a smaller window leaves the link idle (why one TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) stream got only 77–91 Mbps on your 113 Mbps link, while several streams filled it).

3. Faster links make the BDP bigger (more data at risk per loss); distance is fixed by the speed of light — the reason CDNs (Content Distribution Network) put servers close to users (Athabasca's website answered from Virginia in 33 ms; its login server in Oregon took 105 ms).

How to approach it

Topic: Distance, propagation, bandwidth-delay product

Method / formula: d_prop = d/s; BDP = R x d_prop; bits in the link = min(file, BDP); interpret BDP as the "pipe volume"

Q2.3 (20%)

Install Apache as a proxy on your home network and report what you did. Then, with 6 family members, 100 MB (Megabytes) videos, 3 requests per minute, and 5 s for the ISP (Internet Service Provider) router to fetch from the Internet: (a) α = average time for your home router to receive an object from the ISP router; (b) traffic intensity μ with no caching; (c) access delay β = α/(μ−1); (d) total response time 5 + β with a proxy miss rate of 0.5.

Unit 2 · Section 2.2
Answer

Part 1 — the proxy. Your submission states honestly that Apache was not actually installed; it gives the full configuration instead. The key steps (PowerShell/CLI (Command-Line Interface) first):

C:\Apache24\bin\httpd.exe -k install
C:\Apache24\bin\httpd.exe -k start
# httpd.conf: enable mod_proxy, mod_proxy_http, mod_proxy_connect, mod_cache, mod_cache_disk
# httpd-proxy.conf: Listen 3128 / ProxyRequests On / Require ip 192.168.86.0/24
#                   CacheEnable disk "http://" / CacheMaxFileSize 524288000  (default 1 MB would skip 100 MB videos)
curl -x http://192.168.86.118:3128 -sI http://example.com/big.mp4 | findstr /I "X-Cache"   # MISS then HIT

Then point each device's HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) proxy at 192.168.86.118:3128 (Windows: Settings → Network & Internet → Proxy → Manual setup). Honest limitation: most video is HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), which a forward proxy can tunnel but not cache.

Part 2 — the numbers. The question doesn't give the access-link speed, so use your measured 113.4 Mbps (download).

  • Object = 100 MB = 100 × 10^6 × 8 = 8 × 10^8 bits. Requests = 3/min = 0.05 per second.

(a) α = time to push one object across the access link:

α = 800,000,000 / 113,400,000 = 7.055 s

(b) μ = arrival rate × time per object (fraction of time the link is busy):

μ = 0.05 × 7.055 = 0.353       check: demand 0.05 × 8×10^8 = 40 Mbps; 40 / 113.4 = 0.353

The link is busy about 35% of the time — loaded, but stable (μ < 1).

(c) The given formula β = α/(μ − 1) gives 7.055 / (0.353 − 1) = −10.9 s — a negative delay, which is impossible. The standard queuing formula (textbook) is β = α / (1 − μ) (divide by the fraction of time the link is free). Say this in your answer and use:

β = 7.055 / (1 − 0.353) = 7.055 / 0.647 = 10.90 s

(Even at 35% load, waiting adds 3.8 s on top of the 7.1 s transfer.)

(d) No cache: 5 + 10.90 = 15.90 s. With a proxy and miss rate 0.5, half the requests are served from the local disk (≈ 0 s). The other half go out — and the link is now less busy, because only half the requests use it:

μ' = 0.025 × 7.055 = 0.176        β' = 7.055 / (1 − 0.176) = 8.565 s
Average response = 0.5 × (5 + 8.565) + 0.5 × 0 ≈ 6.78 s

(Taking the question literally without recomputing μ: 0.5 × 15.90 = 7.95 s. Show both; 6.78 s is the more correct answer.)

Setup μ β (s) Response time (s)
No cache 0.353 10.90 15.90
Cache, literal 0.353 10.90 7.95
Cache, μ recomputed 0.176 8.57 6.78

Lesson: a cache helps even the requests it can't answer, because it lightens the load on the shared link, and delay depends on 1/(1 − μ).

How to approach it

Topic: Home web cache, traffic intensity

Method / formula: α = L/R; μ = arrival rate x L / R; access delay (use the standard α/(1−μ) and note the sign problem); response time with miss rate 0.5 (recompute μ for misses only)

Q2.4 (10%)

Distribute F = 21 GB (Gigabytes) to N peers. Server upload us = 1 Gbps; each peer downloads at di = 20 Mbps and uploads at u. For N = 10, 100, 1,000 and u = 300 kbps, 7,000 kbps and 2 Mbps, tabulate the minimum distribution time for client-server and P2P (Peer-to-Peer), and comment.

Unit 2 · Section 2.5
Answer

Formulas (plain English in Section 2.5):

D_cs  = max( N·F/us , F/dmin )
D_p2p = max( F/us , F/dmin , N·F/(us + N·u) )

Constants: F = 21 × 10^9 × 8 = 1.68 × 10^11 bits; F/dmin = 1.68×10^11 / 2×10^7 = 8,400 s; F/us = 1.68×10^11 / 10^9 = 168 s.

Sample calculation (N = 100, u = 2 Mbps): N·F/us = 100 × 168 = 16,800 s → D_cs = max(16,800, 8,400) = 16,800 s. N·F/(us + N·u) = 1.68×10^13 / (10^9 + 2×10^8) = 1.68×10^13 / 1.2×10^9 = 14,000 s → D_p2p = max(168, 8,400, 14,000) = 14,000 s.

N u N·F/us (s) D_cs (s) N·F/(us+Nu) (s) D_p2p (s) P2P speed-up
10 300 kbps 1,680 8,400 (2 h 20 m) 1,675 8,400 (2 h 20 m) 1.00×
10 7,000 kbps 1,680 8,400 1,570 8,400 1.00×
10 2 Mbps 1,680 8,400 1,647 8,400 1.00×
100 300 kbps 16,800 16,800 (4 h 40 m) 16,311 16,311 (4 h 32 m) 1.03×
100 7,000 kbps 16,800 16,800 9,882 9,882 (2 h 45 m) 1.70×
100 2 Mbps 16,800 16,800 14,000 14,000 (3 h 53 m) 1.20×
1,000 300 kbps 168,000 168,000 (46 h 40 m) 129,231 129,231 (35 h 54 m) 1.30×
1,000 7,000 kbps 168,000 168,000 21,000 21,000 (5 h 50 m) 8.00×
1,000 2 Mbps 168,000 168,000 56,000 56,000 (15 h 33 m) 3.00×

Comments in plain English:

  • Client-server grows in step with N: the server must send a full copy to everyone, so 10× the peers = 10× the time (4 h 40 m → 46 h 40 m). Peers' upload capacity sits unused.

  • P2P scales itself: every new peer brings upload capacity; the time levels off near F/u. With 1,000 peers at 7 Mbps the swarm supplies 7 Gbps beside the server's 1 Gbps — 8× faster.

  • For small N it makes no difference: at N = 10 both take 8,400 s, because each peer's own 20 Mbps download is the limit.

  • Peer upload speed is the lever: at N = 1,000, going from 300 kbps to 7 Mbps upload cuts P2P time six-fold; client-server doesn't change. Home connections with slow upload (like your 47 Mbps up vs 113 down) limit P2P.

  • Real-world caveats: these are ideal lower bounds; real swarms suffer churn and free-riders (BitTorrent's tit-for-tat and rarest-first fight these). Client-server is simpler and controllable, which is why CDNs (Content Distribution Network) (many distributed servers) dominate commercial delivery.

How to approach it

Topic: Client-server vs P2P distribution

Method / formula: D_cs and D_p2p formulas in a 3 x 3 table for N and u; comment on self-scaling

Assignment 2 (20%) — Units 3, 4 and 5

Every calculation below was re-checked by script; the numbers match your submission (Submissions/comp347/assignment2).

Part 1: Short Answer Questions (30%)

Q1.1Q1.2Q1.3Q1.4Q1.5Q1.6
Q1.1 (5%)

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides reliable data transfer on top of IP (Internet Protocol)'s unreliable best-effort service. In your own words, explain how TCP provides it.

Unit 3 · Section 3.2
Answer

IP is like a postal service that may lose, damage, duplicate or shuffle your letters and never tells you. TCP fixes this at the two ends with a set of tools that work together:

  • Numbering (sequence numbers): every byte gets a number. The receiver can put pieces back in order, spot gaps, and throw away duplicates.

  • Damage check (checksum): each segment carries a checksum; a damaged segment is simply thrown away — so "damaged" becomes "lost", which the next tools handle.

  • Receipts (cumulative ACKs (Acknowledgement)): the receiver keeps telling the sender "I have everything up to byte n; send n next."

  • Timer and resend (retransmission): the sender keeps a timer on the oldest unacknowledged data. If no ACK arrives in time, it resends. The timeout adapts to the network: TimeoutInterval = EstimatedRTT + 4 × DevRTT, and doubles after each timeout.

  • Fast retransmit: three duplicate ACKs for the same byte mean one segment went missing while later ones arrived, so the sender resends it immediately instead of waiting for the timer.

  • Receiver buffering: out-of-order segments are held until the gap is filled, so the application always receives a complete, in-order byte stream.

  • Flow control (receive window): the receiver advertises how much buffer space it has left (rwnd), and the sender never overflows it (which would cause losses).

  • Connection setup and teardown: the three-way handshake (SYN (Synchronize flag), SYN-ACK, ACK) agrees on starting sequence numbers so old or duplicate segments from earlier connections can't be confused with new ones.

  • Congestion control also cuts losses inside the network by slowing the sender when loss signals congestion.

Together: nothing lost, nothing duplicated, no corruption, in order — built entirely at the end hosts on top of an unreliable network.

How to approach it

Topic: TCP reliability over IP

Method / formula: Checksums, sequence numbers, cumulative ACKs, timers with adaptive timeout, retransmission, fast retransmit, flow control

↑ Assignment 2 Part 1
Q1.2 (5%)

The rdt protocols are stop-and-wait, but Go-Back-N lets the sender send multiple packets without waiting for acknowledgements. How does GBN achieve that?

Unit 3 · Section 3.2
Answer

  • A window of N packets. The sender may have up to N unacknowledged packets in flight at once, instead of just one. Packets are numbered with sequence numbers (with k-bit numbers, the window must be ≤ 2^k − 1).

  • Sender bookkeeping: it tracks base (oldest unACKed packet) and nextseqnum (next number to use). Packets base … nextseqnum−1 are sent but unACKed; it may send new packets while nextseqnum < base + N. The window slides forward as ACKs (Acknowledgement) arrive (a "sliding-window protocol").

  • Buffering: the sender keeps copies of all unACKed packets in case they must be resent.

  • Cumulative ACKs: the receiver ACKs "everything up to n received correctly and in order"; one ACK can confirm many packets, and a lost ACK is covered by a later one.

  • Simple receiver: it accepts only the next expected packet; out-of-order packets are discarded and the last in-order packet is re-ACKed. So the receiver needs no buffer.

  • One timer, go back: the sender times the oldest unACKed packet. On a timeout it resends that packet and every packet after it that was already sent ("go back N").

Result: the link stays busy during the round trip, so utilisation rises roughly N-fold compared with stop-and-wait: U = N·(L/R) / (RTT (Round-Trip Time) + L/R).

How to approach it

Topic: How GBN sends without waiting

Method / formula: Window of N unacknowledged packets, sequence numbers, cumulative ACKs, one timer, go back and resend on timeout

Practice: Genre 11

↑ Assignment 2 Part 1
Q1.3 (5%)

What problems was IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) intended to solve? With so many IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) devices still in use, how is the transition from IPv4 to IPv6 being handled?

Unit 4 · Section 4.3
Answer

Problems IPv6 solves:

  • Running out of addresses (the main reason): IPv4 has only 2^32 ≈ 4.3 billion addresses; the regional registries' free pools ran out from 2011 onward. IPv6's 128-bit addresses (2^128 ≈ 3.4 × 10^38) give every device a real, globally unique address and reduce dependence on NAT (Network Address Translation).

  • Faster, simpler router processing: a fixed 40-byte header; no fragmentation at routers (the sender fragments; routers send "Packet Too Big"); no header checksum to recompute at every hop; options moved to optional extension headers.

  • Quality of service: a flow label and traffic class to mark flows needing special handling.

  • Also: auto-configuration (SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration)), better multicast/anycast support, built-in IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) support.

Transition — why it's slow and how it works: you can't switch every device on one day ("flag day"), so methods let both run together:

  • Dual stack: devices and routers run both IPv4 and IPv6 and use whichever the other side supports (DNS (Domain Name System) returns A and AAAA records). This is the most common method.

  • Tunnelling: an IPv6 datagram is carried inside the payload of an IPv4 datagram across IPv4-only parts of the network; the IPv4 section acts like one "link" between two IPv6 routers (6in4, 6to4, Teredo).

  • Translation: NAT64 (Network Address Translation from IPv6 to IPv4)/DNS64 (Domain Name System extension for IPv6-to-IPv4 translation) lets IPv6-only devices reach IPv4-only servers (common on mobile networks).

Adoption keeps growing — large providers (mobile carriers, Google, Comcast, content networks) use IPv6 widely, and today a large share of users reach Google over IPv6 — but IPv4 will stay alongside for years.

How to approach it

Topic: IPv6 motivation and transition

Method / formula: Address exhaustion, faster processing (fixed header, no router fragmentation/checksum), QoS (Quality of Service) flow label; dual stack and tunnelling

↑ Assignment 2 Part 1
Q1.4 (5%)

SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) has seven message types. What are the purposes of the SNMP GetRequest and SetRequest messages? Why were UDP (User Datagram Protocol) datagrams chosen to transport SNMP messages?

Unit 5 · Section 5.7
Answer

  • GetRequest: the managing server asks an agent in a device to read the current value of one or more MIB (Management Information Base) objects (e.g., an interface's byte counter or status). The agent replies with a Response containing the values.

  • SetRequest: the managing server asks the agent to change (write) the value of one or more MIB objects — e.g., change a configuration setting or disable an interface. The agent replies with a Response confirming (or reporting an error).

(Other types: GetNextRequest, GetBulkRequest, InformRequest, Response, Trap.)

Why UDP:

  • Works when the network is sick: network management is needed most when things are broken or congested. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) needs a handshake and holds back data during congestion and retransmission; UDP just sends one message, so the manager can still reach devices.

  • Simple and light: requests are small, independent request/response pairs; a TCP connection per poll would add overhead to thousands of devices, and devices (even tiny ones) don't need to keep connection state.

  • The manager handles reliability itself: it sets a timeout and retransmits if no Response arrives (request IDs (Identifier) detect duplicates); lost periodic polls are simply repeated next time.

  • Speed: no connection setup delay.

How to approach it

Topic: SNMP GetRequest/SetRequest, why UDP

Method / formula: Get reads MIB objects, Set writes them; UDP is light, stateless, works in degraded networks

Practice: Part D, Unit 5 Section 7

↑ Assignment 2 Part 1
Q1.5 (5%)

Many SDN (Software-Defined Networking)-enabled networking devices exist today. What preferable features does an SDN-enabled device usually have?

Unit 4 · Section 4.4 · Unit 5 · Section 5.5
Answer

  • Separation of data plane and control plane: the device mainly forwards packets; decisions come from a remote SDN controller.

  • Flow tables with match-plus-action (generalized forwarding): it can match many header fields (ingress port, MAC (Medium Access Control), VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network), IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, protocol, TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)/UDP (User Datagram Protocol) ports) and apply actions (forward to one/many ports, drop, modify header fields, send to controller), with priorities.

  • Standard southbound interface — OpenFlow (and/or NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol)/YANG (Yet Another Next Generation, a data-modelling language), P4Runtime) — so any compliant controller can program it, avoiding vendor lock-in.

  • Counters and statistics per flow, per port and per table, reported to the controller for monitoring.

  • Fast hardware forwarding at line rate (TCAM (Ternary Content-Addressable Memory)/ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit)), with many flow-table entries and multiple tables.

  • Secure, reliable controller connection (TLS (Transport Layer Security)), with support for backup controllers.

  • Programmability and flexibility: the same box can act as switch, router, firewall, NAT (Network Address Translation) or load balancer; often "white-box" hardware running open software; support for VLANs/tunnels, QoS (Quality of Service) queues, and events such as port-status and packet-in messages.

How to approach it

Topic: Features of SDN-enabled devices

Method / formula: Flow tables with match-plus-action, OpenFlow support, remote controller interface, counters, programmability

Practice: Part D, Unit 5 Section 5

↑ Assignment 2 Part 1
Q1.6 (5%)

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) faces the problem of detecting loops in paths. What are the loops? Why should they be avoided? How does BGP detect them?

Unit 5 · Section 5.4
Answer

  • What a loop is: a routing loop is when routes point in a circle — AS1 thinks the way to a prefix is through AS2, AS2 thinks it's through AS3, and AS3 thinks it's back through AS1. Packets go round and round and never reach the destination.

  • Why avoid them: looping packets waste bandwidth and router capacity, add congestion, and are never delivered; they circulate until their TTL (Time-to-Live) runs out and are dropped. The destination becomes unreachable.

  • How BGP detects them — the AS (Autonomous System)-PATH attribute: every BGP advertisement carries the list of ASes it has passed through. When an AS advertises a route to a neighbouring AS (eBGP (external Border Gateway Protocol)), it adds its own AS number to the front of the AS-PATH. When a router receives an advertisement, it checks the AS-PATH: if its own AS number is already in the list, the route has looped back, and the router rejects it. This detection is exact — unlike distance-vector protocols, which can only guess (count-to-infinity) — because the full path of ASes is carried along.

How to approach it

Topic: BGP loops

Method / formula: Define a loop, why harmful (packets circulate until TTL expires), AS-PATH check rejects routes containing your own ASN (Autonomous System Number)

Part 2: Long Answer Questions (70%)

Q2.1Q2.2Q2.3Q2.4
Q2.1 (10%)

Using the 8-bit bytes 11011001, 01010010, 11001010, 10100100 and 01011001: (a) What is the 1's complement of the sum? (b) Why do UDP (User Datagram Protocol) and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) use the 1's complement of the sum rather than the sum? (c) How does the receiver detect errors? (d) Can any 1-bit error go undetected? A 2-bit error?

Unit 3 · Section 3.2
Answer

(a) Step by step. Rule: add normally; if the sum overflows 8 bits (a carry out of the left end), drop the carry and add 1 to the result ("end-around carry"). Decimal check: whenever a sum passes 255, subtract 256 and add 1 (i.e., subtract 255).

Step Add Raw sum Carry? Running sum
1 11011001 (217) + 01010010 (82) 299 = 1 00101011 yes → 00101011 + 1 00101100 (44)
2 00101100 (44) + 11001010 (202) 246 = 11110110 no 11110110 (246)
3 11110110 (246) + 10100100 (164) 410 = 1 10011010 yes → 10011010 + 1 10011011 (155)
4 10011011 (155) + 01011001 (89) 244 = 11110100 no 11110100 (244)

One's-complement sum = 11110100. Now flip every bit: checksum = 00001011 (decimal 11). Check: 244 + 11 = 255 = 11111111 ✓.

(b) Why the complement: because then the receiver's test is the same simple check every time: add everything — data and checksum — and see whether you get all 1s (a number plus its complement is always 11111111). If the checksum were the plain sum, the receiver would have to add the data and then compare with a separately handled value. With the complement, the same adder does both jobs and the test needs no stored expected value. One's-complement arithmetic is also byte-order independent and easy to update incrementally.

(c) Receiver's check: add all received bytes including the checksum using end-around carry. 11111111 → no error detected; any 0 bit → error, and the segment is discarded (TCP then retransmits after a timeout; UDP just drops it). Here: 11110100 + 00001011 = 11111111 ✓.

(d)

  • Any single-bit error is always detected. Flipping one bit changes the total by ±2^k (1, 2, 4 … 128). With end-around carry the arithmetic works "modulo 255", and none of these values is a multiple of 255, so the sum can't come back to 11111111.

  • A 2-bit error can go undetected. If the same bit position flips 0→1 in one byte and 1→0 in another, the +2^k and −2^k cancel and the sum is unchanged. Example from this data: byte 1 = 11011001 → flip bit 1 (0→1) → 11011011 (+2); byte 2 = 01010010 → flip bit 1 (1→0) → 01010000 (−2). The sum is still 11110100 — the error slips through. (That's why link layers use stronger CRCs (Cyclic Redundancy Check).)

How to approach it

Topic: One's-complement checksum

Method / formula: Add bytes with end-around carry, invert; receiver adds all including checksum → all ones; discuss 1-bit and 2-bit errors

Q2.2 (20%)

(a) Interpret the given Dijkstra table (source u): what does it show, and what do each row and column show? (b) For the network in the figure (fig-Q2-2.png), use Dijkstra's algorithm to compute the shortest paths from x to all other nodes, showing a table like the one given.

Unit 5 · Section 5.2
Answer

(a) Reading the table. It is a trace of Dijkstra's algorithm running at node u, which (link-state routing) already knows every link and cost. It shows u's knowledge improving step by step until it has the cheapest route to every node.

  • Step: the iteration number; one node is finalised per step, so there are as many rows as nodes.

  • N': the set of nodes whose cheapest path from u is final — it grows by one node each step.

  • D(v),p(v) columns: for each other node v, D(v) is the cheapest cost found so far (using only finalised nodes as stepping stones) and p(v) the previous node on that path (used to rebuild the route). "∞" = no path found yet; blank/"—" = already finalised.

  • Each row: pick the not-yet-final node with the smallest D, add it to N', then check its neighbours: D(v) = min(D(v), D(w) + c(w,v)).

  • Reading this one: start: v 2, w 5, x 1 (direct links); y, z unknown. Step 1 adds x (1): w improves to 4 via x, y found at 2 via x. Step 2 adds y (2; tie with v): w improves to 3 via y, z found at 4 via y. Steps 3–5 add v (2), w (3), z (4). Final: v 2 (via u), w 3 (via y), x 1, y 2 (via x), z 4 (via y).

(b) Dijkstra from x. Link costs read from the figure: s–t 1, s–v 5, t–u 9, t–v 6, t–y 5, t–z 3, u–v 1, u–w 1, u–x 2, u–y 1, v–w 3, w–x 3, x–y 5, y–z 11.

Step N' D(s),p D(t),p D(u),p D(v),p D(w),p D(y),p D(z),p
0 x ∞ ∞ 2,x ∞ 3,x 5,x ∞
1 xu ∞ 11,u — 3,u 3,x 3,u ∞
2 xuv 8,v 9,v — — 3,x 3,u ∞
3 xuvw 8,v 9,v — — — 3,u ∞
4 xuvwy 8,v 8,y — — — — 14,y
5 xuvwys — 8,y — — — — 14,y
6 xuvwyst — — — — — — 11,t
7 xuvwystz — — — — — — —

In words:

  • Step 0: x's neighbours — u 2, w 3, y 5.

  • Step 1: add u (2). Via u: v = 2+1 = 3; y = 2+1 = 3 (better than 5); t = 2+9 = 11; w via u = 3 (not better than 3, keep x).

  • Step 2: v and w tie at 3; pick v. Via v: s = 3+5 = 8; t = 3+6 = 9 (better than 11).

  • Step 3: add w (3); nothing improves.

  • Step 4: add y (3). Via y: t = 3+5 = 8 (better than 9); z = 3+11 = 14.

  • Step 5: s and t tie at 8; add s. Via s: t = 8+1 = 9, not better.

  • Step 6: add t (8). Via t: z = 8+3 = 11 (better than 14!).

  • Step 7: add z (11). Done.

Destination Cost Path First hop from x
u 2 x-u u
v 3 x-u-v u
w 3 x-w w
y 3 x-u-y u
s 8 x-u-v-s u
t 8 x-u-y-t u
z 11 x-u-y-t-z u

Checks: t via x-u-t = 11 and x-u-v-t = 9, both worse than 8; z via y-z = 14, worse than 11; s via t = 9, worse than 8. Six of seven destinations leave x through u (u is the well-connected hub).

How to approach it

Topic: Dijkstra

Method / formula: Interpret the given table; then build your own table from x on the figure

↑ Assignment 2 Part 2
Q2.3 (20%)

A CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) router's table: 135.46.56.0/22 → Interface 0; 135.46.60.0/22 → Interface 1; 192.53.40.0/23 → Router 2; default → Router 3. How does a CIDR router route packets? What happens to packets for (a) 135.46.61.10 (b) 135.46.53.16 (c) 192.53.40.6 (d) 192.53.56.7?

Unit 4 · Section 4.2 · Unit 4 · Section 4.3
Answer

How it works: for each packet, compare the destination address with every entry's prefix (only the first /x bits count). Among the entries that match, choose the longest prefix (most specific). If nothing matches, use the default route (think of it as 0.0.0.0/0, which matches everything but always loses to a longer match). If there's no default, drop the packet and send ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) "destination unreachable".

Turn each entry into a range (easiest method). A /22 leaves 10 host bits; the prefix ends 6 bits into the third octet, so it covers a block of 2^2 = 4 values in the third octet. A /23 covers 2 values.

Entry Third-octet range Address range Next hop
135.46.56.0/22 56–59 135.46.56.0 – 135.46.59.255 Interface 0
135.46.60.0/22 60–63 135.46.60.0 – 135.46.63.255 Interface 1
192.53.40.0/23 40–41 192.53.40.0 – 192.53.41.255 Router 2
default everything else — Router 3

(a) 135.46.61.10: third octet 61 is in 60–63 → matches 135.46.60.0/22 → Interface 1. (Binary: 61 = 001111|01; first 6 bits 001111 match 60 = 001111|00, not 56 = 001110|00.) (b) 135.46.53.16: 53 is below 56 → no 135.46 entry matches (53 = 001101|01 ≠ 001110 or 001111) → default, Router 3. (Sharing "135.46" isn't enough!) (c) 192.53.40.6: 40 is in 40–41 → Router 2. (40 = 0010100|0 matches the first 7 bits.) (d) 192.53.56.7: 56 is outside 40–41 (56 = 0011100 ≠ 0010100) → default, Router 3. Note: the two /22 blocks are neighbours and could be combined into 135.46.56.0/21 — but only if they went to the same interface; they don't, so they stay separate.

How to approach it

Topic: CIDR routing, longest prefix match

Method / formula: Convert each prefix to an address range; match each address; longest match wins; otherwise default

↑ Assignment 2 Part 2
Q2.4 (20%)

One TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection uses a 1 Gbps link with no buffering; it's the only congested link. Huge file, big receiver buffer, 1,500-byte segments, two-way propagation delay (RTT (Round-Trip Time)) 15 ms, always in congestion avoidance. (a) Maximum window (segments)? (b) Average window and average throughput? (c) Time to regain the maximum window after a loss? (d) How to choose a buffer size to keep the link always busy?

Unit 3 · Section 3.3
Answer

Given: R = 10^9 bps; MSS (Maximum Segment Size) = 1,500 × 8 = 12,000 bits; RTT = 0.015 s.

(a) Maximum window. With no buffer, the most data that can be in flight without loss is what fits "in the pipe" — the bandwidth-delay product:

R × RTT = 10^9 × 0.015 = 15,000,000 bits
W = 15,000,000 / 12,000 = 1,250 segments

One more segment and there's nowhere to put it → loss.

(b) Average window and throughput. In congestion avoidance the window climbs by 1 segment per RTT from W/2 up to W, then halves on loss — a sawtooth. The average of a straight ramp from W/2 to W is the midpoint:

Average window = (625 + 1,250) / 2 = 0.75 × 1,250 = 937.5 segments
Average throughput = 937.5 × 12,000 bits / 0.015 s = 750,000,000 bps = 750 Mbps

So one TCP connection uses only 75% of the link — a quarter is lost to the sawtooth.

(c) Time to climb back. After a loss the window drops to 1,250/2 = 625 and grows by 1 segment per RTT:

(1,250 − 625) RTTs = 625 × 0.015 s = 9.375 s

More than 9 seconds to recover from one lost packet — why faster long-distance paths need newer algorithms (CUBIC, BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time)).

(d) Buffer size. Choose a buffer equal to the bandwidth-delay product:

Buffer = R × RTT = 15,000,000 bits = 1.875 MB ≈ 1,250 segments

Why: now the window can grow to pipe + buffer = 2 × 1,250 = 2,500 segments before a loss. After halving, it's 1,250 — still exactly enough to fill the pipe — so the link never goes idle and utilisation becomes 100%. A bigger buffer doesn't add throughput, only extra waiting (bufferbloat). (With many flows, about R × RTT / √N is enough.)

Part Result
(a) Max window 1,250 segments (15 Mbit)
(b) Average window / throughput 937.5 segments / 750 Mbps
(c) Recovery time 9.375 s (625 RTTs)
(d) Buffer ≈ 1,250 segments = 1.875 MB (Megabytes)
How to approach it

Topic: TCP window, throughput, recovery, buffer

Method / formula: W = R x RTT / MSS; average 0.75 W; recovery W/2 RTTs; buffer ≈ R x RTT

Q1.1 (5%)

What is the role of the anchor MSC (Mobile Switching Center) in GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) networks?

Unit 7 · Section 7.3
Answer

In GSM, the MSC (mobile switching centre) is the switch that handles calls for a region. The anchor MSC is the MSC the mobile was using when the call began. If the phone moves during the call into the area of a different MSC, the call is not re-routed from scratch; instead it stays routed through the anchor MSC, which extends the call to the new MSC.

  • The anchor MSC stays in the call path for the whole call; only the last leg (anchor MSC → current MSC → base station) changes as the phone moves through more MSCs.

  • This makes inter-MSC handoffs simple and quick — the caller's side of the call (the route from the caller's network to the anchor, via the home network) never changes.

  • It's GSM's version of an "anchor" in mobility: the fixed point where the moving part of the path is attached. (The cost is that the path can become longer than necessary.)

How to approach it

Topic: Anchor MSC in GSM

Method / formula: The MSC first visited when a call starts stays on the path during handoffs; only the last leg changes

↑ Assignment 3 Part 1
Q1.2 (5%)

What are the main characteristics of LTE (Long-Term Evolution) radio access networks? How does LTE differ from previous generations of cellular networks?

Unit 7 · Section 7.2
Answer

LTE radio access network (E-UTRAN (Evolved UMTS Terrestrial Radio Access Network)) characteristics:

  • OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access) downlink (SC-FDMA (Single-Carrier Frequency Division Multiple Access) uplink): the channel is divided into many narrow sub-carriers (frequency) and short time slots; the base station (eNodeB) schedules "resource blocks" (frequency × time) to each device every millisecond — a combination of FDM (Frequency Division Multiplexing) and TDM (Time Division Multiplexing).

  • MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output) (multiple antennas) and adaptive modulation/coding → high data rates (tens to hundreds of Mbps; LTE-Advanced > 1 Gbps with carrier aggregation) and low latency (~10 ms).

  • Flat architecture: the eNodeB does its own radio resource management and handover control — there is no separate radio network controller; eNodeBs talk directly to each other (X2 interface) and to the core (MME (Mobility Management Entity), S-GW (Serving Gateway)).

  • All-IP (Internet Protocol), packet-switched: everything, including voice (VoLTE (Voice over Long-Term Evolution)), is IP data.

  • Link layer sublayers PDCP (Packet Data Convergence Protocol), RLC (Radio Link Control), MAC (Medium Access Control); power-saving sleep modes.

Differences from earlier generations:

2G (Second Generation cellular) (GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications)) 3G (Third Generation cellular) (UMTS (Universal Mobile Telecommunications System)) 4G (Fourth Generation cellular) LTE
Radio TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access)/FDMA (Frequency Division Multiple Access) CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access) (WCDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access)) OFDMA (with MIMO)
Voice Circuit-switched Circuit-switched (+ packet data) Packet (VoLTE over IP)
Architecture BTS (Base Transceiver Station) → BSC (Base Station Controller) → MSC (Mobile Switching Center) NodeB → RNC (Radio Network Controller) → MSC/SGSN (Serving GPRS Support Node) eNodeB → EPC (Evolved Packet Core) (MME, S-GW, P-GW (Packet Data Network Gateway)); no controller
Data speed ~10–100 kbps (GPRS (General Packet Radio Service)/EDGE (Enhanced Data rates for GSM Evolution)) ~0.4–40 Mbps (HSPA (High Speed Packet Access)+) ~10–300+ Mbps
Latency high ~100 ms ~10–20 ms
How to approach it

Topic: LTE radio access network

Method / formula: OFDM (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing), scheduled time/frequency slots, all-IP, compared with circuit-switched 2G and 3G

↑ Assignment 3 Part 1
Q1.3 (5%)

What does CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) stand for? How does it work? Explain why RTT (Round-Trip Time) on an Ethernet LAN (Local Area Network) is an important parameter for CSMA/CD to work properly.

Unit 6 · Section 6.3
Answer

CSMA/CD = Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection — the access rule of classic shared Ethernet ("listen before you talk, and stop if you hear someone else").

1. Carrier sense: listen; if the cable is idle, start sending; if busy, wait until idle.

2. Collision detection: keep listening while sending. If another signal is detected, a collision has happened.

3. Abort and jam: stop sending the frame and send a 48-bit jam signal so everyone notices.

4. Binary exponential backoff: after the m-th collision, pick K at random from {0, …, 2^m − 1} and wait K × 512 bit times, then try again. More collisions → wider range → less chance of colliding again.

5. If the whole frame goes out with no collision, it's done (no ACK (Acknowledgement)).

Why RTT matters: a sender can only detect a collision while it is still transmitting. In the worst case, A starts sending, and just before A's signal reaches the far end, B starts too. The collision's signal must travel all the way back to A — taking one full round trip (2 × propagation delay) from when A started. If A's frame is shorter than that, A finishes and walks away thinking it succeeded, while its frame was destroyed. So Ethernet requires:

frame transmission time ≥ RTT (2 × d_prop)     i.e.   minimum frame size ≥ 2 × d_prop × R

This rule sets Ethernet's minimum frame size (64 bytes = 512 bits), the backoff slot (512 bit times), and the maximum cable length. At higher speeds, frames get shorter in time, so the network must be shorter or the minimum frame larger (Gigabit Ethernet's 512-byte slot with carrier extension).

How to approach it

Topic: CSMA/CD and RTT

Method / formula: Sense, transmit, detect, jam, binary backoff; frame must last one RTT so the sender is still transmitting when a collision echo returns

Practice: Genre 17

↑ Assignment 3 Part 1
Q1.4 (5%)

What does CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance) stand for? How does the protocol work? How can collisions be avoided?

Unit 7 · Section 7.1
Answer

CSMA/CA = Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance — the access rule of Wi-Fi (802.11). Wireless stations can't detect collisions while sending (their own signal drowns out others, and hidden stations can't hear each other), so the aim is to avoid them and use ACKs (Acknowledgement).

1. If the channel is sensed idle for DIFS (Distributed Inter-Frame Space) (a fixed short wait), the station may begin.

2. Otherwise it picks a random backoff and counts down only while the channel is idle (freezing while busy).

3. When the counter reaches 0 it sends the whole frame.

4. The receiver checks the CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check), waits SIFS (Short Inter-Frame Space) (shorter than DIFS) and sends an ACK.

5. No ACK → assume a collision/error → choose a backoff from a larger range and retry.

How collisions are avoided:

  • Random backoff before sending (even after the channel frees up), so stations waiting for the same idle moment are unlikely to pick the same instant.

  • Freezing the countdown while others transmit, so stations don't jump in mid-frame.

  • SIFS < DIFS priority, so ACKs and replies always get the channel first.

  • RTS (Request to Send)/CTS (Clear to Send) reservation (optional): the sender sends a short RTS; the AP (Access Point) answers with CTS, heard by all stations (including hidden ones), which then stay quiet for the stated duration (NAV (Network Allocation Vector)). Only the short RTS frames can collide, not the long data frames.

How to approach it

Topic: CSMA/CA

Method / formula: DIFS, backoff counting only while idle, SIFS, ACK, RTS/CTS reservation

Practice: Genre 18

↑ Assignment 3 Part 1
Q1.5 (5%)

What techniques can be used for error detection and error correction, respectively, at the data link layer?

Unit 6 · Section 6.2
Answer

Error detection (find out that something is wrong):

  • Single parity bit — one extra bit so the count of 1s is even (or odd); catches any odd number of flipped bits.

  • Checksums — add up the data in words (weak; mostly used at transport layer).

  • CRC (cyclic redundancy check) — divide the data by an agreed generator using XOR (Exclusive OR) arithmetic and send the remainder; catches all bursts up to r bits long and most others. Used by Ethernet and Wi-Fi (CRC-32), in hardware.

Error correction (find where it's wrong and fix it):

  • Two-dimensional parity — row and column parity bits; one bad row + one bad column pinpoint a single flipped bit to fix.

  • Forward error correction (FEC) codes — Hamming codes, Reed-Solomon, convolutional codes, turbo and LDPC (Low-Density Parity-Check code) codes (Wi-Fi 6, 5G (Fifth Generation cellular)), which let the receiver correct errors without a resend.

  • Retransmission (ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest)) — detect, discard and have the sender resend (802.11 ACKs (Acknowledgement)), or hybrid ARQ (FEC + retransmission, LTE (Long-Term Evolution)/5G).

How to approach it

Topic: Error detection and correction

Method / formula: Parity, 2-D parity, checksum, CRC (detection); 2-D parity and FEC (correction)

Part 2: Long Answer Questions (70%)

Q2.1Q2.2Q2.3Q2.4Q2.5
Q2.1 (15%)

Start with the simple CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access) protocol in the textbook, study more advanced CDMA schemes, choose one and explain in your own words how it works. Describe CDMA's advantages over TDM (Time Division Multiplexing) and FDM (Frequency Division Multiplexing). Include the titles and sources consulted.

Unit 7 · Section 7.1
Answer

1. The textbook's simple CDMA. Everyone transmits at the same time on the same frequencies; each sender gets a unique code of M "chips" (+1/−1). To send a bit d (+1 or −1), send d × code (M chips). The channel adds all senders' chips together. The receiver multiplies what it gets by the wanted sender's code, adds up and divides by M. Because codes are orthogonal (other senders' codes multiplied by yours sum to zero), everyone else cancels out and the wanted bit remains. (See the worked example in Section 7.1's formulas.)

2. A real scheme — Direct-Sequence CDMA as used in IS-95 (Interim Standard 95) / cdma2000:

  • Spreading: voice data at 9.6 kbps is multiplied by a code at 1.2288 Mchips/s (128 chips per bit — the "processing gain"). The signal spreads across 1.25 MHz and looks like faint background noise to anyone without the code.

  • Two kinds of code: Walsh codes (truly orthogonal; 64 of them) separate the users within one cell on the downlink, where the base station sends to everyone in perfect sync. Long pseudo-random (PN (Pseudo-random Noise)) codes separate different base stations and the users on the uplink, where phones can't be perfectly synchronised — they're only "nearly" orthogonal, so each extra user adds a little interference.

  • Power control: a phone near the tower would drown out a far-away phone (the near-far problem). The base station tells every phone to raise or lower its power 800 times a second, so all arrive at about equal strength. Without this, CDMA doesn't work.

  • RAKE receiver: reflected copies of the signal (multipath) arrive at slightly different times; the receiver's "fingers" lock onto several copies and combine them — turning a problem into extra signal.

  • Soft handoff: all cells use the same frequency, so a phone can talk to two or three base stations at once while moving and drop the old one only when the new one is solid ("make before break").

3. Advantages over TDM and FDM:

FDM TDM CDMA
How users are separated Frequency bands Time slots Codes — everyone uses all frequencies all the time
Guard bands/times Needed Needed Not needed
Capacity limit Hard (N bands = N users) Hard (N slots) Soft — more users just raise the noise slightly
Idle users Band wasted Slot wasted Silent users add no interference → more room for others
Frequency reuse Neighbouring cells need different frequencies (~1/7 each) Same Every cell uses the whole band (reuse of 1)

Also: resistance to narrowband interference and eavesdropping (looks like noise), multipath benefit via RAKE, soft handoff (fewer dropped calls), no strict slot synchronisation between users. Downsides: needs very precise power control, complex receivers, and capacity limited by self-interference — one reason 4G (Fourth Generation cellular)/5G (Fifth Generation cellular) moved to OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access).

4. Sources consulted (from your submission's reference list):

  • Kurose, J. F., & Ross, K. W. (2021). Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th ed.). Pearson — Sections 6.3.1 and 7.2.1.

  • Gilhousen, K. S., et al. (1991). On the capacity of a cellular CDMA system. IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) Transactions on Vehicular Technology, 40(2), 303–312. https://doi.org/10.1109/25.289411

  • 3GPP2 (3rd Generation Partnership Project 2). (2009). Physical layer standard for cdma2000 spread spectrum systems (C.S0002-E v1.0).

  • TIA (Telecommunications Industry Association)/EIA (Electronic Industries Alliance). (1993). IS-95 Mobile Station–Base Station Compatibility Standard; Viterbi, A. J. (1995). CDMA: Principles of Spread Spectrum Communication. Addison-Wesley.

How to approach it

Topic: CDMA scheme

Method / formula: Explain encoding/decoding and orthogonal codes; compare with TDM/FDM; cite sources

Q2.2 (15%)

Host A sends payload 1011 0110 1010 1011 to B using a two-dimensional checksum so B can detect and correct any 1-bit error, while keeping the checksum as short as possible. With even parity, what is the checksum? Show your work, prove it's the shortest, and prove any 1-bit error can be detected and corrected.

Unit 6 · Section 6.2
Answer

Step 1 — choose the grid (shortest checksum). 16 data bits in r rows × c columns (r × c = 16). The checksum has one bit per row and per column: length = r + c.

Grid Checksum length Corrects 1-bit errors?
1 × 16 17 No (just one row = ordinary parity)
2 × 8 10 Yes
4 × 4 8 Yes — shortest
8 × 2 10 Yes
16 × 1 17 No

Proof it's the minimum: for a fixed product, the sum is smallest when the two numbers are equal (the arithmetic–geometric mean rule): r + c ≥ 2√(r × c) = 2√16 = 8, with equality only when r = c = 4. The table checks every possible grid.

Step 2 — compute even parity (parity bit = 1 if the row/column has an odd number of 1s):

c0 c1 c2 c3 Row parity
r0 1 0 1 1 1 (three 1s)
r1 0 1 1 0 0 (two 1s)
r2 1 0 1 0 0 (two 1s)
r3 1 0 1 1 1 (three 1s)
Column parity 1 (three 1s) 1 (one 1) 0 (four 1s) 0 (two 1s)

Checksum = row parities 1001 + column parities 1100 = 1001 1100 (8 bits). A sends 24 bits: 1011 0110 1010 1011 | 1001 1100. (Overhead 50% — the price of correcting rather than just detecting.)

Step 3 — proof that any 1-bit error is detected and corrected. Every data bit belongs to exactly one row and one column.

  • Error in a data bit (row i, column j): exactly one row parity (i) and one column parity (j) fail. Their crossing identifies the bit → flip it back.

  • Error in a row-parity bit: that one row fails, no column fails → the parity bit itself is wrong; the data is fine.

  • Error in a column-parity bit: one column fails, no row fails → data is fine.

These cases cover all 24 bits, and each gives a different, recognisable pattern, so every single-bit error is detected and corrected.

Example: bit (row 2, column 1) flips 0 → 1: row 2 becomes 1110 (three 1s → should be parity 1, but received 0 ✗); column 1 becomes 0,1,1,0 (two 1s → should be 0, received 1 ✗). Crossing = (2,1) → flip back.

(Two-bit errors: all are detected — at least two rows or two columns fail — but can't be corrected, because the pattern could come from two different pairs of bits.)

How to approach it

Topic: Minimal 2-D parity

Method / formula: Choose the grid with the smallest row + column count; even parity; prove single-bit correction

Q2.3 (20%)

A 1 Gbps Ethernet has nodes A and B joined by 180 m of cable with three repeaters; each has a 1,024-bit frame to send to the other. Propagation 2×10^8 m/s; backoff in multiples of 512 bits; each repeater adds 20 bit-times. At t = 0 both transmit. After the first collision and a 48-bit jam, A draws K = 0 and B draws K = 1. (a) One-way propagation delay (including repeaters)? When is A's frame completely delivered at B? (b) If only A sends and the repeaters are replaced by switches, each with an 8-bit processing delay plus store-and-forward, when is A's frame delivered?

Unit 6 · Section 6.3
Answer

Useful unit: at 1 Gbps, 1 bit time = 1 ns.

Item Calculation Time
Cable propagation 180 m ÷ 2×10^8 m/s 900 ns
Repeaters 3 × 20 bit times 60 ns
Frame 1,024 bits 1,024 ns
Jam 48 bits 48 ns
Backoff slot 512 bits 512 ns

(a) One-way delay = 900 + 60 = 960 ns = 9.6 × 10^-7 s.

Timeline:

Time (ns) What happens
0 A and B both see an idle cable and start sending.
960 Each one's first bit reaches the other → both detect the collision.
960 → 1,008 Both stop and send the 48-bit jam.
1,008 Jams finished. A's backoff = 0 × 512 = 0; B's = 1 × 512 = 512 ns (ends at 1,520).
1,968 The end of B's jam reaches A (1,008 + 960). The cable is now idle at A; A's backoff is already over, so A starts retransmitting.
1,968 → 2,992 A sends its 1,024-bit frame.
3,952 A's last bit reaches B (2,992 + 960). Delivered.
t = 960 (collision) + 48 (jam) + 960 (wait for B's jam to clear at A) + 1,024 (frame) + 960 (last bit travels)
 = 3,952 ns = 3.952 µs = 3.952 × 10^-6 s

Why B doesn't interfere: B's backoff ends at 1,520 ns, but B senses A's jam still arriving (960–1,968 ns), so it waits; A's new frame reaches B at 1,968 + 960 = 2,928 ns, before B could start. A wins because it drew K = 0.

Worth noting (the point behind Q1.3): CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) needs frame time ≥ round trip = 2 × 960 = 1,920 bit times. A 1,024-bit frame is shorter, so collision detection isn't guaranteed in general — it worked here only because both started at exactly t = 0. That's why Gigabit Ethernet extended the slot to 512 bytes.

(b) Switches, only A sending. No collision, jam or backoff. But a switch is store-and-forward: it must receive the whole frame before sending it on, adding a full frame time (1,024 ns) plus 8 ns processing at each of 3 switches. Repeater delays disappear; cable propagation (900 ns total) remains.

t = 1,024 (A sends) + 3 × (1,024 + 8) (switches) + 900 (cable)
 = 1,024 + 3,096 + 900 = 5,020 ns = 5.02 µs = 5.02 × 10^-6 s

Why slower than (a)? Each store-and-forward switch costs a whole frame time (3 × 1,024 ns), while repeaters cost only 20 bit times each. Switches buy separate collision domains and full-duplex links at the price of latency (cut-through switching would reduce it).

How to approach it

Topic: CSMA/CD timeline with repeaters and switches

Method / formula: Work in bit times; propagation + repeater delays; jam; backoff K x 512; switched case with store-and-forward and processing delays

Q2.4 (10%)

An 802.11 station always reserves the channel with RTS (Request to Send)/CTS (Clear to Send). At t = 0 it wants to send 1,024 bytes of data; all other stations are idle. When is the transmission complete? When is the acknowledgement received?

Unit 7 · Section 7.1
Answer

The question gives no rates or timings, so state assumptions (802.11b values, as the textbook uses): rate 11 Mbps; DIFS (Distributed Inter-Frame Space) = 50 µs, SIFS (Short Inter-Frame Space) = 10 µs; RTS = 20 bytes; CTS = ACK (Acknowledgement) = 14 bytes; propagation ignored (≈0.3 µs); no backoff (channel idle).

Air time of each frame = bits ÷ rate:

Frame Bits Time
RTS 160 160 / 11×10^6 = 14.545 µs
CTS 112 10.182 µs
DATA 8,192 744.727 µs
ACK 112 10.182 µs

Timeline:

Step Event Duration (µs) Time (µs)
1 Wait DIFS 50 50.000
2 Send RTS 14.545 64.545
3 SIFS 10 74.545
4 AP (Access Point) sends CTS (others go quiet) 10.182 84.727
5 SIFS 10 94.727
6 Send DATA 744.727 839.455
7 SIFS 10 849.455
8 AP sends ACK 10.182 859.636
Transfer complete  = DIFS + RTS + SIFS + CTS + SIFS + DATA = 839.455 µs ≈ 0.839 ms
ACK received       = 839.455 + SIFS + ACK = 859.636 µs ≈ 0.860 ms

Plain-English notes: the data itself is 744.7 µs of the 859.6 µs; the RTS/CTS handshake adds about 45 µs — cheap insurance for a long frame, but wasteful for small frames (hence the RTS threshold). Effective throughput ≈ 8,192 bits / 859.6 µs ≈ 9.5 Mbps on an "11 Mbps" link. With other values (e.g., 802.11g: 54 Mbps, SIFS 10 µs, DIFS 28 µs) plug into the same formula.

How to approach it

Topic: 802.11 RTS/CTS timing

Method / formula: DIFS + RTS + SIFS + CTS + SIFS + DATA, then + SIFS + ACK; state the rate and timing values you assume

Q2.5 (10%)

Research Bluetooth and describe and comment on the Bluetooth frame format — its features and limitations. Is there anything in the frame format that inherently limits the number of active nodes to eight? Explain.

Unit 7 · Section 7.1
Answer

Context: Bluetooth (IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.15.1, maintained by the Bluetooth SIG (Special Interest Group)) is short-range wireless in the 2.4 GHz band. A piconet has one controller (master) and some peripherals (slaves). It uses frequency hopping (79 channels of 1 MHz, 1,600 hops/second, 625 µs slots). The controller polls: a peripheral may send only in the slot right after the controller addresses it — no collisions, no contention.

Classic (BR/EDR (Basic Rate / Enhanced Data Rate)) baseband packet format:

Field Size Purpose
Access code 72 bits (68 without trailer) Identifies the piconet (derived from the controller's address); synchronisation and paging
Header 18 bits, sent as 54 bits (each bit repeated 3 times for error correction) Link control (below)
Payload 0–2,745 bits Data, with its own payload header and usually a 16-bit CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check)

Header fields:

Field Bits Purpose
LT_ADDR (active member address) 3 Which peripheral the packet is to/from
TYPE 4 Packet type (single or multi-slot, voice/data, FEC (Forward Error Correction) or not)
FLOW 1 Flow control ("stop, my buffer is full")
ARQN (Automatic Repeat reQuest Number) 1 ACK (Acknowledgement)/NAK (Negative Acknowledgement) of the previous packet
SEQN (Sequence Number) 1 1-bit sequence number (alternating-bit protocol) to spot duplicates
HEC (Header Error Check) 8 Header error check (CRC)

Features: very robust header (tripled + 8-bit CRC — if the header is lost, the whole packet is useless); simple immediate stop-and-wait ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest) with single bits; multi-slot packets (3 or 5 slots) for higher throughput; access code isolates neighbouring piconets; separate handling of voice (reserved slots, no retransmission) and data (retransmitted).

Limitations: large fixed overhead (126 bits before any data — more than the payload for small packets); small payloads and low rates (about 1–3 Mbps); all traffic goes through the controller (peripherals can't talk directly); short range (~10 m typical); crowded 2.4 GHz band.

The 8-node limit — yes, it comes from the frame format: the LT_ADDR field is only 3 bits, so it can express 2^3 = 8 values (0–7). Address 0 is reserved for broadcast from the controller, leaving 1–7 for peripherals. The controller itself needs no address (every packet is to or from it). So a piconet can have at most 7 active peripherals + 1 controller = 8 active nodes. More devices can be parked (inactive, up to 255 with a separate 8-bit parked address) and swapped in, or piconets can be linked into a scatternet. (Bluetooth Low Energy uses a different design without this 3-bit field.)

How to approach it

Topic: Bluetooth frame format

Method / formula: Research the frame; note the 3-bit active-member address, which allows only 7 active slaves plus the master = 8 active nodes
